what_happened: To let Rust services reach the dashboard, loopback trust was rejected because nginx proxies LAN requests from 127.0.0.1; instead a dedicated 256-bit token file (0600, dir 0700) authorizes exactly two METHOD+path routes with constant-time compare, failing closed, and /system forwards only plain title/message/severity/source.
root_cause: Behind a local reverse proxy, a 127.0.0.1 source address does not identify a local service.
lesson: Internal services must authenticate with a narrowly scoped machine credential (exact routes, constant-time compare, fail closed, read from a file, never in argv) that cannot send actions, links or approval payloads to the owner, and a loopback source address must never be treated as trusted.
tripwire: internalServiceAuth.test.ts (19); live: a valid internal token on /notifications/send still returns 401 (scope holds).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node will also put a proxy in front of its backend.

class: secret in a world-readable systemd unit
what_happened: CONTROL_PLANE_OWNER_TOKEN, which gates approvals, recovery writes, chantools and channel.db restore, was set with Environment= in a root 0644 systemd drop-in readable by any local user through systemctl cat/show.
root_cause: The secret was injected through the unit file instead of an owner-only environment file.
lesson: Secrets must never appear in unit files or argv: services read them from 0600 files, runtime env files are written under umask 077, and rotation is scripted and verified (new value accepted, old rejected).
tripwire: scripts/rotate-owner-token.sh; name-only scan of unit files; live fingerprints; systemctl cat/show checked clean after the owner's sudo step.
applies_to_new_node: yes — systemd on Fedora IoT; podman/quadlet secrets offer the same choice.

class: secret redaction misses a quoting form
what_happened: While auditing unit environments, the AI session printed the owner token's value into its tool output because a redaction regex missed the quoted form, so the token had to be rotated, not just moved.
root_cause: Redaction relied on a pattern that did not cover every quoting form.
lesson: Agents inspecting configuration must use name-only scans and never print values, the redaction layer must be tested against quoted, unquoted and export forms, and any secret exposed to a session must be rotated.
tripwire: Token rotated; name-only scans used. Should exist: a redaction test suite.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant and coding agents must never see secret values.

class: runtime state erased on service restart
what_happened: Control-plane restarts erased /run/rikuri/ai-tier.env and an update-freeze marker, because the unit's RuntimeDirectory was removed on stop.
root_cause: systemd deletes a service's RuntimeDirectory on stop unless RuntimeDirectoryPreserve is set.
lesson: State in /run that other components rely on must survive service restarts (RuntimeDirectoryPreserve=yes) or live in persistent state, and unit drop-ins must be validated with systemd-analyze verify.
tripwire: 40-runtime-dir.conf with RuntimeDirectoryPreserve=yes; a marker file in /run/rikuri survived a restart.
applies_to_new_node: yes — systemd services on both nodes.

class: repair without preserving the broken artifact
what_happened: Before building self-heal, three live breakages were repaired by hand: backup-config.json corrupt since 2026-08-10 (drives had received nothing since, while daily reports said 'blockchain: Failed: Could not read backup-config.json'), a truncated embedding model, and a stopped testnet pair; each broken artifact was kept and each repair applied atomically.
root_cause: I1 racing non-atomic writers, I2 a download interrupted by a stop with no checksum, I3 an upgrade runner that restores only the mainnet stack — none of which alerted.
lesson: Live repairs must preserve the broken artifact for forensics, apply changes atomically, verify in a fresh process, and be followed by a class fix and a tripwire; a failure line in a daily report is not an alert.
tripwire: Class fixes in 2026-09-16-backup-device-config-store.md and 2026-09-16-backup-truth-and-alerts.md; smoke gate for the testnet pair.
owner_decision: Decision Q0 = "repair all three by hand first".
applies_to_new_node: yes — incident handling on both nodes.

class: downloaded artifact used without checksum verification
what_happened: The embedding model was truncated (15,013,666 vs 22,972,370 bytes) after a download was interrupted by a stop; the RAG canary failed with 'Protobuf parsing failed', the doc-watcher logged 476 'Failed to index', and running processes kept the bad bytes in memory until restarted.
root_cause: The model cache lived inside node_modules and was never verified against a checksum.
lesson: Every downloaded model or binary must be fetched to a temporary name, verified against a pinned checksum, atomically moved into a cache outside dependency folders, verified on load, and a failed load must alert.
tripwire: Hand repair with sha256sum -c against the LFS oid; checksum-on-load was a planned P4 guard, not built in this record.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant on both nodes will load local models.

class: upgrade restores only part of what it stopped
what_happened: The 2026-09-15 OS-upgrade runner's docker stop fallback stopped lnd-testnet and bitcoin-testnet and restored only the mainnet stack, so tapd was down 39 hours while smoke reported PASS ('off is a valid state').
root_cause: The runner did not record and restore everything it stopped, and smoke did not compare running state with enabled state.
lesson: An upgrade must record every service it stops and restore exactly that set, and health checks must FAIL when an enabled service is not running.
tripwire: scripts/smoke.sh now FAILs a stopped testnet pair while rikuri-testnet-stack is enabled and an enabled-but-inactive rikuri-tapd (proven with a docker shim giving RED).
applies_to_new_node: yes — OS image updates with automatic rollback still need the service set restored and checked (greenboot-style health checks).

class: declarative config uses vocabulary the engine silently ignores
what_happened: A survey of 22 DRBs found approval tier T0 used 6 times but absent from the engine's union (blocked only by fallthrough) and 10 signal problems across 4 DRBs; DRB-NETWORK-OFFLINE-01 gated on three signals nobody implemented, so it fired vacuously before the 09-16 fix and could never fire after.
root_cause: Nothing validated DRB JSON against the fields, tiers, operators, signals and runbooks the engine actually understands.
lesson: Every declarative self-heal definition must be validated in CI against the engine's real vocabulary — fields, approval tiers, operators, signal names parsed from the collector source (not a hand-copied list, with a plausibility count) and existing remediation runbooks — with gaps in gating groups reported as more severe than discriminator gaps and a debt baseline that only shrinks.
tripwire: drbSchemaGate.test.ts (16; proven by reintroducing 'required_anyy' and an invented gating signal into a real DRB) + ragdocs/drb-schema-baseline.json, landed empty.
owner_decision: The owner chose to fix the violations rather than baseline them; deleting DRB-NETWORK-OFFLINE-01 was owner-approved.
applies_to_new_node: yes — any declarative self-heal catalog on the new node.

class: broad staging over a shared working tree sweeps other sessions' changes
what_happened: Two other commits each swept in part of this work via broad staging (the DRB file deletion without its routing row; a concept-card fix), so committed drbRouting.ts routed to a nonexistent DRB for 11 days; this record's change landed 11 days late in three pieces.
root_cause: Sessions committed with git add -A / -u over a tree shared with other sessions, and a deletion shows as ' D', which a broad add picks up unnoticed.
lesson: Commits must stage by explicit path and be reviewed for deletions, one coherent change must land with its record in one commit, and a fresh build from HEAD must be verified rather than only the working-tree build running on the node.
tripwire: Procedure lesson; re-verified against HEAD before committing. Should exist: a pre-commit check that flags staged deletions and files outside the change's declared scope.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new repo is worked on by concurrent sessions.

class: disproportionate self-remediation and silent-then-sudden pages
what_happened: Three DRBs remediate by restarting the whole dashboard (for backup-stale this is disproportionate and was part of the original incident), and DRB-HOST-CLOCK-DRIFT-01 — 332 attempts, zero successes, page_on_total_failure true — will now page at P0 about a condition that had failed silently for months.
root_cause: Remediations were chosen without proportionality review and escalation had never been wired, so long-running failures were invisible.
lesson: Self-remediation must be proportionate to the suspected fault (never restart the management plane because one scheduler might be down), and when a new escalation is enabled the owner must be told in advance which long-failing conditions will start paging.
tripwire: Attempt budget now caps the dashboard restart at 3/day and escalates; the remediation choice itself was not revisited (open item).
applies_to_new_node: yes — self-heal design on the new node.

class: health signal measures a hard-coded path that does not exist
what_happened: The backup 'mounted' signal ran `mountpoint -q /mnt/backup`, which was always false because the node's real drives were /mnt/storage (fstab NVMe) and /media/junc/BACKUP1 (udisks USB); disk_percent always threw, readonly/free_pct were unimplemented, /api/backup/status never returned backup_disk_mounted (so the Guardian's 'Backup disk is not mounted' issue could never fire), and staleness used the newest copy anywhere, local copies included (incident I1 blind spot). StorageDetection also never refreshed a known device, so a drive turning read-only kept its first reading.
root_cause: Signals were written against an assumed mount path instead of the destinations the owner actually selected, and nothing checked that the signal could ever change value.
lesson: The node must derive backup health from the owner-selected destinations identified by filesystem UUID (attached vs mounted vs unplugged, writable, free space, last successful backup per drive, re-read on every check), must never count a local copy as a backup, and with no drive selected every backup signal must report 'unknown' rather than healthy.
tripwire: backupDriveSignals.test.ts (10: signals on injected drive lists + issue-to-DRB routing); live /api/backup/status showing backup_disk_mounted, drives_stale_hours and drives_not_writable for the real drives.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node also writes backups to external/USB drives; a backup monitor that can never fire is the I1 failure.

class: staleness inferred from an event-driven source file's mtime
what_happened: DRB-BACKUP-STALE-01 fired on the age of LND's channel.backup (which LND rewrites only when channels change) or on the local config artifact, and its remount hypothesis was tier T0 (blocked).
root_cause: The age of a file that only changes on events was used as a proxy for 'the backup job ran'.
lesson: The node must measure backup staleness from the backup job's own last successful write to each mounted, writable destination (and separately alarm when the scheduler itself has been silent), never from the mtime of a source file such as the SCB.
tripwire: DRB-BACKUP-STALE-01 v2 symptom = drives stale >= 26 h OR scheduler silent >= 6 h; diagnosisEngine.test.ts backup scenarios (4 red on the old DRB file, incl. the stale guard).
applies_to_new_node: yes - the SCB-only-changes-on-channel-events property is LND's, not the old node's.

class: one generic remedy (restart/delete) applied to causes it cannot fix
what_happened: The backup DRB proposed restarts for a stale or full drive, and RB-BACKUP-DEST-CLEANUP-01 deleted `rikuri-backup-*` directories that did not exist while measuring `df /` (wrong disk); its issue type BACKUP_DEST_DISK_FULL was raised by nothing.
root_cause: Remediations were attached to the symptom rather than to a diagnosed cause, and no test checked that a remedy could change the measured condition.
lesson: Each backup failure cause must map to its own remedy: scheduler stopped -> restart the scheduler; drive attached but unmounted -> remount; drive read-only or full -> tell the owner (no automatic delete, no restart). Retention already prunes old copies, so automatic cleanup of a backup drive must not exist.
tripwire: diagnosisEngine.test.ts backup scenarios 'remount first' and 'a full drive is not fixed by a restart' (red on the old DRB); the cleanup runbook was deleted after proving only the two DRBs referenced it.
applies_to_new_node: yes - applies to any self-healing over backup destinations.

class: service lacks the privilege its remedy needs; remedy guesses devices
what_happened: `udisksctl mount` from the control-plane service was refused by polkit (auth_admin, checked with pkcheck against the service PID), so a service could not remount a USB backup drive; the old remount runbook only echoed /mnt/backup advice.
root_cause: The remedy was designed without checking the authorization model of the process that would run it.
lesson: An automatic remount must act only on selected drives by UUID (validated before building paths), never guess a device and never run `mount -a`, use udisks for removable drives, and run under an explicit, opt-in, minimal grant (polkit filesystem-mount only, for the node user) whose effect is verified with pkcheck against the actual service process; fstab drives are left to the owner.
tripwire: backupRemountScript.test.ts (6, read-only paths; exit 0 / 1 failed-or-not-writable / 3 not attached); `rikuri-backup-remount.sh --check`; pkcheck before/after the owner installed the rule. Unmount/remount was NOT exercised live.
applies_to_new_node: yes - Fedora IoT uses udisks2 + polkit as well; a minimal polkit rule is the right grant shape on an immutable host.

class: ran reported as fixed (action failure ignored)
what_happened: The Rust runbook executor ignored non-zero action exits, treated failed validation as informational, never stopped on a non-matching pre-check, left timed-out children running and always set ExecutionResult.error to None: RB-DNS-SEED-INJECT-01 logged 'completed' 4x while every command failed, RB-MEMORY-GRACEFUL-RESTART-01 'completed' 71x with a validation that could never pass, and RB-CONTAINER-RESTART-01 timed out 89x at 60 s (LND stops in up to 90 s).
root_cause: The executor had no failure semantics: 'the steps were attempted' was recorded as success.
lesson: The node's remediation executor must fail a runbook when a pre-check does not match, an action exits non-zero or times out, or the post-check never passes; it must run undo on failure, kill the whole process group on timeout, and record the failed step and reason as the outcome.
tripwire: Rust runbook module tests (35) with 9 mutations back to the old behaviour each red; runbookExecution.test.ts (5 red on the old TS engine); live: a proposal whose pre-check did not match was recorded failed with its reason and the service untouched.
applies_to_new_node: yes - any self-healing on the new node needs honest step semantics.

class: fix counted without re-detection
what_happened: MonitoringLoop counted every fire as an 'automated attempt' (no runbook, waiting for approval, refused) and never checked whether a fix worked; its per-runbook cooldown also blocked the same runbook for other services.
root_cause: 'Fired' and 'fixed' were the same counter and no detector was asked again.
lesson: A fix must count only when the detector that raised the problem no longer sees it (verify-by-redetect over consecutive ticks); 'fires' and 'attempts' (a runbook actually ran) must be separate; the outcome must be written back to the decision; cooldowns must be keyed by runbook plus its target parameters.
tripwire: monitoringVerify.test.ts (9, 8 red on the old loop); live PUT /v1/decisions/:id/outcome stored.
applies_to_new_node: yes - core self-healing invariant.

class: shell injection through template parameter substitution
what_happened: A user value placed inside a runbook's own single quotes was quoted again and ended up unquoted in the shell; repo_root was a caller-overridable parameter; undeclared parameters overrode system values; POST /v1/runbook/execute ran any runbook with any values and no tier check (and had no caller). The TS engine escaped nothing.
root_cause: String templating into shell commands without quote-context awareness, type checks or a declared parameter schema.
lesson: Runbook parameters must never become shell code: one-pass quote-context-aware substitution, undeclared parameters dropped, system values never overridable, string values restricted to one plain word ([A-Za-z0-9._:@+-], no leading '-', <= 128 chars) because escaping cannot protect a value handed to a nested `sh -c`; runbooks run only through tiered proposals, never through a raw execute route.
tripwire: Shared fixture control-plane/tests/fixtures/runbook-template-cases.json used by both engines; a real-shell test proving a value stays literal in 5 quoting contexts; live POST /v1/runbook/execute -> 405.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the rebuilt backend must not reintroduce templated shell; better still, use argv arrays.

class: declarative remediation catalogue drifts from the host
what_happened: An audit of all 65 RB-*.json found runbooks referencing paths that do not exist (stop bitcoind, then `mv data/bitcoin` -> abort -> bitcoind left stopped), RB-LND-WT-CLIENT-TUNE-01 writing a bare `sweep-fee-rate=` key (LND expects wtclient.sweep-fee-rate) then restarting LND, `expect` split on every `|`, `sleep 60` validations that always timed out, and stop timeouts shorter than the service's grace period.
root_cause: Runbook JSON was never validated against the real files, the host layout or the daemons' option names.
lesson: Every declarative runbook must pass a catalogue test over the real files (expects compile, no long sleeps in checks, every placeholder declared or system, no parameter shadows a system value, stop/restart timeouts >= the service's stop grace), and any runbook that stops a funds or chain daemon must have an undo that restarts it; config-writing runbooks must be tiered for owner approval.
tripwire: Rust catalogue test over the real RB-*.json (21 violations before the JSON fixes, 0 after); TS command audit.
applies_to_new_node: yes - applies to whatever remediation catalogue the new node ships.

class: probe relies on a tool absent from the image, so it always reports failure
what_happened: The Tor cascade check ran `nc -zw2 tor 9050` inside the bitcoin container, but the Bitcoin Core 31.1 image has no `nc`, so Tor was always 'unreachable' and bitcoind was restarted after every Tor restart (and through the cookie cascade electrs, LND and mempool too): 36 cascades since 2026-08-10. bitcoind resolves its Tor proxy address once at start and the tor container had no static IP.
root_cause: A liveness probe was written without verifying the probe tool exists in the target image, and a failing probe was treated as evidence of a fault.
lesson: After a Tor restart the node must restart bitcoind only when bitcoind's startup-resolved proxy IP (from getnetworkinfo) is no longer one of Tor's current IPs; unknown proxy, unknown Tor address or RPC failure -> skip and log 'not restarting blind'; a probe must never depend on a binary that is not in the image.
tripwire: Pure tor_cascade::decide with 4 Rust tests (incl. the 2026-09-16 same-address case); live Tor restart left bitcoin/electrs/lnd/mempool StartedAt unchanged with a logged 'bitcoind left alone' decision.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node runs bitcoind behind Tor; restart cascades must be evidence-based (and a stable Tor address avoids the stale-proxy case).

class: remedy selected by directory order
what_happened: For TOR_HIDDEN_SVC_FAIL the Rust /match endpoint returned the first runbook file in read_dir order (RB-TOR-RESTART-01) instead of the curated RB-TOR-ONION-RECOVER-01; DiagnosisTrigger's RAG branch was dead code.
root_cause: Selection relied on filesystem enumeration order instead of an explicit, ordered choice.
lesson: Remedy choice must come from a curated, ordered per-issue list, each entry confirmed loadable before use; a generic match is only a fallback, sorted deterministically, never filesystem order.
tripwire: runbookSelection.test.ts (2 fail on the old DiagnosisTrigger); a gate that every curated runbook is loadable (it caught a misnamed crash-loop runbook).
applies_to_new_node: yes - any rule-to-remedy mapping in the rebuilt backend.

class: classifier lets a service name outvote the symptom
what_happened: A +3 score for the service name alone let 'electrs stopped' classify as an index problem, which produced a destructive-reindex approval request (incident I6).
root_cause: Keyword scoring gave service-name matches weight regardless of whether the symptom matched.
lesson: Issue classification must go exact type -> `<service>_down` mapping -> symptom scoring, where a service-name bonus applies only to types with a real symptom score; a service name alone must never select a destructive remedy.
tripwire: issueClassification.test.ts (26-row table + 2 guards; 10 fail on the old classifier).
applies_to_new_node: yes - any alert classifier feeding remediations.

class: hard-coded daemon container name wrong under an alternate engine; no-op reported as success
what_happened: The proposal engine mapped `bitcoin` to the container `bitcoin`, which is wrong when the node runs Knots (bitcoin-knots); `add_peers` returned success without doing anything.
root_cause: Container identity was duplicated per caller instead of resolved by one engine-aware lookup, and an unimplemented action returned success.
lesson: The node must resolve the bitcoind container through one engine-aware lookup shared by every caller, the container map must refuse unknown names, and an unimplemented action must fail rather than report success.
tripwire: containers::{running_bitcoin_container, bitcoin_container} shared by cascade and proposal engine; proposal tests 6/6.
applies_to_new_node: maybe - matters if the new node offers more than one bitcoind engine or network; the no-op-is-not-success rule applies everywhere.

class: approval path never round-trips (missing auth header, silent 403)
what_happened: Every approval answered 403 since about 2026-07: the control plane required X-Owner-Token on approve/deny but the dashboard sent only its Bearer token and Telegram sent no headers at all. 730 of 741 queued decisions were never resolved (oldest 2026-03-23); the last successful approval anywhere was 2026-04-30.
root_cause: The approval chain was never tested end-to-end against the real authorization requirement, and nothing alarmed when approvals stopped succeeding.
lesson: Every owner approval path (dashboard, phone/Telegram) must be tested end-to-end against the server's real authorization requirement, and the node must surface approval requests that fail or go unanswered instead of letting them pile up.
tripwire: approvalRoundTrip.test.ts (6, all red on the old code); live approve without the owner token -> 403, with it -> executed; startup sweep closed the 730 orphans.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node will have held actions that need owner approval.

class: pending approvals held only in memory; expiry not enforced
what_happened: Pending proposals lived only in memory, so a control-plane restart dropped them and the button then said 'not found'; expiry was filtered on read but not enforced on approve, so an expired proposal was still executable; the history record dropped the `approval` field so buttons vanished on reload.
root_cause: Durable state needed for a privileged action was kept in process memory, and the deadline was checked at the wrong point.
lesson: Held proposals must be persisted with their deadline, restored at startup and closed by a periodic sweep; approve must refuse an expired proposal and record why, and an unparseable deadline counts as expired (never run on a date that cannot be read).
tripwire: Rust tests pending_approvals_survive_and_close_out, undecided_requests_are_closed_out, expiry_is_decided_safely; live: a held T2 proposal survived a control-plane restart ('restored 1 pending approval').
applies_to_new_node: yes - any approval queue on the new node.

class: remote action buttons without sender authorization
what_happened: Telegram callback buttons had no sender check: any member of a chat the bot was in could approve a held action or press an `upgrade:` button that starts a host service upgrade.
root_cause: The callback handler trusted the button press itself as authorization.
lesson: Every remote action (approve, deny, upgrade) arriving through a chat or notification channel must verify it comes from the owner's configured chat/identity before doing anything.
tripwire: approvalRoundTrip.test.ts cases 'a press from another chat refused' and 'an upgrade button from another chat refused'.
applies_to_new_node: yes - if the new node keeps phone/Telegram actions.

class: tests mutate process-wide environment concurrently and reach a live service
what_happened: The Rust workspace suite failed about one run in three: several tests set process-wide env vars, a concurrent read came back empty, and an internal notification escaped to the live dashboard on :5000 (answered 401).
root_cause: Tests shared mutable global environment across threads and the default endpoints pointed at the live node.
lesson: Tests must never mutate process-wide environment while other tests run, and a test must never be able to reach a live node service: inject configuration, or serialize env-dependent tests and default endpoints to non-live values.
tripwire: `cargo test --workspace -- --test-threads=1`; env-dependent dashboard_internal tests merged into one; 2/2 serial runs green (was 1-in-3 flaky).
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node's test suite will also run on or near the live machine.

class: parallel approval stores with divergent guarantees
what_happened: The audit found seven other approval stores: in-memory approvalManager, an unreachable autonomy approvalService (GET-vs-POST mismatch, shipped default token secret), an approval-mode store that could not be filled, an aiAgent store with no caller, watchdog fleet approvals that 401, plus marketplace and agent-wallet stores that already used SQLite + step-up + HMAC.
root_cause: Each feature grew its own approval mechanism instead of using one.
lesson: The node must have exactly one approval store with one shape: durable, step-up-authenticated, signed, with expiry; features submit to it rather than inventing their own.
tripwire: None added in this record (consolidation deferred to the next P3 increment); a check that only one approval route/store exists should exist.
applies_to_new_node: yes - a clean rebuild is the moment to have a single approval path.

class: duplicate uncoordinated monitors and remediators
what_happened: run_service_monitor was spawned both in the control plane and in the root-owned node-watchdog: six monitors ran twice with independent cooldowns writing two decision databases (29k and 20.7k rows); CascadeManager and CookieWatcher were duplicated so one cookie change restarted electrs -> lnd -> mempool twice; the agent's own dashboard probe loop was a third restarter on top of systemd WatchdogSec. The watchdog's copy was also misconfigured (wrong RPC URL and cookie path) and silently blind.
root_cause: Monitoring code was linked into two binaries with no single owner for each check and repair.
lesson: Each check and each repair must run exactly once, in one owning process; the node must document 'who watches what' (systemd, control plane, agent) and a second process must not restart the same service.
tripwire: Live: exactly one 'Service monitor started' line; test the_agent_still_serves_health_and_the_fleet_registry plus the route-surface test below.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node will also have systemd plus an app-level monitor; ownership must be explicit.

class: unauthenticated root command-execution endpoint with no caller
what_happened: The node-agent's POST /fix ran `sh -c <command>` as root, skipped the auto_execute gate its sibling enforced, and its auth middleware was a no-op because no RIKURI_AGENT_API_TOKEN was configured; /auto-fix, /diagnose (LLM) and /restart/all (`docker compose down && up -d`) sat beside it. No caller existed anywhere; its fix catalogue was stale (e.g. `fix_cookie` = `rm -f ~/.bitcoin/.cookie`).
root_cause: Privileged surfaces were left deployed after their callers disappeared, and auth failed open when unconfigured.
lesson: The node must expose no endpoint that runs repair commands as root; unused privileged routes are deleted, not disabled; authentication must fail closed when its secret is not configured; a test asserts the exact route surface of every privileged process.
tripwire: the_agent_exposes_no_remediation_endpoints (proven red by re-adding /fix); live POST :5100/fix, /auto-fix, /diagnose, /restart/all -> 404.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the rebuilt backend and any root helper must have a pinned, tested route surface.

class: disable flag read by a different binary (flag says off, loop runs)
what_happened: The operator disabled the dashboard probe loop with a systemd drop-in RIKURI_DISABLE_WATCHDOG=1, but only the other crate (node-agent) read that flag, so this binary kept probing and restarting.
root_cause: The flag's reader and the process it claimed to configure diverged and nothing logged the flag's effect.
lesson: Every enable/disable flag must be read by the process it configures and its effect must be logged at startup, so a dead flag is visible.
tripwire: Live startup log 'Dashboard watchdog disabled via RIKURI_DISABLE_WATCHDOG=1'.
applies_to_new_node: yes - systemd drop-ins will configure the new node's services too.

class: detector findings never reach the incident record (split record)
what_happened: The control plane's service monitor, the detector that watches Docker events, disk, peers, the dashboard and backups, wrote findings only to its decisions table, so a problem only it saw never became an incident and repairs it ran itself (prune, DNS seeds, dashboard restart) were invisible to the record that judged whether anything had been done.
root_cause: Each language/process kept its own log of findings with no shared vocabulary or write path.
lesson: Every detector in every process must write to one incident record through one narrow, authenticated, field-validated machine route using one shared issue vocabulary; an unknown issue type is a loud 400, a repair the detector ran itself counts as an attempt, and the route can only write the record (never run a fix).
tripwire: incidentReport.test.ts (37, incl. a cross-language gate that reads the Rust issue constants and fails on any unknown here); live: no token -> 401, unknown type -> 400, resolved -> closes.
owner_decision: Ok replace AI Fixes and Rust-side detectors write incidents
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node will have detectors in more than one process.

class: fault report gated on the wrong condition (exit code)
what_happened: The control plane's whole container-down report sat inside `if exit_code != 0`, and `docker stop` exits 0, so the most ordinary way a container goes down produced nothing; it was found by noticing the journal stayed silent.
root_cause: A death was equated with a non-zero exit.
lesson: A container that goes down must be reported regardless of its exit code; the detector must also watch start events so it closes what it opens, and wait a short grace (20 s) before calling a restart-policy blip a problem.
tripwire: Live induced faults: `docker kill` (137) and `docker stop` (0) both opened an incident at +20 s and closed it on the start event.
applies_to_new_node: yes - podman/docker on the new node report stop exit codes the same way.

class: repair outcome accounting is not truthful
what_happened: The Docker prune decision row said 'executed' even when Docker refused and discarded the bytes reclaimed; an attempt counter frozen with the incident state showed '0 fix attempt(s)' beside a visible fix_result row; a successful Rust report logged nothing on either side; an incident id derived from the clock collided when a problem cleared and returned in the same millisecond.
root_cause: Outcome fields were filled optimistically and identity derived from time alone.
lesson: Every repair must record what actually happened (refusal, measured effect such as bytes reclaimed), attempt counts must not be frozen with state, every cross-process report must leave a log line on the side that acted, and record IDs must not be derived from the clock alone.
tripwire: Unit tests for the id collision and attempt counting; live fault 1 exposed the counter bug.
applies_to_new_node: yes - general to the rebuilt backend.

class: owner page shows a feature sandbox instead of the node's real problems
what_happened: The 'AI Fixes' page showed a sandbox for two candidate-fix recipes (its comment claimed nine) and nothing about the problems the node actually had, while the incident record existed and no page rendered it.
root_cause: The UI was built around a feature rather than around the owner's question 'what is wrong and what is being done'.
lesson: The owner-facing incident page must render the incident record in three sections (waiting for you, happening now, recently resolved), show 'all clear' only when nothing is open, run nothing itself, and approve/deny only through the proposal id on the awaiting-approval timeline row.
tripwire: frontend tests/Guardian.test.tsx (8).
owner_decision: Ok replace AI Fixes and Rust-side detectors write incidents
applies_to_new_node: yes - the rebuilt frontend needs an incident view.

class: no incident owner (one row per attempt counted as many incidents)
what_happened: There was no incident record: one tapd-down problem recorded every 30 min appeared as '100 incidents, 99 unresolved' while the node scored 94/100; guardian_past_fixes had 1,281 rows with issue_type empty on 1,278; guardian_logbook had the shape of an incident record but 0 rows ever, yet diagnose.ts answered 'is this recurring?' from it (always 'no'); recovery alerts were dropped.
root_cause: Problems were logged per action and the only opened->verified->resolved model lived in memory.
lesson: Every problem must be one incident with an append-only timeline (opened -> diagnosed -> fix -> verified -> resolved), one open incident per `service:ISSUE_TYPE` signature, repeated sightings only bump a timestamp, a recurrence after resolution is a new incident, recovery alerts close it, and only a detector may close it.
tripwire: incidentStore.test.ts (11), incidentDispatch.test.ts (11), monitoringVerify.test.ts (13); live induced faults ending in one resolved incident.
applies_to_new_node: yes - foundation for any self-healing on the new node.

class: health check repairs directly, bypassing tiers, and on the wrong target
what_happened: A live induced `docker stop mempool-web`: health detected CONTAINER_DOWN:mempool-web, the synthesizer rewrote the target to mempool-api and the runbook restarted that healthy container, while healthService.triggerAIAutoFix restarted the real one directly with no tier check, no runbook and no decision row (enabled at runtime by approvalModeService in full-auto mode).
root_cause: Health both detected and repaired, and its mempool status named whichever container `find` hit first.
lesson: Health must only detect; every repair goes detector -> one dispatcher -> tiered proposal -> executor and is recorded, and the fix must target the exact container that is down.
tripwire: Live: the same induced fault produced ONE incident naming mempool-web and restarted only mempool-web; triggerAIAutoFix and the direct restart loop were deleted.
applies_to_new_node: yes - no side-door repairs in the rebuilt backend.

class: late write reopens a closed record
what_happened: In live run 2 the fix's rows landed 4 s after the recovery alert resolved the incident and flipped it back to 'fixing'; 'fix started' was written at completion, 35 s late.
root_cause: State transitions were not monotonic and events were recorded at completion instead of when they happened.
lesson: A resolved incident's state must be frozen (its timeline stays append-only) and the chosen fix must be recorded when chosen, not when it finishes.
tripwire: incidentStore tests; live run 3 showed the full honest timeline; the inconsistent row was corrected with a note row rather than deleted.
applies_to_new_node: yes - general state-machine rule.

class: external agent tool exposure without scoped, authoritative execution
what_happened: Plan (G0 done, G1-G4 not started) to expose the node's tools to external MCP clients. Characterization showed internalTools.ts (39 tools tagged LOW..CRITICAL, 'MUST NEVER be sent to cloud LLMs') separated from external public-knowledge tools by a privacyRouter, and a 4-tool hand-rolled stdio server that existed but did not run and was not gated.
root_cause: Design decision, not a defect: the risk is an agent tool surface that bypasses the control plane or leaks private node data.
lesson: The AI/agent tool surface must default to read-only with per-token scopes, exposed only on a private network (Tailscale), every mutation executed by the authoritative control plane, 'dangerous' tools never exposed directly but projected onto the owner approval queue, and private node data never sent to cloud LLMs.
tripwire: Planned regression guard (spec section 5 row 3): no exposed tool may be authority 'ts' + permission 'dangerous'; not yet built.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node's AI assistant is sandboxed; the same scoping and approval-queue rule should bound any tool it or an external agent can call.

class: module move breaks string specifiers invisible to typecheck
what_happened: Moving dashboard/backend/src/mcp to nodeTools/knowledge: a mid-way run showed 115 suites/1893 tests vs the 116/2013 baseline because a `jest.mock('../mcp/internalTools')` was missed; `require('../tools')` would have silently loaded a different existing module (src/tools/); a stale tracked compiled dist/mcp could have masked a broken import at runtime.
root_cause: Specifier rewrites covered only import/require/from forms, moved files carried @ts-nocheck, and the build left stale output.
lesson: A behaviour-neutral refactor must be proven by identical test-suite and test counts before/after, runtime-loading of moved modules, driving the real protocol, and a clean build directory; every string module specifier form (require, jest.mock, dynamic import) must be swept.
tripwire: Test-count equivalence (stop the line on any drop); `build:clean`; protocol drive-test (initialize + tools/list).
applies_to_new_node: yes - the clean rebuild should avoid string requires and @ts-nocheck so typecheck can see moves.

class: architecture conclusion drawn from file names without reading the routing layer
what_happened: A competitive brief claimed 'two subsystems named MCP that mean opposite things'; reading the code showed three, and the internal/external split was a deliberate privacy design in privacyRouter.ts that the brief's author never opened. A cleanup runlog that stopped on 2026-07-28 would also have given a wrong (pessimistic) state.
root_cause: Claims were made from headers and stale logs instead of the running system.
lesson: Before acting on any claim about the node's architecture or state, verify it against the running system and the code that actually routes behaviour, not file names or stale logs.
tripwire: Process rule; the record re-checked every other claim in the brief against the live node.
applies_to_new_node: yes - process lesson for the rebuild.

class: same mapping derived independently in two places (decision silently no-ops)
what_happened: The owner's 'stay on Bitcoin' decision was stored keyed by the UI's service name (`bitcoin`) while the check looked it up by engine (`knots`): the POST returned success:true and the consensus card stayed prominent.
root_cause: The service->engine mapping was derived separately in the route and in the check.
lesson: A stored owner decision must be written and read through one shared key-mapping function, and verified by observing its effect rather than the write's success response.
tripwire: upgradeService.engineForService() shared by both; live round trip decline -> acknowledged -> restart -> still acknowledged -> undo.
applies_to_new_node: yes - general rule for persisted owner choices.

class: persisted owner choice silently lost or resurrected
what_happened: There was no mechanism at all to answer the consensus question; the new store was designed to survive restarts and be loud on corruption.
root_cause: Design decision.
lesson: Owner decisions must persist atomically (.tmp + rename), resolve their path per call, be tested by reading the file on disk (a module round-trip would pass with an in-memory cache), and a corrupt store must be a loud error, never treated as 'no decision' (which would resurrect a nag and hide the corruption); an answered prompt collapses with its date and an undo but never vanishes.
tripwire: 6 unit cases incl. atomicity (no .tmp left) and the corrupt-file path; frontend UpgradesConsensus.test.tsx (answered release goes quiet but stays on the page, undo reachable).
applies_to_new_node: yes - any owner-decision store on the new node.

class: auth tier does not match the direction of risk
what_happened: Declining a consensus-changing update was added to the loginless benign-mutation allowlist; gating it behind the fund-movement password would have put a password prompt on saying 'no thanks', the same default-closed trap that once demanded a password to change the colour theme. By contrast, applying a relay posture stays login-required.
root_cause: Design decision.
lesson: Authentication tiers must follow the direction of risk: refusing a change (the safe direction) must not require step-up, while actively changing node behaviour must; benign loginless mutations must be exact METHOD /path allowlist entries, not regexes.
tripwire: The route was collapsed to one static POST so the allowlist entry is exact.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the rebuilt backend's auth policy.

class: upgrades modelled as semver distance only (chain change offered as minor)
what_happened: The Upgrades page offered Knots 29.4.20260508 as upgradeType 'minor', readyToUpgrade true, 'OPTIONAL - New features available' (21-day wait long elapsed); one click would have rewritten the consensus-critical pin in docker-compose.knots.yml and restarted bitcoind onto the BIP-110/RDTS fork.
root_cause: 'Newer' was treated as 'better after a wait'; the model had no concept of a release that changes which network you are on, and the runtime upgrade path was a second, independent route around the CI pin gate.
lesson: The node must classify every bitcoind release for consensus change, fail closed for audited engines (an unreviewed release counts as consensus-changing), never offer a consensus-changing release through the one-click upgrade path, and the CI pin gate and the runtime guard must share one list.
tripwire: consensusBuilds.test.ts (7 cases, incl. fail-closed on a hypothetical unreviewed release; Core/electrs/lnd classify 'none'); knotsConsensusPin.test.ts imports the shared module.
applies_to_new_node: yes - any bitcoind engine can ship a consensus change; the new node's update path needs this classification regardless of engine.

class: client recomputes a server-authoritative safety decision
what_happened: After the API correctly returned upgradeType 'consensus' and readyToUpgrade false, the page still rendered the green Upgrade button and '✓ Ready to upgrade', because Upgrades.tsx computed readiness locally from releaseDate vs the wait period and never consulted the server.
root_cause: The frontend trusted its own countdown over the server's decision.
lesson: The UI must gate every action on the server's authoritative decision (here readyToUpgrade and consensusChange) and never recompute safety locally; a guard must be verified in the running UI, not only at the API.
tripwire: dashboard/frontend/tests/UpgradesConsensus.test.tsx: button absent for a consensus release while the local countdown says ready, badge CHANGES NETWORK not MINOR, and a control case where an ordinary release of the same age still offers the button.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the rebuilt frontend.

class: owner choice explained only in jargon, without downstream effects
what_happened: The relay panel listed three postures with an `available` flag and raw option strings as the only concrete detail, saying nothing about what happens to sending, receiving, Lightning, electrs, mempool or disk.
root_cause: The panel answered 'which setting' but never 'what happens to my node'.
lesson: Every owner-facing choice must be explained in plain language (what is carried, what size, what stays safe, effects on wallet, Lightning, electrs, mempool, disk), with raw options only behind a 'Technical settings' disclosure, and the one genuine danger (here: replay risk on the Knots fork) stated explicitly while the safe option carries no symmetric scare.
tripwire: A test greps every owner-facing string for datacarrier|permitbaremultisig|rejectparasites|bitcoin.conf|=<digit>; tests assert effects.storage /no change/ and effects.lightning /no effect/ for every posture and that the Knots card names replay.
owner_decision: I think we just have 2 different cards, each for each engine. … For a novice, we don't understand the technical things like datacarrier=1…
applies_to_new_node: yes - but the 'relay policy does not change your disk usage' copy was justified for an unpruned node (-prune=0); it must be re-checked for the pruned Pi.

class: page-scoped CSS class used elsewhere (className invisible to every gate)
what_happened: The relay-posture buttons used `className="pill-btn secondary"`, but `.pill-btn` existed only as `.guardian-page .pill-btn`, so the buttons rendered as bare elements, effectively invisible on the dark theme; the owner concluded the choice did not exist although the API returned all three as available.
root_cause: A className string is invisible to typecheck, build and text-asserting tests.
lesson: The frontend must have a gate that every button carries at least one globally-defined styling class (modifier classes exempt).
tripwire: buttonClassesExist.test.ts (v3, per-button rule), proven to fail naming 'pill-btn secondary' and pass with no false positives; scoped to pages/settings only, literal classNames only.
applies_to_new_node: maybe - depends on the new frontend's styling system; the class of defect exists wherever styles are referenced by string.

class: gate passes on the very bug it was written for
what_happened: The first version of the button-class gate asked whether `.foo` appears anywhere in CSS, which `.guardian-page .pill-btn` satisfies, so it passed on the bug; v2 was too strict and flagged legitimate modifiers; v3 moved the rule to per-button.
root_cause: The gate was not run against the defect before being trusted.
lesson: Every new gate or test must be proven red on the exact defect it targets (planted regression) and green on legitimate variants before it counts; a gate that cries wolf will be disabled.
tripwire: Planted-regression proof recorded for each gate (re-introducing the original string fails the suite).
applies_to_new_node: yes - cross-cutting rule for the rebuild's test suite.

class: upstream ships a chain-splitting consensus change in a point release; pin never re-audited
what_happened: The pinned Knots image 29.3.knots20260508 was an RDTS (BIP-110) build: in August 2026 it rejected mainnet block 961,642 and followed the BIP-110 fork to its final block 961,633, although `consensusrules=rdts` was set nowhere. A summary had also wrongly claimed 29.4.knots20260508 was RDTS-free; floating tags latest/29/29.4 all resolved to RDTS builds; four docs named a different pin than the compose file.
root_cause: Pinning was followed, but a pin bump had no consensus-review step and secondary summaries were trusted over primary sources.
lesson: Every bitcoind image pin must be on a default-deny allowlist of reviewed builds, never a floating tag, checked against primary release notes and at binary level (`-help`/`-version` in a throwaway container with no datadir), and every image reference in the repo must agree.
tripwire: knotsConsensusPin.test.ts (allowlist enforcement, mainnet-pin identity, no floating tags, and 'gate still guards something'); proven red on the old pin (2 of 4 failing).
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node also pins daemon images; a consensus review on every bump applies to any engine.

class: scan gate silently shrinks (swallowed read errors, zero matches pass)
what_happened: The first draft of the pin gate walked the filesystem, tripped over unreadable runtime dirs (data/lnd/...), and its natural fix, swallowing EACCES, would let a path drop out of the scan silently.
root_cause: A filesystem walk was used where the set of files under review is defined by version control.
lesson: A repository scan gate must enumerate git-tracked files deterministically, never swallow read errors, and fail if it finds nothing to guard.
tripwire: knotsConsensusPin.test.ts scans git-tracked files only and asserts the scan found at least one pin.
applies_to_new_node: yes - pattern for any repo-scanning gate.

class: shared block store carries another engine's invalid-block verdicts
what_happened: Knots wrote InvalidChainFound marks for majority-chain blocks into the block index shared (bind-mounted) by both engines; after switching back, Core inherited the invalid verdict and refused the majority chain until the owner ran `bitcoin-cli reconsiderblock <hash>`. The record's own plan to discard the dead Knots chainstate was corrected: that forces revalidation from genesis.
root_cause: Two engines with different consensus rules shared one block index.
lesson: Before any engine switch that shares a block store, the node must check getchaintips for invalid entries, back up blocks/index, keep the old chainstate (let it reorg forward), and treat 'block <hash> was previously marked invalid' as the known failure signature whose remedy is reconsiderblock, never a reindex.
tripwire: Product preflight GET /api/bitcoin/engine/switch/preflight; getchaintips check (0 invalid entries found); the switch itself remained owner-gated and unverified.
applies_to_new_node: maybe - only if the new node supports switching engines over a shared block store.

class: stale knowledge base gives dangerous advice
what_happened: The assistant's RAG advised 'prefer upgrading Knots to 29.4', an RDTS build that leaves the Bitcoin chain; the guide was rewritten and the stale advice verified gone from the live vector store, not just the file.
root_cause: Knowledge documents were not re-checked when the facts behind them changed.
lesson: When a safety-relevant fact changes, the assistant's knowledge must be corrected in the live store and verified by querying that the stale advice returns nothing.
tripwire: ChromaDB query get(where_document contains 'prefer upgrading Knots to 29.4') -> 0 chunks; new chunks verified present.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node's sandboxed assistant will also answer from a knowledge store.

class: two orthogonal choices presented as one (engine vs policy conflated)
what_happened: The owner asked: "Is by Standard you mean Bitcoin Core? And Strict is Bitcoin Core: 83? The last Maximum is Knots? I'm a little confused which is which." The panel never named the engine, showed an `available` boolean without saying why or what to do, and never said sending and receiving work identically on all postures.
root_cause: The panel showed availability as a bare flag and did not separate the engine choice from the policy choice.
lesson: Every option must state which software it needs and what to do when unavailable, the panel must lead with the running engine and the 'does not affect your money' statement (one shared string used by UI and assistant docs so they cannot drift), and no option may change the engine on its own.
tripwire: Unit tests: every posture names its engine(s); Standard and Strict both say 'either engine'; Maximum names Knots; the shared no-effect sentence mentions sending, receiving and channels.
applies_to_new_node: maybe - applies if the new node offers relay-policy or engine choices; the shared-string-for-UI-and-docs rule applies generally.

class: preset defined by the absence of settings
what_happened: 'Standard' was defined as `options: {}` (let engine defaults apply), but Core and Knots default differently (datacarriersize 100000 vs 83, permitbaremultisig 1 vs 0, rejectparasites n/a vs 1), so Core+Standard and Knots+Standard were two postures under one name and Knots+Standard was almost Core+Strict. The owner reported: "I'm still not clear if Core's Strict and Knots' Standard are the same, or are they slightly different."
root_cause: A preset's meaning depended on defaults the node does not control.
lesson: Every policy preset must be defined by explicit values per engine/version, and a test must assert that a preset available on more than one engine resolves to the same effective option set (engine-only options explicitly neutralised).
tripwire: Cross-engine equivalence test for every shared posture; 'Standard is not the absence of settings' case; live read-back of the resolved settings per posture.
applies_to_new_node: yes - applies to any config preset, even on a single engine across version upgrades whose defaults change.

class: test reaches the live node via env-var indirection
what_happened: During a test run ~/.bitcoin-knots/bitcoin.conf was rewritten to '# posture: strict': relayPosture.test.ts did `delete process.env.KNOTS_DATA_DIR` to inspect real default paths, and those overrides were the only thing keeping the suite off the live config. It was the second occurrence of the class in this repo (3a1c01bf). It had no runtime effect only because the container still used its CLI args, and was noticed because the panel reported active: None.
root_cause: Isolation depended on an environment variable that a test could unset.
lesson: A test must never be able to write to the live node's configuration or data: production write paths must refuse under test when the resolved path is outside the temp directory, and tests must never unset isolation overrides.
tripwire: applyPosture throws under NODE_ENV=test if the path is outside os.tmpdir(), with a test proving the guard fires; the offending test now asserts the engines resolve to different files instead.
applies_to_new_node: yes - tests and live node share a machine; isolation must be enforced, not configured.

class: daemon setting defined in two places with ambiguous precedence
what_happened: Knots' relay policy came purely from compose command-line args (its bitcoin.conf held 3 comment lines), while Core's came from bitcoin.conf, which set none of the options.
root_cause: Policy was split between CLI args and the config file per engine.
lesson: Each daemon setting must live in exactly one place (bitcoin.conf for both engines); the node rewrites only its own marked block (replacing it, never stacking duplicates), preserves the operator's lines outside the markers, and migrates by writing the new source first and removing the old one second.
tripwire: Unit tests: re-applying replaces the managed block; operator lines survive; smoke echoes the active posture in its summary line.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node will also manage bitcoind config.

class: unsupported choice silently downgraded
what_happened: Design for applying postures: Maximum on Core (which lacks rejectparasites) must be refused, not mapped to the nearest posture.
root_cause: Design decision: a posture that looks applied but filters nothing is worse than an error.
lesson: An option the running engine cannot serve must be refused with an error and write nothing, never silently downgraded.
tripwire: Unit test asserting refusal and that no file is even created.
applies_to_new_node: yes - general rule for applying owner choices.

class: control shipped before the path that makes it take effect
what_happened: The spec sequenced the UI (C2) before the apply path (C3); they were built as one increment so the UI never offered a choice that did nothing, and the UI states that a change needs a bitcoind restart rather than implying it is live.
root_cause: Design decision.
lesson: A control must not ship before the path that makes it take effect, and a change that needs a restart must say so at the point of choice.
tripwire: Unit tests on the apply path; smoke reports the active posture.
applies_to_new_node: yes - general rule.

class: policy retyped per engine; renderer not checked against what runs
what_happened: Relay policy was retyped per engine: Knots ran strict policy from our own compose args, Core ran permissive defaults, and a dead `_createKnotsConfig()` would have written a third copy into a conf file that did not match it.
root_cause: There was no single typed source for policy and no check tying the source to the running config.
lesson: Relay policy must be one typed data module with one renderer; a drift guard must compare rendered output with what actually runs, and detecting a half-applied policy must return 'unknown' (null) rather than the nearest posture.
tripwire: relayProfiles.test.ts (6, incl. detectPosture(['datacarrier=0']) -> null) and a drift guard comparing rendered Maximum args to docker-compose.knots.yml.
applies_to_new_node: maybe - applies if the new node exposes relay postures.

class: Tor proxy setting fails to apply at bitcoind start
what_happened: Unrelated pre-existing finding, not fixed: Core's debug.log carried '[error] Invalid -proxy address or hostname: 'tor:9050'' (2026-08-18, 2026-08-23) because the docker hostname `tor` is not always resolvable at bitcoind startup.
root_cause: bitcoind's proxy depended on a container hostname resolving at start.
lesson: The node must verify after every bitcoind start that the configured Tor proxy actually applied (getnetworkinfo), alarm if not, and not depend on a container hostname that may not resolve at start.
tripwire: None added; a post-start getnetworkinfo proxy check should exist.
applies_to_new_node: yes - a proxy that silently fails to apply is a privacy failure on any Tor-routed node.

class: config option meaningless to the running binary
what_happened: `mempoolfullrbf=0` sat in Core's bitcoin.conf (template and live), but a binary option diff showed it is a Knots-only option that Core 31.1 does not have.
root_cause: Config was carried across engines without checking the binary's option surface.
lesson: Every bitcoind config line must be validated against the running binary's option surface (`-help`).
tripwire: None added; flagged for follow-up.
applies_to_new_node: yes - config templates drift across bitcoind versions.

class: weakening a gate to make it pass
what_happened: After consensusBuilds.ts became git-tracked, the pin gate flagged an example image reference in its own doc comment; adding the file to EVIDENCE_PATHS would have passed by shrinking the gate, so the comment was reworded instead.
root_cause: The easy fix was an exemption.
lesson: A failing gate must be satisfied by fixing the source, never by adding an exemption or shrinking its scope.
tripwire: The pin gate itself, with no exemption added.
applies_to_new_node: yes - cross-cutting rule.

class: advisory-only rules for AI sessions
what_happened: Every existing rule for AI coding sessions was advisory. A deterministic PreToolUse guard was added (identical guard.py across repos, per-repo guard-config.json): secret-file reads deny, force-push deny, protected paths ask, funds/money-daemon mutations and stop/restart ask, a fix-lock that makes tests read-only during a fix, and any guard failure -> ask with the error (never fail open).
root_cause: Instructions can be skipped; only a hook is deterministic.
lesson: AI sessions working on the node must be bound by a deterministic hook that denies secret reads and force-pushes, asks before protected-path edits and money-daemon mutations, locks tests during a fix, protects itself, fails to 'ask' on its own errors, and has tests that routine commands stay silent (a false-positive gate trains the owner to click yes).
tripwire: test_guard.py replaying per-repo worked examples; mutant allow-all guard -> 36 failures + 1 error, mutant with fix-lock disabled -> 4 failures; live `claude -p` canary read refused in each repo.
owner_decision: implement Claude SDLC's procedure from now on for projects that make sense.
applies_to_new_node: yes - if the new node is built with AI sessions, the guard applies (it is already shared with Rikuri-PI).

class: frozen dependency left on trust
what_happened: The pinned Knots build 29.3.knots20260507 (on Core 29.3) is frozen by design. Review: no published advisory confirmed to affect it, but it lacked Core 29.4 (incl. a chainstate rewrite bug causing excessive disk I/O, i.e. SSD wear, and a fix in the same component as a High-severity use-after-free) and the 29.x line reaches end of life when v32.0 ships (~Oct 2026). Core discloses Medium/High issues about a year after the fix, so a CVE-only trigger would fire a year late.
root_cause: 'We'll keep an eye on it' had no mechanism.
lesson: Every pinned daemon that is not tracking upstream must carry a dated review of record with automatic re-open triggers (a new release on its base branch not accounted for, the base branch reaching end of life, the review date passing; interval <= 92 days), the review must cover the tag actually pinned, and withdrawal is a person's decision recorded in data that informs the owner and never switches the engine automatically.
tripwire: knotsPinReview.test.ts (13 evaluator cases incl. could-not-check is 'unknown', the review must cover the pinned tag so re-pinning without re-review fails CI, interval <= 92 days); knotsPinWatch.test.ts (8, against the real incident store and validator); daily Guardian cycle; smoke check; 7/7 planted regressions caught.
applies_to_new_node: yes - any frozen or slow-moving image (bitcoind, LND, electrs) on the new node needs a review cadence; vital if Knots is offered.

class: lazily-initialised singleton trusted for runtime truth
what_happened: Run for real, the pin watcher returned 'not-running' on a Knots node: the engine-service singleton had not loaded its state file yet and defaulted to Core, so the watcher would have resolved its own incidents and gone quiet. Unit tests could not see it because they injected the engine.
root_cause: Runtime truth was read from a cached object's default before initialisation.
lesson: Which engine/network is running must be read fresh from the authoritative source on each call (the same source scripts and smoke use), never from a lazily-initialised singleton's default; features must be run once for real, not only with injected dependencies.
tripwire: Live standalone run of the cycle returned 'current' after switching to getActiveEngineId().
applies_to_new_node: yes - general rule for the rebuilt backend.

class: unknown reported as all-clear; a watcher that can never succeed stays silent
what_happened: The evaluator was built so that a failed check yields 'unknown' (never 'current') and changes nothing, to avoid flapping; the record notes the remaining gap: if egress to GitHub is broken for weeks, no incident is ever raised about that.
root_cause: Absence of success was not itself monitored.
lesson: A check that cannot run must report 'unknown' and never all-clear, and the node must alarm when the last successful run of any watcher is older than N days.
tripwire: Evaluator case 'could-not-check is unknown'; frontend case 'unknown never reads as all-clear'; the last-success-age alarm is owed (not built).
applies_to_new_node: yes - every periodic watcher on the new node.

class: tests bound to today's data punish the next review
what_happened: Mutation runs showed several tests tied to the current review data (a hard-coded overdue date, '29.5' as the new release), so performing the next review would have broken them.
root_cause: Behaviour tests used live data instead of fixtures.
lesson: Behaviour tests of a periodic review must use fixed fixtures, and a simulated next review must pass the suite.
tripwire: Fixture-based behaviour tests; a simulated next review (re-dated to 2027, 29.5 accounted for) passes all 21.
applies_to_new_node: yes - general testing rule.

class: owner control panel rendering untested while its data is tested
what_happened: Every visible defect the owner found in the relay-posture panel (invisible buttons, unnamed engines, jargon) was a rendering defect the data-layer tests could not see; a rendering test had been owed across three changes.
root_cause: Tests stopped at the data layer.
lesson: Owner-facing control panels must have rendering tests through the real component, each guarded behaviour mutation-proven, including: the active choice offers no button, the other engine's card offers no button (never a second path to an engine switch), a save says it takes effect on the next restart and never that it is live, and a refused save shows the error, not success.
tripwire: dashboard/frontend/tests/RelayPosturePanel.test.tsx (11 cases); 7 of 7 planted regressions caught, each by its own case.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the rebuilt frontend's control panels.

class: persistently red CI with no alarm
what_happened: CI on the working branch was red for 7 weeks (since 2026-08-03) and nothing said so: CI never installed the shared/ workspace package's locked deps, so 4 backend suites could not load (better-sqlite3, zod) while it worked locally where shared/node_modules existed. Later a verifier found the new smoke CI check once PASSed on a stale run (2026-08-01).
root_cause: A workspace package outside the CI install path, hidden by no alarm on a red CI.
lesson: CI must install every workspace package's locked dependencies from a fresh clone, and the local gate must fail when the branch's latest CI run is red, warn when it cannot tell, and never pass on a run that is not for the current commit.
tripwire: smoke.sh check 9 reads the branch's latest decided CI run via gh (proven FAIL on a red run, WARN with GH_TOKEN=invalid); fresh-clone reproduction. The stale-run pass is a known gap.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node's CI and gate.

class: declared state standing in for runtime truth
what_happened: After the owner chose Strict on Core the panel said 'in use' while the running node reported maxdatacarriersize 100000 and permitbaremultisig true (Standard): the config had been written 3.5 minutes after bitcoind last started, and bitcoind reads its config only at start. The same class had hit the pin watcher the day before.
root_cause: 'In use' was derived from the saved config file, not from the running process.
lesson: Status shown as 'in use' must come from the running process: the RPC's own report where available (Core getmempoolinfo permitbaremultisig / maxdatacarriersize), otherwise the daemon's start time vs the config's last write (Knots omits the fields); 'cannot ask' must read 'checking', never 'in use'; a restart-to-apply control appears only while saved != running and disappears only when the node confirms.
tripwire: relayPostureStatus.test.ts; RelayPosturePanel.test.tsx ('a SAVED setting the node has not loaded is not in use'); smoke posture check reads the live status.
owner_decision: let the restart button surface only after I click the switch from standard to strict (may be popup with authentication), then disappear after implementation.
applies_to_new_node: yes - every status display on the new node.

class: 'up' taken as 'recovered': self-healing fights a deliberate restart
what_happened: The maintenance window was lifted as soon as bitcoind answered, before LND (which restarts itself on the new cookie) was back; the diagnosis trigger saw LND 'syncing', and the Rust proposal engine auto-ran RB-CONTAINER-RESTART-01, a second LND restart. The Rust service_monitor also ignores the maintenance flag. No funds were at risk only because mainnet LND had 0 channels.
root_cause: Recovery was judged by the restarted daemon alone, not by its dependents.
lesson: A deliberate restart must hold a maintenance window until every dependent that was running before is ready (bitcoind live, LND synced_to_chain, electrs healthy), with each probe time-bounded and the whole wait ending inside the window's TTL; reaching the bound must warn visibly or fail, and every monitor and remediator must honour the window.
tripwire: Real-wiring tests with a fake clock; planted regression 'window lifted when bitcoind answers' caught; owner's live acceptance: no incident and no self-heal action during the restart.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node's planned restarts and OS updates need the same window.

class: restart of a funds-adjacent daemon not step-up protected or bounded
what_happened: The restart-to-apply route first relied on login only; the owner then chose server-checked step-up. Verification also found two concurrent clicks both accepted, and the generic POST /api/system/restart-service/bitcoin route not engine-aware (on a Knots node it would start the idle Core container) and without a maintenance window.
root_cause: Owner decision plus verifier findings on an exec path.
lesson: Any owner action that restarts a funds-adjacent daemon must be server-enforced step-up (password + 2FA, a single-use token bound to that request), derive its container server-side, refuse (409) when its precondition does not hold rather than act as a general restart, allow one at a time (claimed before the first await), and use a bounded clean stop.
tripwire: Tests pin the route as step-up and every other /bitcoin/engine write as login-required; tests/stepUpFetch.test.ts (the app-wide step-up had no test before); live unauthenticated or Bearer-only POST -> 401 step_up_required.
owner_decision: should require password
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node's backend auth model.

class: expired session is a dead end for an authenticated action
what_happened: The owner's first nine clicks (4 saves, 5 restarts) all got '401 Token expired'; the panel showed 'Token expired' and offered no way to log in.
root_cause: No re-authentication path existed on that action.
lesson: An authenticated action that meets an expired session must open re-authentication and retry exactly once, cancelling must say nothing changed, and an expiry mid-operation must be stated.
tripwire: Frontend tests: expired session -> password -> exactly one retry; cancel sends nothing; expired login mid-restart is shown.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the rebuilt frontend.

class: control-path probe unbounded; 'cannot tell' read as 'no'
what_happened: Verification found: a status pre-check that could wait forever, `lndCall` with no timeout, 'cannot tell' treated as 'not running', and a planted unbounded-wait regression that crashed Node or spun for 6 minutes and kept jest from exiting.
root_cause: Status questions were awaited without time limits and absence was inferred from errors.
lesson: Every status probe in a control path must be time-bounded, only an explicit 'no such container' may count as absent ('cannot tell' is never a negative), and tests of waits must use a fake clock that fails fast past a bound.
tripwire: Fake-clock tests; a fake clock that throws past a day of fake time (planted unbounded wait -> 2 fails, jest exits in 2 s).
applies_to_new_node: yes - general rule.

class: gate failure leaves no record of which check failed
what_happened: Smoke had one transient FAIL that two reruns did not reproduce, and it keeps no record of which check failed; its CI check also once passed on stale data.
root_cause: The gate reported only an aggregate result.
lesson: The node's gate must persist which check failed, with its evidence, for every run.
tripwire: None added (routed as its own change).
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node's smoke/health gate.

class: edge event read as a level fault
what_happened: Incident lnd:LND_SYNC_STALLED stayed open from 2026-09-18 with 11 LND restarts: each followed LND reporting 'syncing' for a few seconds while processing a new block (e.g. block 968341 at 02:41:11Z, health poll at 02:41:16Z), which keyword matching ('sync', /lnd.*sync/) turned into a stall and a restart.
root_cause: A momentary 'started syncing' edge was classified as a stall without evidence that height had stopped moving.
lesson: A transient 'syncing' edge must never open an incident or trigger a fix; an LND stall must be a level condition: synced_to_chain false AND LND height below bitcoind's AND LND height not advancing over N consecutive checks (synced_to_graph excluded), followed by one restart and then the owner.
tripwire: lndSyncStall.test.ts (16, 12 failed on the old code); 11/11 planted regressions caught; live: 'Lightning (LND) syncing' after a Bitcoin restart triggered nothing.
owner_decision: 3. Fix without guardian to ask first
applies_to_new_node: yes - on a funded node each unneeded LND restart takes channels offline.

class: opener and closer name the same thing differently
what_happened: Incidents were opened as `lnd:*` but recovery alerts said `lightning`, and noteRecovery compared the raw alert name, so a recovery never closed the incident.
root_cause: Two components derived the service name independently.
lesson: Incident opening and recovery matching must normalise through one canonical service-name mapping.
tripwire: lndSyncStall tests 'lightning_recovered closes lnd:*'; planted regression 'naming mismatch put back' caught.
applies_to_new_node: yes - general rule for the incident record.

class: incident orphaned by a restart never closes
what_happened: The legacy incident could never close because closing depended on in-memory loop state lost on dashboard restart; the fix closes it from LND's current level state after two synced looks, with honest wording ('Not a stall … the 11 restarts were not needed'). A general staleness sweep still does not exist.
root_cause: Closure depended on edge history held in memory.
lesson: The detector that owns an incident must close it from current level state on two consecutive good looks (recording the evidence, e.g. both heights), and the node must have a general staleness sweep for incidents no detector will revisit.
tripwire: lndSyncStall R3 tests; live close 97 s after deploy with heights recorded.
applies_to_new_node: yes - general rule for the incident record.

class: network-unaware remediation target
what_happened: Verification found that in testnet4 mode an LND stall would restart the mainnet `lnd` container (targeting predated the change and the old edge path had the same flaw).
root_cause: Remediation targets ignored which network the node was in.
lesson: Every remediation target must be network-aware; when the rule cannot target the right network it must stand down and log once.
tripwire: Loop 5 tests: testnet4 detection and close stand down; planted regressions caught.
applies_to_new_node: maybe - matters if the new node runs more than one network side by side.

class: missing or stale input silently disables a detector
what_happened: A lightning snapshot without synced_to_chain would make the rule go quiet; a frozen health snapshot counts as 'not moving' because health calls LND without a timeout; health alerts emitted before the diagnosis listener attaches at startup are dropped silently.
root_cause: Detectors assumed their inputs were present and fresh.
lesson: A detector must log loudly when an input field is missing, must check the age of the snapshot it judges, and must not lose alerts raised before its listener attaches.
tripwire: A warning when synced_to_chain is missing (test watches the mocked logger); snapshot-age check and startup-race fix are owed.
applies_to_new_node: yes - general detector rule.

class: PID-1 shell wrapper does not deliver the stop signal
what_happened: electrs-start.sh and mempool-start.sh had the LND wrapper flaw. electrs's image uses StopSignal SIGINT and dash as PID 1 exits on INT at once (0.1 s, exit 130), so the container died and electrs was SIGKILLed without being asked (risking an hours-long index rebuild); mempool's start.sh runs node in the foreground, so even a TERM to the shell orphaned node (seen exiting 137). A stop during electrs's 15 s pre-start sleep was also SIGKILLed because dash defers traps until `sleep` ends.
root_cause: The wrapper was PID 1, ran the program as a child, trapped nothing, and slept uninterruptibly.
lesson: Every container entrypoint wrapper must trap TERM and INT, forward the stop to the real program (and to its children when an image script runs it in the foreground), wait until it has exited, exit 0 for a requested clean stop (0/130/143) and pass other codes through, and use interruptible sleeps (`sleep N & wait $!`); it must be tested as PID 1 in the real image with that image's StopSignal.
tripwire: wrapperStop.test.ts on the real scripts with fakes (9 of 12 failed on the old scripts; follow-up 4 failed); PID-1 probes in the real images (electrs 0.1 s/130 -> 2.0 s/0, mempool 10.1 s/137 -> 2.1 s/0); control-plane 'died' count 0 after apply.
owner_decision: 1. yes fix both
applies_to_new_node: yes - podman/docker on Fedora IoT have the same PID-1 signal semantics; prefer `exec` or a real init that reaches the program.

class: probe artifact named like a service triggers a false alarm
what_happened: A stopped probe container named `wrapper-probe-mempool` matched the health check's `name.includes('mempool')`: 'Mempool Explorer is down', self-healing restarted the healthy mempool-api, and an incident closed 10 s later as 'auto'.
root_cause: Probe naming collided with substring-based identity in the health check.
lesson: Test and probe artifacts created on a live node must use neutral names (e.g. rk-scratch-*) that cannot match any service matcher, and must be removed afterwards.
tripwire: Naming rule recorded (rk-scratch-* used in later probes); root cause fixed in 2026-09-26-health-exact-container-names.md.
applies_to_new_node: yes - experiments will run on the live new node too.

class: guard can be switched off through an unprotected side channel
what_happened: An independent verifier found that a Write to `.claude/settings.local.json` (git-ignored, so no review sees it, and able to set disableAllHooks) was a silent allow, as were `rm -rf .claude/hooks` and `rm -rf .claude/state` (which silently releases the fix-lock); round 2 found wildcard deletes still allowed. User-level ~/.claude/settings.json remains outside any repo policy.
root_cause: The policy protected the guard's files one by one but not the other ways to switch it off.
lesson: A safety gate must protect every way of disabling it (local settings files, its directories and state, wildcard and traversal deletes), each with a worked example seen failing before the fix; remaining unprotectable paths must be listed as known gaps.
