tripwire: guard-config.json worked examples (FAILED failures=5 before the globs, then 2 more in round 2); guard tests on Python 3.12 and 3.9; guard.py/test_guard.py cmp-identical across repos.
owner_decision: Yes, go ahead and close the hole.
applies_to_new_node: yes - if the new node's repo uses the AI-session guard.

class: precondition checked after the lock it should gate
what_happened: Twice (in a comment on 09-22, in a new test on 09-24) a `require(` broke the quality ratchet and was found only after the fix-lock was engaged, each time costing the owner an extra approval to release it.
root_cause: The ratchet ran after, not before, the point where tests become read-only.
lesson: Engaging the fix-lock must run the repo's preflight (the ratchet) first, with argv and no shell, and refuse with the failing command's output if it fails, leaving no lock.
tripwire: test_guard.py: failing preflight refuses and leaves no lock, passing engages, no key engages, malformed key refuses; live planted require( -> 'fix-lock NOT engaged'.
owner_decision: ok with 2 rules
applies_to_new_node: yes - if the new node's repo uses the guard and a ratchet.

class: editing a bind-mounted script that a running PID 1 is reading
what_happened: scripts/lnd-start.sh was edited in place while bind-mounted (same inode) into the running LND container, where `sh` reads the script as it runs, shifting the bytes under a live PID 1; it was caught and restored before harm.
root_cause: Shells read scripts incrementally, and the bind mount made the repo file the live file.
lesson: Scripts mounted into running containers are live files: develop on copies, check the running shell's read position, and write the live file once at apply time; better, bake entrypoints into immutable images.
tripwire: Instruction-level rule in CLAUDE.md ('Bind-mounted scripts are LIVE files'); no automated check.
owner_decision: ok with 2 rules
applies_to_new_node: yes - on Fedora IoT, baking wrappers into images avoids the class; if any script is bind-mounted the rule applies.

class: PID-1 wrapper forwards no stop signal (LND SIGKILLed on every stop)
what_happened: Every Docker stop or restart of lnd SIGKILLed LND (14 forced kills since 2026-09-18), on every path: self-healing, the Rust cascade (killed after its 30 s timeout), compose and the owner. lnd-start.sh ran `lnd &` and `wait` under busybox ash as PID 1 with no trap, and PID 1 ignores TERM without a handler.
root_cause: A PID-1 wrapper that starts its program in the background and forwards no signal.
lesson: LND must be stopped gracefully on every path: its wrapper traps TERM/INT, forwards TERM to LND, waits for LND's own shutdown and exits with LND's status, a stop before LND starts ends promptly, the cookie watcher dies with it, and a hung LND is still killed at the runtime's timeout. (`exec lnd` was rejected because the wrapper runs the cookie watcher; compose `init: true` was rejected because tini forwards only to the shell.)
tripwire: lndStartScript.test.ts (real script, fake lnd; 2 failed on the old script); PID-1 probe in the real image (10.2 s/137 -> 2.2 s/0); live `docker restart lnd` 0.8 s, 'Shutdown complete', exit 0.
owner_decision: Go ahead and work on the fix for LND stop
applies_to_new_node: yes - a funded LND on the new node must never be SIGKILLed by routine restarts.

class: credential visible on a process command line
what_happened: Verification found LND's command line carries `--bitcoind.rpcpass=<cookie>`, readable with `ps` inside the container and from the host; the cookie rotates on every Bitcoin restart, which limits but does not remove the exposure.
root_cause: The wrapper passed the RPC secret as an argument.
lesson: Credentials must never be passed on a process command line; LND should read bitcoind's cookie file itself (e.g. --bitcoind.rpccookie, which may also remove LND from the cookie-restart cascade).
tripwire: None added (owner decision pending); a check that no daemon's argv contains a secret should exist.
applies_to_new_node: yes - applies to every daemon on the new node.

class: two mechanisms own the same restart and neither checks the other
what_happened: After every Bitcoin restart LND restarted itself via its cookie watcher (00:12:42) and the control plane's cookie cascade restarted it again (00:12:48), costing ~30 s more Lightning downtime (and the same for electrs and mempool); the cascade used a flat 30 s stop timeout below LND's 90 s grace, called a missing container 'restarted successfully' and counted skipped as restarted.
root_cause: Two mechanisms each owned 'restart on a new cookie' and neither looked at whether the other had already done it.
lesson: The cookie cascade must skip a dependent whose start time is after the cookie change (an unknown start time means restart), log every skip, stop each container with its own configured grace period (with the client call timeout above it), and report restarted / skipped / failed separately by name; a dependent restarted only to reconnect (mempool-web) is never skipped.
tripwire: Inline Rust tests in cascade.rs (already_has_new_cookie, stop_timeout_secs, skip_rule_applies, restart_call_timeout, summary_line; 8/8, seen failing as E0425 first). The live skip at the next Bitcoin restart was not yet observed.
owner_decision: 2. Ok let control plane skip
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node also has cookie-dependent services; or remove LND from the cascade by having it read the cookie file.

class: fuzzy identity: substring fallback acts on a neighbour
what_happened: dockerService.getContainer() fell back to the first container whose name contained the requested one: with lnd absent, a restart of 'lnd' would act on lnd-testnet, and 'bitcoin' on bitcoin-testnet; the upgrade sandbox asked for the group name 'mempool' and passed its existence check on whichever mempool-* container Docker listed first.
root_cause: Targets were resolved by name similarity instead of identity.
lesson: Every container action (start, stop, restart, logs, stats) must resolve its target by exact name after a small explicit alias table and otherwise refuse with 'not found' and do nothing; a group name is not a container.
tripwire: exactContainerTarget.test.ts (8; 5 failed on old code); planted regressions caught; live GET /api/services/mempool -> 404, /lnd and /lightning -> 200.
owner_decision: So must pass along the name for health check. Refuse if container name doesn't match.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node will have mainnet/testnet or full/pruned siblings with similar names.

class: alert loses the failing component's identity
what_happened: A mempool-db outage raised by the monitoring loop carried only the service 'mempool', which the classifier mapped to mempool-api, so RB-CONTAINER-RESTART-01 would restart the wrong container, although health's snapshot already knew the down container's name.
root_cause: The alert carried an aggregate service name instead of the container.
lesson: Every alert must carry the exact failing container from the health snapshot through classification to the runbook parameters.
tripwire: exactContainerTarget.test.ts: the loop's mempool-db finding and alert carry `container` and the real synthesizer classifies onto mempool-db.
applies_to_new_node: yes - general rule.

class: deployed artifact differs from committed code
what_happened: The verifier found the live dashboard dist contained another session's uncommitted DRB schema-gate code, because `npm run build` compiles the whole working tree; every rebuild (likely since 2026-09-17) shipped it.
root_cause: Deployment built from a dirty working tree.
lesson: The node must deploy only from a committed, clean tree and be able to report the exact commit it is running.
tripwire: None added (routed to the owner).
applies_to_new_node: yes - image-based deploys with OS rollback should be built from tagged commits.

class: relaxing a safety gate
what_happened: After many prompts, the owner relaxed four guard approvals in rikurinode: fix-lock release, docker restart of lnd/bitcoin/knots/testnet/tapd and systemctl restart of tapd, and edits to the guard and CI workflows. The costs were stated first and the AI recommended keeping three of them; stops, kills, lncli stop, money-moving commands, settings files and the constitution still ask.
root_cause: Owner policy choice.
lesson: Relaxing a gate must be an explicit owner choice with its costs stated beforehand, scoped exactly to what was chosen, reversible in one config file, and every relaxed action that bypasses a protection (fix-lock release) must be logged and audited; the funds-daemon restart gate should be raised again when mainnet channels open.
tripwire: test_guard.py config-aware tests, test_every_release_is_logged, test_release_policy_must_be_a_boolean; .claude/state/fix-lock.log; verifier step 5 (fix-lock audit).
owner_decision: Can we release the fix-lock, allow restart LND/bitcoin/tapd; edit guard, or CI from requiring permission? … We'll put these back on when appropriate
applies_to_new_node: yes - the same trade-off will recur on the new node once it holds funds.

class: identity by substring in the health check
what_happened: Health selected 'the electrs container' and 'the mempool containers' by substring (`name.includes('electrs')`, `includes('mempool')`); on 2026-09-26 a stopped probe container named wrapper-probe-mempool produced 'Mempool Explorer is down', self-healing restarted the healthy mempool-api, and the incident closed 10 s later as 'fixed automatically'. The old code also lost the down container's name when its stats threw.
root_cause: Health trusted 'a container whose name contains X'.
lesson: Health must count exactly the stack's named containers and ignore every other container; a down container must be reported and named even when its stats cannot be read.
tripwire: healthContainerIdentity.test.ts drives the real performHealthCheck() with a decoy container (5 of 6 failed on old code); live decoy-mempool-probe changed nothing.
owner_decision: 4. yes
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node's health checks.

class: fix silently changes unchosen behaviour (aggregate status, metric source)
what_happened: The verifier FAILED the first commit: the node's overall status stayed 'healthy' while electrs or mempool-web was down (the old code set 'degraded' only in catch blocks reached by accident), and moving the explorer's stats to mempool-api (normally 80-141% CPU, ~90% memory) fired mempool_high_cpu 3x and came within 2.2 points of MEMORY_HIGH, whose auto-executing runbook could have restarted LND.
root_cause: Aggregate health was a side effect of error paths, and a metric source change was not treated as a behaviour change.
lesson: Aggregate health must be computed explicitly from component states, never as a side effect of exceptions, and any change in which component a metric is read from is a behaviour change that needs the owner's choice and a threshold review.
tripwire: Correction-loop tests: stopped electrs / mempool-web / mempool-db -> 'degraded'; all running -> 'healthy'; stats source pinned; 5/5 planted regressions caught incl. the verifier's misses.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node's health aggregation.

class: generic resource remediation can restart the funds daemon
what_happened: RB-MEMORY-GRACEFUL-RESTART-01 (tier T1, auto-executes) restarts the worst container at >= 90% memory, excluding only bitcoin, bitcoin-knots and electrs, so LND was eligible; it did not fire.
root_cause: The exclusion list was a denylist written before LND held funds.
lesson: Generic resource remediations must use an explicit allowlist of restartable containers that excludes funds daemons (LND, tapd) unless the owner opts in.
tripwire: None added (owner decision pending); a test that no resource runbook can target LND or tapd should exist.
applies_to_new_node: yes - the new node will run LND with funds.

class: absent component reported as healthy
what_happened: Verification found a stack container that is absent (not merely stopped) is invisible: mempool reported healthy with mempool-api missing.
root_cause: Health iterated over containers that exist instead of over the containers that should exist.
lesson: Health must enumerate the expected stack and report a missing member as down; absence is not health.
tripwire: None added (separate change).
applies_to_new_node: yes - general rule.

class: secret passed on a process command line
what_happened: LND was started with --bitcoind.rpcuser=__cookie__ --bitcoind.rpcpass=<cookie password>, so anything that could list processes, inside the container or on the host, could read Bitcoin Core's RPC password. The same sweep found the testnet pair (lnd-testnet, bitcoin-testnet) carrying a static RPC login (rikuri-testnet) on their command lines, committed in docker-compose.testnet.yml.
root_cause: The start wrapper read the cookie itself and passed its value to LND as an argument instead of giving LND the cookie's path.
lesson: The node must never put a credential (RPC password, cookie value, token) on any process's command line or exported environment; LND must be pointed at the cookie with --bitcoind.rpccookie=<path> (supported by LND 0.21.3), the wrapper may read the cookie only to refuse an empty one (never logged or exported), and testnet stacks get the same credential hygiene (no committed static logins), since lnd-testnet holds testnet sats and backs tapd.
tripwire: lndStartScript.test.ts: a fake lnd logs its argv; tests assert rpccookie is present and neither rpcpass nor the cookie value, in both launch branches (3 planted regressions caught); a later test asserts the password reaches neither LND's environment nor the wrapper's output (a planted `export COOKIE_PASS` is caught). Live: list host processes with a bitcoind.rpcpass / -rpcpassword flag (flag names only, never values). The testnet static login was left as a Skipped owner item.
owner_decision: "4. yes" (2026-09-26), to having LND read Bitcoin's cookie file itself.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node pairs LND with bitcoind on both the x86 and the Pi 5 node; cookie-path auth and no secrets in argv apply to every service.

class: credential rotation not picked up by a long-running client
what_happened: The owner asked: "Does that mean it's better to have LND read Bitcoin's cookie? Would that affect the cascade order?" A throwaway regtest bitcoind + LND 0.21.3 showed that after a bitcoind restart (new cookie) LND kept failing with HTTP 401 for 2.5+ minutes; the verifier independently re-ran it and saw 401 for 3+ minutes.
root_cause: LND reads the cookie file once at startup and does not re-read it when bitcoind rotates it on restart.
lesson: The node must restart LND after every bitcoind restart (the cookie rotates each time), keeping the bitcoind-then-LND restart cascade and its watchers even with rpccookie; an exposed cookie stays valid until the next bitcoind restart.
tripwire: Regtest experiment by builder and verifier (recorded). Should exist: an integration test or monitor that detects LND's 401s against bitcoind after a bitcoind restart and asserts LND is restarted; re-run on each LND upgrade.
applies_to_new_node: yes — same LND/bitcoind pairing; the restart cascade must survive into the new node and be re-checked per LND version.

class: stop signal lost during a wrapper's startup phases
what_happened: The LND wrapper (container PID 1) exited 143 with "shutting LND down cleanly…" when stopped before LND started, its cookie-wait sleep was not interruptible, and a stop landing between `lnd … &` and `LND_PID=$!` could be lost. The verifier found that race path differs by shell: busybox (production) exits 143 in 0.05 s, dash (the jest host shell) hung until killed, 3/3.
root_cause: The wrapper only handled TERM once the child PID was known, used plain sleeps, and its tests ran under a different shell than production.
lesson: A service start wrapper must handle a stop in every phase: interruptible waits, an honest exit 0 for a stop before the service starts, and a held stop (STARTING/STOP_PENDING) when the signal arrives before the child's PID is known; wrapper tests must run under the production shell.
tripwire: lndStartScript.test.ts: early stop prompt (< 1.5 s) and exit 0; planted plain sleep and early 143 caught; PID-1 probe in the real image (normal stop 2.1 s/0, stop during cookie wait 0.1 s/0). The microsecond race cannot be hit deterministically; covered by code read and the verifier only.
applies_to_new_node: maybe — depends on whether the new node keeps a shell wrapper as PID 1 or lets systemd/the container runtime supervise LND directly; the phase-by-phase stop rule applies either way.

class: automated remediation with a target chosen at run time (fuzzy identity)
what_happened: On a memory alert, the automatic (T1) runbook RB-MEMORY-GRACEFUL-RESTART-01 restarted whichever container was highest at >=90% of its memory limit anywhere on the node (only bitcoin, bitcoin-knots and electrs excluded), which could be LND even when something else raised the alert. Found by the health-check verifier.
root_cause: The target was picked by a shell command inside the runbook step, invisible to the policy engine that decides automatic vs owner-approved.
lesson: Every automatic repair must name its exact target before submission, and the trusted policy engine (not the caller) must decide automatic vs held from that actual parameter: restarting a funds-holding service (lnd, lnd-testnet, tapd) for resource pressure is held for the owner, other containers stay automatic, a missing or empty target fails closed (held), and the precheck re-verifies the condition at run time (the owner may approve hours later).
tripwire: control-plane/tests/runbook_owner_hold.rs loads the real runbook JSON (lnd, lnd-testnet, tapd held; mempool-api automatic; missing target held) plus runbook_route routing tests; memoryRestartTarget.test.ts for the backend pick (nothing proposed when none qualifies); 9 planted regressions caught. Recorded gap: a regression bypassing runbook_route inside submit_runbook needs a whole-submit harness.
owner_decision: "Why exclude. Shouldn't the runbook restart LND or is that a double restart?" then "2. Ok, use your suggestion" (2026-09-26): ask first when the picked container holds funds, automatic for everything else.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node will have automated repair; funds-holding services need a target-based hold decided in the trusted core.

class: restart policy for a funds service must differ by failure mode
what_happened: After the memory-restart hold was built, the owner decided that a DOWN LND (RB-CONTAINER-RESTART-01) is restarted without waiting for approval, while the memory-pressure restart of a RUNNING LND stays held.
root_cause: A stopped LND already has its channels offline, so waiting on approval prolongs the outage, whereas restarting a running LND takes channels offline for a minute or two.
lesson: The node must restart a stopped LND automatically and ask the owner before restarting a running LND for resource reasons; each rule is a visible, one-line, reversible policy entry in the runbook data.
tripwire: The hold list in the runbook JSON (hold_for_owner) pinned by runbook_owner_hold.rs; RB-CONTAINER-RESTART-01 carries no hold.
owner_decision: "Don't wait for my approval to restart LND." (2026-09-27)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the same distinction applies to LND supervision on both new nodes.

class: deployed binary not built from the verified source
what_happened: Verifier round 1 found the running control plane was a build from 10:08Z, made before the 10:15Z runbook_route refactor (its binary still contained "is T3 (manual-only)"); the restart had waited ~11 h for owner approval, so a stale build went live.
root_cause: The binary was built and staged early, the source then changed, and the deploy did not check build freshness.
lesson: A deploy must ship a fresh build of exactly the verified source: refuse to stage if any source file is newer than the build, and after restart confirm the running executable is byte-identical to the build.
tripwire: Stage refused if any control-plane/src file is newer than the build; `strings` check for a removed string; `cmp /proc/<pid>/exe target/release/control-plane`. Lesson-loop CLAUDE.md line: "Runbook JSONs are LIVE too, and a control-plane deploy ships a FRESH build".
applies_to_new_node: yes — image-based deploys should carry the source commit and be checked by digest against what was tested.

class: older engine silently ignores a new safety field
what_happened: The new optional hold_for_owner field (serde default) would be ignored by the old control-plane binary, which would then run the named-target runbook with no hold. The runbook JSON v2.0 was on disk from 10:15Z; the old binary loaded it lazily at 18:47Z and held v2.0 without the hold until 21:22Z (harmless only because the old backend never passed a funds container).
root_cause: Policy files are live the moment they are written and the engine accepts unknown fields, so only deploy order protected the safety property.
lesson: Safety-relevant policy data must never be loadable by an engine that does not enforce it: deploy the enforcing engine before the data, version the policy schema and refuse unknown safety keys, and treat on-disk policy files as live code.
tripwire: Manual deploy order (Rust binary, then runbook reload, then backend). Should exist: a schema-version or deny-unknown-fields check on safety keys so an old engine refuses new policy.
applies_to_new_node: yes — any policy/config shipped separately from the engine (including across OS image rollbacks) has this mixed-version risk.

class: approval request misstates the risk of the action
what_happened: The approval message for a held LND restart said "Tier T1 … safe, reversible" and "Risk level: low", did not name the container, and in round 1 the held message read ". ." ; the T0 deny text also said T3.
root_cause: The message text was derived from the runbook tier, not from the hold decided for the actual target.
lesson: An owner approval request must name the exact target and why it is held ("Why it asks you"), and must never call a funds-service action low-risk or "safe, reversible" because of its tier.
tripwire: Approval-text tests (held lnd and ask-first lnd show "Why it asks you", no "Risk level", no "safe, reversible"; mempool-api reads as before); round-2 planted regression "a held run called low-risk" caught; verifier rendered texts from the deployed dist. Residual: the notification's riskLevel metadata still says "low".
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node will ask the owner for approvals; wording must reflect the actual target.

class: test pins a helper but not that the entry point uses it
what_happened: The Rust test covered owner_hold_reason but not that submit_runbook called it, so a regression dropping the call would have passed; the fix-lock was released to add runbook_route routing tests. The same gap recurred in 2026-09-28-repairs-outlive-the-request.md, where a handler-bypass mutation of run_to_completion survived.
root_cause: Unit tests targeted the decision function in isolation; its wiring into the real entry point was untested.
lesson: A safety decision must be tested through the entry point that applies it (or a single routing function the entry point provably calls), and a mutation that bypasses the call must turn a test red.
tripwire: runbook_route tests seen failing before the refactor; planted "the route skips the gate" caught. Should exist: a whole-submit harness (decision log, pending store) and handler-level tests so a bypass is caught.
applies_to_new_node: yes — applies to every safety gate in the rebuilt backend.

class: two knobs for one quantity drift apart
what_happened: mempool-api's container got 1720 MB from auto-scale-memory.sh (2048 MB x host share) while compose pinned Node's heap at --max-old-space-size=2304 (set for a 3 GB container on 2026-08-16). The container had hit its limit 21,921 times, had 352,571,392 B in swap, and reached ~98% within ~6 h of a start; the approved "restart at >=95%" watch alone would have restarted it about every 6 hours.
root_cause: The container size (auto-scale, which overrides compose's 3G) and the heap (compose) were set in different places and the heap was never updated.
lesson: A runtime heap must be derived at start from the container's own cgroup memory.max (here 80%), replacing any inherited heap flag, with a digits-only owner override, and logged; container limit and heap must never be set independently.
tripwire: mempoolApiMemory.test.ts: heap from a fake cgroup file on a scratch copy of the wrapper, auto-scale sizes from a fake meminfo (RIKURI_MEMINFO), compose has no fixed heap, health -> loop -> classifier -> runbook; planted regressions (heap 100% of limit, inherited flag kept, auto-scale back to 2048, heap pinned again) caught. Live: node runs with --max-old-space-size=2064 in a 2580 MB limit; memory.events max 21921 -> 0 after the restart.
owner_decision: First approval "1. Ok with your proposal" (alert only at >=95% for 3 checks in a row; restart mempool-api itself, never "the heaviest container"; no CPU alert); after the investigation, chose "Heap follows limit".
applies_to_new_node: yes — mempool on the x86 full node; small hosts get a smaller heap (~589-614 MB on 8 GB), where the 2026-08-16 big-mempool crash could recur (owner-accepted cost, the watch restarts it).

class: memory metric counts reclaimable page cache
what_happened: After the heap fix, page cache still filled mempool-api's cgroup to the limit at each of mempool's disk-cache writes and was then reclaimed; the planned watch read raw usage (86.6% vs docker stats 75%) and would have drifted to 95% and restarted a healthy mempool-api. Generic figures showed bitcoin 46.6% by usage vs 14.3% in docker stats.
root_cause: The backend's memory_percent was cgroup usage including inactive file cache, not the working set.
lesson: Container memory alerts and restart decisions must use the working set (usage minus inactive_file, as docker stats does, for cgroup v1 and v2) as the single figure everywhere; cgroup limit hits and swap (memory.events max/oom, swap) must also be watched because they appear in no log.
tripwire: memoryWorkingSet.test.ts (cgroup v2/v1, no cache figure, a bogus cache figure); health case "the watch reads the working set" (usage 99, working set 80 -> 80); 4 planted regressions caught; live watch 75.5% vs docker stats 75.0%. Not built: a watch on memory.events max growth. Generalised to every container (92% alert and memory-restart pick) in 2026-09-30-dashboard-measurements.md.
owner_decision: "Fine with 95% limit for now." (2026-09-27, on measuring the 95% as docker stats shows it)
applies_to_new_node: yes — cgroup v2 under any container engine on Fedora IoT has the same cache accounting.

class: pipeline exit status masks a failing test suite
what_happened: The backend was deployed with a red suite: `(npm run test:unit | grep | tail) && build && restart` succeeded because the pipeline's status was tail's; 1 test was failing.
root_cause: The deploy was chained on a filtered pipe whose last command always succeeds.
lesson: A deploy must be gated on the test runner's own exit code (run alone, or under pipefail), never on a filtered pipeline.
tripwire: From round 2 the suite runs alone with pipefail and the deploy is conditional on its code (record lesson). Should exist: a deploy script that refuses unless the full gate exited 0.
applies_to_new_node: yes — process rule for building and deploying the new node.

class: operator override silently ignored
what_happened: A *_MEMORY_LIMIT in .env is silently overridden: rikuri-stack.service and the post-upgrade bring-up load auto-scale's file as EnvironmentFile and the process environment beats .env (confirmed on Compose v5.5.1 with a scratch project); the auto-scale comment and generated header claimed the opposite. Only the stack watchdog used .env/compose defaults without auto-scale.
root_cause: Two configuration sources for one setting, with undocumented precedence and a false comment.
lesson: Each resource limit must have one documented source of truth that scales with host RAM (baseline x host share, with floors); an operator override must either win or be reported as ignored at startup, never dropped silently, and every start path must apply the same sizing.
tripwire: False comment and header corrected; docs no longer promise .env wins. Should exist: a startup check comparing configured overrides with effective limits, and one start path for all bring-ups.
owner_decision: "The original memory limit for each service depends on the size of RAM for a node … if there is only 8 or 16 GB, that needs to be limited or controlled. Not sure what .env has." (2026-09-27)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the Pi 5 pruned node has much less RAM than the x86 node, so per-host scaled limits from a single source matter more.

class: editing a script while a running shell executes it
what_happened: mempool-start.sh (like the LND wrapper in 2026-09-26-lnd-rpccookie.md) is a live bind-mounted file executed by a container's PID 1; the change had to be developed on a scratch copy and written once in place, after confirming the running shell had already read the tail (its final wait at byte 9038 of 9404, ending in an unconditional exit).
root_cause: Wrapper scripts are bind-mounted from the mutable repo checkout into running containers, so any edit is a live edit of executing code.
lesson: The node's service wrappers must ship inside immutable images or versioned files that take effect only at a restart, never as live bind mounts of a working tree read incrementally by a running shell.
tripwire: Manual live-file rule (scratch copy, tail check, single write; repo = host = container same inode and sha256). Should exist: a check that no running container bind-mounts a script from the repo checkout.
applies_to_new_node: yes — image-based OS and containers remove live bind-mounted scripts by construction; keep it that way.

class: evidence claims stated imprecisely
what_happened: Verifier rounds 2-6 failed the record only on its claims: "max still 247" when it was 903, mixed MB/MiB, undated live numbers, "swap does not grow" contradicted by memory.swap.peak (19,578,880 B), "~15 min" that was ~7.5, and an acceptance clause ("never reaches its limit") that was not met and had to be dropped openly; round 7 passed.
root_cause: Live figures were written from memory or integer prints without timestamps, units or sources, and the acceptance line was set before the mechanism was understood.
lesson: Every live figure in an engineering record must be a dated snapshot with exact units and its source, and an unmet acceptance criterion must be amended openly, never reinterpreted.
tripwire: Units/time-zone header at the top of the record; independent verifier re-reads every number. (Process rule, no automated check.)
applies_to_new_node: yes — process rule for the rebuild's records.

class: approval gate latency stalls routine work
what_happened: Two control-plane restarts on 2026-09-26/27 waited ~11 h and ~6 h in the AI-session guard's approval prompt; the owner said "I'm getting fewer ask for approval but still some."
root_cause: The guard asked the owner for every control-plane restart, though a restart returns in about 2 s and pending approvals survive it.
lesson: Development guardrails must weigh the cost of waiting: a routine, quickly reversible restart of a safety service may run without the owner, while stopping, killing, disabling or masking it and restarting the whole stack keep asking.
tripwire: Guard worked examples flipped first and seen failing (18 tests, 2 failures), then the one regex alternative removed; live hook replayed with Claude Code's JSON (restart allow; stop control plane, restart rikuri-stack, docker stop lnd ask).
owner_decision: "Ok yes, make the one line change." (2026-09-27)
applies_to_new_node: maybe — development tooling for the rebuild repo, not node runtime.

class: safety gate strictness fixed for every project phase
what_happened: The owner found the guard too restrictive while projects are in development (asks waiting overnight) and asked that users be able to adjust it easily; a "development"/"stable" profile was added to the guard shared by four repos.
root_cause: The guard had one strictness level suited to software close to completion.
lesson: The development guard must have a one-command, logged strictness profile kept in committed config: in development only money-moving, irreversible or secret-exposing asks survive (marked always_ask, e.g. lncli/bitcoin-cli sends, rm wallet.db/chain data, fund-moving curl), denies (secret reads, force-push, test edits under a fix-lock) never relax, every relaxed ask is logged, loosening asks the owner and tightening is free.
tripwire: test_guard.py replays every worked example under both profiles (expect / expect_dev) plus Profiles tests; planted regressions (always_ask ignored, secret touch relaxed, relaxed log off, loosening free) caught; guard.py/test_guard.py cmp-identical in all four repos; live hook replay per repo (restart allowed and logged; lncli sendcoins and rm wallet.db ask; cat .env and git push --force deny).
owner_decision: "I think for now we'll just follow the Auto mode for Claude or Codex. It's too restrictive the way I set this up." … "They need to be able to adjust this permission system easily. These restrictions are more suited for something close to completion." Chosen: development still asks only before money moves ("sending funds/payments, Iceman live trading, deleting wallet or chain data"); all four repos switch now.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the rebuild repo's AI sessions need the same gate, with money-moving and wallet/chain-data deletion always asking.

class: gate reports clean when it could not run (fail-open)
what_happened: The repo's dependency audit printed a stderr line and exited 0 ("clean") when cargo audit or npm audit failed to run; live, the committed script with cargo off the PATH printed "dep-audit clean", exit 0. It also had a hidden `cargo install cargo-audit` side effect.
root_cause: Tool and network failures were caught and logged but never changed the exit code.
lesson: A security gate must distinguish clean (0), findings (1) and could-not-audit (2), list every part not audited, and never report clean when a tool, a network source, a malformed answer or a lockfile-coverage check failed; a missing tool fails loudly with its install command.
tripwire: scripts/dep-audit/run.test.js: 20 hermetic black-box tests of the real CLI with fake cargo/npm on PATH and a fake OSV on localhost (pass in a loopback-only network namespace), 13 of 15 red on the committed script, npm's real failure JSON captured from npm 10; run on every push in ci.yml. Live: DEP_AUDIT_OSV_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9 and cargo off PATH both give exit 2 "NOT audited".
owner_decision: "fix the audit as well" (2026-09-28)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the rebuild needs a dependency gate that cannot pass silently.

class: one advisory database treated as the whole truth
what_happened: The audit read only RustSec (cargo audit) while GitHub's advisory database had yamux, jsonwebtoken, openssl and serde_with advisories RustSec lacked; it dropped cargo-audit warnings (hiding unsound RUSTSEC-2026-0221 in event-listener, compiled into the control plane) and allowlisted only by exact RUSTSEC id.
root_cause: The gate trusted a single scanner and filtered out its warnings.
lesson: Dependency auditing must query a merged source (OSV: RustSec + GHSA) for each exact locked version alongside the native tool, print one line per advisory merged across aliases, allowlist by any alias with a recorded reachability reason, fail on "unsound" as well as vulnerabilities (unmaintained/yanked as notices), and print allowlist entries that matched nothing.
tripwire: Same run.test.js suite (merge-once, allowlist by alias, unsound is a finding, stale entries, coverage); first real run surfaced the yamux GHSA (allowlisted with reachability evidence) and event-listener was bumped 5.4.1 -> 5.4.2 and redeployed. Stated cost: crate names and versions go to api.osv.dev.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's Rust/JS dependencies need the same merged view.

class: status check reads a stale CI run
what_happened: smoke.sh check 9 read a stale CI run from GitHub several times (August cleanup/main runs 7e53e3cf, 29878dbc, 93ef5797), turning the gate falsely GREEN once and falsely RED twice; it recurred in later records.
root_cause: The check accepted whatever run GitHub's API listed without confirming that run's commit belongs to the branch being checked.
lesson: A gate that cites CI status must confirm the cited run's commit is the current commit (or in its history) and treat anything else as not proven.
tripwire: Proposed to the owner, not built: check that the cited run's commit is in the branch's history.
applies_to_new_node: yes — any CI-status check in the rebuild's smoke/gate.

class: test lock identifies tests by file name only
what_happened: The fix-lock made tests read-only by file glob (tests/*, *_test.rs), but Rust keeps most unit tests inline in #[cfg(test)] modules (132 of rikurinode's 222 .rs files), so a session could still edit the very test meant to prove a fix; it was first noticed in 2026-09-28-repairs-outlive-the-request.md and 2026-09-28-runtime-alerts-round-two.md (auth tests).
root_cause: A gate that knows a test by its file name cannot see tests kept beside the code.
lesson: A test-immutability lock must cover in-source test regions (from the first test marker to end of file, plus attribute/comment lines attached above it), refuse added, removed or changed lines that make production code behave differently under test (cfg(test), cfg!(test), cfg_attr(test, …), not(not(test)), assert-macro shadows), deny shell writes to any covered file, deny when a file cannot be read, and only ever add denies while a lock is engaged.
tripwire: test_guard.py InlineTests (20 tests on a synthetic config; 45 in all), config worked examples (92 in rikurinode), planted regressions each round; verifier compared 36,728-36,888 unlocked decisions against HEAD with 0 differences; live hook refused an Edit inside mod repair_lifetime_tests.
owner_decision: "Ok for fix to the gurad" (2026-09-28)
applies_to_new_node: yes — any language with in-source tests in the rebuild needs this coverage.

class: pre-execution hook models the tool's effect inexactly
what_happened: Seven verifier rounds found ways the guard's simulation of an Edit differed from Claude Code's Edit tool: loose matching (curly quotes, unicode escapes) applied edits the guard judged no-ops; a deletion also swallows the next newline and can join the marker onto the line above; lone CR vs universal newlines; blank-file detection by JS trim() vs Python strip() (U+FEFF).
root_cause: The hook simulated edits with its own assumptions instead of the tool's actual algorithm.
lesson: A hook that judges a tool call must model the tool's exact behaviour where it matters, check every plausible outcome when unsure, deny when it cannot model the outcome (no exact match, non-UTF-8, unreadable), and be re-verified after every tool upgrade.
tripwire: test_the_edit_tool_is_modelled_exactly, test_an_empty_old_string_is_judged_both_ways, test_crlf_is_folded_as_the_tool_does; verifier harnesses ran the tool's own code; re-check procedure for Claude Code upgrades recorded (2.1.221 function names).
applies_to_new_node: maybe — only if the rebuild repo keeps the same AI-session guard.

class: pattern-based tripwire cannot see every disguised switch-off
what_happened: Accepted as the limit of a tripwire: an attribute trailing on the code line above the marker, an inner #![cfg(any())], multi-line cfg attributes, a bare #[test] fn outside a cfg(test) module, cfg!(debug_assertions), [lib] test = false, runtime test detection, and 31 shell write forms (other redirects, wrappers, sed -Ei, git apply/stash/reset, cargo fmt …) that reach test files.
root_cause: A line- and regex-based rule cannot enumerate every way the language and the shell can disable or rewrite tests.
lesson: Fix verification must compare the "N passed" count before and after a fix (a switch-off shows as a drop), and cheats that keep the count unchanged must be caught by review; the lock is a tripwire, not a wall.
tripwire: Procedure docs require the before/after "N passed" comparison; known gaps listed in the guard docstring ("Bash matching is a tripwire, not a wall") and the record's Skipped list.
applies_to_new_node: yes — process rule for verifying fixes in the rebuild.

class: evidence judged through a truncated view
what_happened: The survey claimed "all 133 uses in rikurinode are exactly #[cfg(test)]", but head had cut one off (commerce-service/src/registry/reviews.rs:409, #[cfg(any(test, feature = "test-helpers"))]). Test runs in this batch also hung when `| head` closed jest's pipe, and `pkill -f` matched its own shell (2026-09-29-btc-price-exchanges-first.md).
root_cause: Conclusions were drawn from truncated output, and piping into head changed the behaviour of the command under test.
lesson: Evidence must be counted by a script over the full output, never judged through head, and test output must go to a file rather than into a truncating pipe.
tripwire: CLAUDE.md line "Count evidence with a script; never judge it through head" (process rule; the head-pipe hang was repeated once after the line was written).
applies_to_new_node: yes — process rule.

class: work tied to the lifetime of the request that asked for it
what_happened: The Tor onion repair (RB-TOR-ONION-RECOVER-01) was cut off at exactly 2:00 on 09-24 and 09-28 when the dashboard's 120 s fetch gave up; the control plane ran the repair inside the HTTP handler with kill_on_drop, so the script was killed and no decision row, outcome or notification was written (on 09-24 it had already restarted Tor). 43 runbooks could outlast the 2-minute wait.
root_cause: The control plane executed repairs inside the request handler, so the caller's patience decided whether a repair finished; it also held the shared app-state read lock for the whole repair.
lesson: Once accepted, a repair must run to completion in a task detached from the HTTP caller and always write its decision, outcome and notification; a panic inside it must come back as an error, and shared locks must be released before the long work starts.
tripwire: repair_lifetime_tests (inline in control-plane/src/http_server.rs): work not cancelled with the caller, a panic returned as an error (2 red on the old helper). Live: the real runbook submitted and hung up after 5 s completed and recorded decision 29536. Gap: the handlers' use of the helper is not pinned (a handler-bypass mutation survived).
owner_decision: "Let's fix the tor onion." (2026-09-28)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's repair engine must decouple execution from callers.

class: cancellable request leaves LND stopped
what_happened: The verifier found POST /v1/backup/channeldb/now stops LND, copies channel.db and starts LND inside the request, so a hang-up mid-copy left LND stopped.
root_cause: Same class as the repair: a multi-step operation that stops a funds service ran in the request's lifetime.
lesson: Any operation that stops LND (a channel.db backup or otherwise) must run detached from its caller and must always bring LND back up, whatever happens to the request.
tripwire: now_handler moved onto run_to_completion (covered by the helper's tests and review); not triggered live because it would stop LND. Should exist: a test that cancels the request mid-copy and asserts LND is running again.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node will back up channel state; LND left stopped is a funds-availability incident.

class: every kind of no-answer reported as the same failure
what_happened: The dashboard's submitProposal returned null for a timeout, a refused connection and an HTTP error alike, logging "Control plane unreachable — self-heal degraded to notify-only" and recording the runbook as "not submitted" while the control plane was healthy and the repair still running.
root_cause: The client collapsed distinct failure modes into one value.
lesson: A client must classify a missing answer (still running: timed out while /health is OK; unreachable; HTTP error), report each truthfully, record a started repair as an attempt, and never blame the server for a job that is still running; approvals that time out report approved-and-running if the proposal is no longer pending.
tripwire: repairStillRunning.test.ts (12) and approvalRoundTrip.test.ts additions: 17 red on the old code; live: 0 "Control plane unreachable" lines after the restart.
applies_to_new_node: yes — every client of the new node's control plane.

class: removing a timeout exposes concurrent duplicate runs
what_happened: Once repairs could run past 2:00, a ~12 min Tor repair would overlap the monitoring loop's re-fire at ~10 min; the cooldown is stamped only when a run ends, so two copies could run at once (the verifier caught this regression).
root_cause: The old timeout kill had been an accidental concurrency limit.
lesson: The repair executor must allow one in-flight run per runbook and target, refuse a second as "already running" (not counted as an attempt), and release the slot on every end including cancellation.
tripwire: In-flight guard tests in execute_runbook (red then green); NEVER_STARTED vocabulary treats the refusal as not an attempt; live: two overlapping Tor submits, decision 29540 refused "already running", 29541 completed.
applies_to_new_node: yes — any long-running repair in the new node.

class: client wait longer than a proxy's timeout
what_happened: Approvals through the nginx vhost on :3002/ryzen.local are cut at 60 s while the approval path waited 120 s (the owner would see HTTP 504); before the fix, dashboard and Telegram approvals used a 45 s axios timeout that killed long approved repairs and told the owner they failed.
root_cause: Timeouts were chosen per layer without checking the layers in front of it.
lesson: Every client wait must be shorter than every proxy timeout in front of it, and a wait that ends first must report "still running", not failure.
tripwire: APPROVAL_WAIT_MS = 40 s (+5 s pending check); fake-timer test answers before 50 s (red then green).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's UI behind a reverse proxy.

class: notification or approval failure swallowed
what_happened: Telegram approval edits were sent as MarkdownV2 with the original text unescaped, so Telegram rejected them and the error was swallowed; separately, drbIntegration.syncRustProposalStatus approves with no owner or API token, is always refused, and logs it only at debug (pre-existing, not fixed).
root_cause: Send and approve failures were caught without being surfaced.
lesson: Every notification and approval call must escape text for the channel's format and surface its failure; a refusal logged only at debug level counts as a silent failure.
tripwire: Escaping tests for the approve and deny edits (red then green). The drbIntegration sibling and heartbeat.submitToRust (45 s axios, timeout reported as "Failed to submit proposal") recorded, not fixed.
applies_to_new_node: yes — owner notifications are the node's alert channel.

class: security control documented but never tested
what_happened: verify_token had no tests; writing them showed the control plane accepted a JWT with no iss although a comment promised an issuer pin (set_issuer checks iss only when present). The jsonwebtoken advisory GHSA-h395-gr6q-cpjc (nbf/exp of the wrong JSON type treated as absent) was reproduced in the shipped 9.3.1 (not exploitable here: HS256 with a server-held secret, exp required).
root_cause: The auth path relied on library defaults that validate a claim only when present, and nothing tested refusals.
lesson: Token verification must require exp and iss (set_required_spec_claims), and refusal tests plus a real issue-then-verify round trip must exist before any auth-library upgrade, each shown red on the old code and green on the new; prefer a crypto backend already in the build (jsonwebtoken 10.4 with aws_lc_rs, the library TLS uses) over a second stack.
tripwire: 13 tests in control-plane/src/auth.rs auth::tests (refusals; register -> login -> verify_session round trip); a 4-variant table (9.3.1/10.4 x with/without the code change) shows each test fixed by what it claims; the session-row check mutation-proven; live POST /v1/auth/verify refuses bad tokens.
owner_decision: "Ok yes" (2026-09-28), to: fix openssl and serde_with, upgrade jsonwebtoken properly with auth tests, record yamux as unreachable, and prove-then-remove ai-orchestrator.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the rebuilt backend's auth must be test-pinned before any library change.

class: test build overwrites production artifacts
what_happened: `cargo test --release --workspace` rebuilt the target/release binaries as test-feature builds (control-plane, node-watchdog and commerce-service hashes changed), which the deploy steps and install-node-watchdog.sh would then have installed.
root_cause: Tests and production builds shared one output directory.
lesson: Production artifacts must be built in a dedicated step immediately before install (or in a separate build, e.g. the image build) and verified by hash, never taken from a directory a test run writes into.
tripwire: Production binaries rebuilt last and their sha256 recorded before install; proposed: deploy steps run cargo build --release immediately before installing.
applies_to_new_node: yes — image builds for the new node must not reuse test-build artifacts.

class: dead prototypes kept in the tree generate alerts
what_happened: dashboard/ai-orchestrator (a 2025 Python prototype) carried 4 Dependabot alerts with zero references, no container, unit or process; the first deadness proof grepped only the folder name and missed "AI Orchestrator … default 8000" port reservations in two port scripts (found by the verifier). node-agent was also a stale, unrun binary with no issuer pin and no tests.
root_cause: Prototypes and unrun services were never retired, and the deadness proof searched one name only.
lesson: Unused services and prototypes must be retired, and proof of deadness must search every name a component goes by (folder, product name, env vars, ports, units, processes) before deletion.
tripwire: Repo-wide grep including Python imports, the product name and the env var; bash -n on edited scripts.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the clean rebuild should not carry prototypes or unrun services.

class: scheduled security gate silently never runs
what_happened: The weekly dep-audit.yml existed only on cleanup/main, but GitHub runs scheduled workflows only from the default branch (pro-ai-agent, 326 commits behind), so it had never run once (GitHub answered 404); Dependabot scanned the same stale branch and showed 315 alerts describing two-month-old code.
root_cause: The deployed branch was not the default branch and nothing checked that the gate had actually run.
lesson: The deployed branch must be the repository's default branch, and every scheduled gate must be monitored for a recent successful run; absence of a run is itself an alert.
tripwire: Proposed smoke check "the weekly dep-audit has a run in the last 8 days" (not made; needs the owner). The owner switched the default branch; GitHub then listed "Dependency audit".
owner_decision: "Yes, go ahead with both 1 and 2 first" (2026-09-28) — (1) make cleanup/main the default branch, (2) fix the real runtime list as one tracked change.
applies_to_new_node: yes — CI for the rebuild must prove its scheduled gates run.

class: vulnerability signal diluted by dead and non-runtime lockfiles
what_happened: 315 alerts were 217 flaws in 58 packages across 14 lockfiles, 166 in build/test tools; control-plane/Cargo.lock and node-agent/Cargo.lock were read by nothing (workspace members use the root lock) yet carried 40 + 15 alerts; none of the 3 criticals was in code running on the node.
root_cause: Stale lockfiles and non-runtime tooling sat in the scanned tree, mixing dead code with live code.
lesson: The repo must contain only lockfiles that are actually built, audits must be scoped to runtime dependencies of code the node runs, and every unfixable finding must be triaged with reachability evidence on an allowlist; fixes use pinned overrides and patch bumps, not npm audit fix --force.
tripwire: dep-audit gate exit 0 with the allowlist fingerprinted (sha256 unchanged); cargo metadata proof that member lockfiles were unread; npm audit --omit=dev per project.
applies_to_new_node: yes — keep the rebuild's lockfiles minimal and audited.

class: running binary lags source; a security rebuild ships unrelated changes
what_happened: The running commerce-service binary dated from 2026-07-12; a fresh build for the dependency fixes also shipped c276611d (libp2p 0.54 -> 0.56, sqlx default-features = false), which had passed CI but never run on the node. node-watchdog and commerce-service needed the owner's sudo to reinstall.
root_cause: Services were installed by hand and not redeployed when their source changed.
lesson: Running services must be rebuilt and redeployed from current source routinely so a security rebuild never carries months of untested changes; when it does, those changes are disclosed to the owner before install and a rollback artifact is kept.
tripwire: Installed binaries compared with target/release and checked for fixed crate versions; rollback kept at /usr/local/bin/commerce-service.pre-2026-09-28; journals checked for 0 errors after restart.
applies_to_new_node: yes — images with automatic OS rollback cover rollback, but drift between running images and source still needs a check.

class: major upgrade risk understated by its BREAKING note
what_happened: nodemailer 9 -> 10 (needed for one moderate advisory) was first described as only "Node 20 or newer", but 10.0.0 is a full TypeScript rewrite with separate ESM and CommonJS builds; rustls 0.23.45 forced aws-lc-sys 0.40 -> 0.45. The verifier caught both.
root_cause: Only the BREAKING section of the changelog was read.
lesson: A major or forced transitive upgrade on an owner-alert or TLS path must be read in full and proven live on the real path (an SMTP transporter.verify() that authenticates and sends nothing, a real gRPC request, TLS refreshes), and direct-dependency floors must be raised so a lock regeneration cannot fall back to a vulnerable version.
tripwire: Live: SMTP verify PASS (authenticated, nothing sent) on nodemailer 10.0.12; gRPC HTTP/2 200 grpc-status 12; TLS threat-feed refreshes after restart; floors ^2.4.0, ^10.0.12, ^1.12.1, ^17.13.8.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's alert channel and TLS stack.

class: reverse-proxy vhost missing the websocket route
what_happened: socket.io live updates handshake on :5000, via the IP on :80 and on rikuri.local, but configs/nginx/ryzen.conf (serving :3002 and ryzen.local) has no /socket.io location, so live updates never worked on those URLs; browser console handshake errors recurred in later records.
root_cause: Two nginx configs diverged and only one routed websockets.
lesson: Every vhost that serves the UI must route its websocket path, and smoke must perform a websocket/socket.io handshake through each served URL.
tripwire: Manual polling handshake per URL (evidence log). Should exist: a per-vhost handshake check in smoke. Not fixed (nginx install needs the owner's sudo).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's UI will sit behind a reverse proxy.

class: stale value served as live after its only source failed
what_happened: The owner saw 84,346 while Kraken, Coinbase and mempool.space showed ~83,2xx. CoinGecko, the only live source, had refused the node for ~10 h (810 x HTTP 403, then 429); priceService served its last good value (about 4.6 h old) with no age limit, still flagged live: true.
root_cause: A single-source fetch fell back to its cache silently, with no freshness model.
lesson: Every externally sourced value must carry its source, the source's own timestamp, age and a stale flag; it is "live" only within a stated limit (10 min, one env knob), is shown as stale after that, is served as explicitly unavailable when none exists, an older value from a fallback never replaces a newer one, and the owner is alerted (PRICE_FEED_STALE) when it stays stale.
tripwire: priceService.test.ts (26 of 58 red first), PriceFreshness.test.tsx, priceFeedStale.test.ts (evaluator) and the issueClassification row; drill with Kraken and Coinbase refused showed mempool's price marked stale with every source's error. The Guardian alert path was not triggered live.
owner_decision: "rikurinode's Bitcoin price on Bitcoin section is wrong (showing 84,346, instead of 83,260). Are we not connected to the source or is the source compromised?" Chosen: "Exchanges first (Recommended)" — Kraken, then Coinbase, then the node's own mempool.
applies_to_new_node: yes — any external figure the new node shows needs source, age and stale handling.

class: hardcoded placeholder substituted for a missing external value
what_happened: The pricing advisor (L402 sat-anchor suggestions) fetched CoinGecko itself and silently used 100,000 on failure; the AI fee explanation also used a silent 100,000; in round 2 one L402 input in USD mode with no price showed sats labelled "USD" and saved typed dollars as sats.
root_cause: Each reader had its own fallback that invented a value instead of refusing.
lesson: No reader may substitute a made-up number for a missing price: it refuses (HTTP 503 naming the explicit override parameter), omits the derived figure, or falls back to sats clearly labelled; USD-to-sats conversions refuse while the price is stale.
tripwire: btcPriceReaders.test.ts; endpointPrice helper ("sats *" with a tooltip); L402 headless check with the price forced stale; stale price reads as 0 so existing L402 zero-guards refuse. Residual: FALLBACK_BTC_USD = 100_000 still feeds channelAnalyticsService break-even before any price arrives (flagged not live).
applies_to_new_node: yes — any sats/fiat conversion on the new node (fees, L402 or channel economics) must refuse on a stale price.

class: assistant presents stale data as current
what_happened: The AI knowledge store saved the stale price stamped with the time of saving, so the assistant presented it as current; after the first fix the assistant still called an old saved row "Current Bitcoin Price" with no date, printed market cap and volume beside it, and printed a missing 24h change as "+0.00%".
root_cause: The store recorded save time instead of the value's own time, and the answer templates had no stale branch.
lesson: The assistant's knowledge store must save only live values with their own timestamp and real source, and every answer must name source and time, say STALE with date and age for an old row, drop dependent figures beside a stale value, and print a missing figure as absent, not zero.
tripwire: btcPriceReaders tests (stale saved row says STALE with date and "4 h ago", not "Current"; no market cap/volume beside a stale price; change stored as null); verifier ran the real dist direct answer, tool context and system prompt.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant reads node data through tools; freshness must travel with every value it reads.

class: retry without backoff keeps a rate limit in force
what_happened: priceService retried CoinGecko on every request with no backoff, which kept the 403/429 refusal in force; a slow CoinGecko could also delay the price by up to 8 s.
root_cause: No per-source failure state, no shared in-flight refresh, and secondary fetches awaited inline with the primary.
lesson: Each external source must have its own backoff (1 min doubling to 30 min, honouring Retry-After), concurrent callers share one in-flight refresh, failures retry only after their backoff, and secondary data never delays the primary value beyond a short cap (1.5 s; 5 s source timeout).
tripwire: priceService backoff test (catches a backoff that does not double) and slow-CoinGecko test; live journal "coingecko failed (HTTP 429); not asking it again for 60 s"; verifier saw FX/CoinGecko retries at 60/120/240/480 s.
applies_to_new_node: yes — every outbound poller on the new node.

class: sibling sweep misses browser and AI readers of the same source
what_happened: The first fix covered the backend only; the verifier found the browser still called CoinGecko directly (useLocalCurrency for the local-currency line and L402/marketplace conversions) and the AI path lacked source and time, needing two more rounds; Fear & Greed and the chart fallback still go from the browser to third parties (out of scope, stated).
root_cause: The sweep for callers of the external source searched backend code only.
lesson: When fixing an external data source, sweep backend, frontend and every reader of the saved value (including the assistant), and route third-party calls through the node so the owner's browser never contacts them directly.
tripwire: Playwright network log showed no browser CoinGecko calls; record lesson-loop rule: "for an external source, sweep backend AND frontend, and every reader of the saved value".
applies_to_new_node: yes — privacy and consistency rule for the new node's UI.

class: metric labelled with a different window than its source field
what_happened: Kraken's ticker "o" is the open since 00:00 UTC, not 24 h ago, so the 24h change needed OHLC candles; hourly candles made the figure jump each hour and were replaced by 5-minute candles; a source with no 24h change used to show "0.00 %" in red.
root_cause: Each source field's semantics were not checked against the label shown.
lesson: Each displayed figure must come from a source field whose semantics match its label (a true rolling 24 h from fine candles), and a figure a source lacks must be hidden, never shown as zero.
tripwire: Test for 5-minute candles; verifier matched Kraken's 5-minute candles with the live figure; the 24h change hidden when a source has none.
applies_to_new_node: maybe — only if the new node shows market data.

class: third-party dependency for a figure the node can compute
what_happened: CoinGecko answered HTTP 403 to the node and the owner found it unreliable; market cap was replaced by price x issued supply computed from the node's own block height through the exact subsidy schedule (20,091,275 BTC at block 969,207, matching CoinPaprika within 0.001%), and 24h volume by spot volume on Kraken + Coinbase + Bitstamp.
root_cause: Market cap had been fetched from an aggregator although the supply follows exactly from the chain.
lesson: Figures derivable from the node's own chain must be computed locally: issued supply from GetBlockSubsidy in whole satoshis summed to height max(blocks, headers), only on mainnet, with the reason stated when unavailable ("not_mainnet" / "no_height"), and marked stale together with the price they depend on.
tripwire: btcSupply.test.ts; the verifier recomputed the supply at 16 heights and matched the node height against three sources; drill with CoinGecko blocked changed nothing; the no-height path seen in a separate process.
owner_decision: "Market cap and 24h volume: CoinGeko doesn't seem reliable. It goes down sometimes, same thing happens for CoinGeko app on its smartphone app. Any alternative?" Chosen: "Computed on the node (Recommended)" for market cap and "Regulated exchanges only" for 24h volume.
applies_to_new_node: yes — works on the pruned Pi 5 node too, since only the height is needed.

class: partial aggregate presented as the whole
what_happened: The verifier found a fresh partial 24h volume read "Kraken + Bitstamp" with Coinbase (~58% of the three) silently missing, while the RAG claimed the card named the missing exchange; 2026-09-29-market-intel-freshness-arkb.md had the same class (a 10-session ETF sum skipping missing days under a whole-window label).
root_cause: The missing-component state was surfaced only once the whole aggregate went stale.
lesson: An aggregate missing any component must be labelled partial, naming the missing component and its error in a warning style, and a sum over a window must read unavailable if any period is missing; it is never shown as the complete figure.
tripwire: Freshness.partial tests (key dataPartial, 5 locales); drill with Bitstamp blocked showed a labelled two-venue volume with last_error naming Bitstamp; page render in the warning style.
applies_to_new_node: maybe — wherever the new node shows multi-source aggregates.

class: cold fallback never exercised until the primary fails
what_happened: The ETF-flow issuer fallback (IBIT/FBTC snapshots) ran only while Farside was down, so the first session of an outage could get no estimate; once kept warm, the verifier found its failures were silent (FBTC daily, Yahoo refusing its price) and a long Farside outage left a false backup alarm on the books.
root_cause: The backup path had no schedule and no success bookkeeping of its own.
lesson: A fallback must run on a schedule while the primary works (here at most once per 12 h), persist its own last attempt, last success and last error, alert only when the fallback itself has failed for a stated period (IBIT not captured for 3 days), clear that state when the fallback succeeds, and never overwrite primary data.
tripwire: etfWarmSnapshots.test.ts; warm_attempted_at / warm_ok_at / warm_error bookkeeping; etfBackupProblem() 3-day rule drilled across a weekend and a Monday holiday with no false report.
owner_decision: "1. Ok" (2026-09-29), approving keeping the ETF issuer fallback warm (cost stated: one extra headless-browser visit to iShares and etfdb plus a Yahoo call per day).
applies_to_new_node: maybe — the warm-standby rule applies to any fallback on the new node (e.g. secondary backup targets), market intel only if rebuilt.

class: knowledge answer buried in a large chunk
what_happened: The RAG did not answer "why is the volume so low": the answer sat inside a long "What it does now" chunk and Chroma returned the Privacy and "Why this exists" chunks; giving market cap and volume their own section plus question-shaped entries made all three owner-style questions return them first.
root_cause: Docs were written for reading, not for chunked retrieval.
lesson: Assistant knowledge docs must be split into short, question-shaped sections, and retrieval must be checked with owner-style questions after each change.
tripwire: Retrieval checks of owner-style questions against Chroma after re-index (new sections first); rag:build chunk counts.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant will rely on retrieval.

class: silent staleness; expiry deletes the last value
what_happened: Market Intelligence metrics (Fear & Greed, MAs, returns, funding, ETF flows, treasuries, credit) each came from one source; a failed refresh wrote one log line, the card kept the old value (2 of 7 showed an age, none marked stale), and after 3x TTL the row was deleted so the card read "No data yet", which looks like "never fetched". No Guardian alert existed.
root_cause: Refreshers had no success/failure bookkeeping, and the cleanup treated age as garbage.
lesson: Each feed must record success (with source) or failure (with reason); it is stale after 2x its refresh interval or when the data's own date is too old; the last value is kept and marked stale, never deleted; one Guardian entry names every stale metric with its age and error and closes when all are fresh.
tripwire: marketFeeds.test.ts, marketIntelFreshness and marketDataStale tests (MARKET_DATA_STALE); forced-stale drill (funding 45 min, ETF data 6 days) raised one finding naming both; all fresh -> none.
owner_decision: "Do we need fallback for other existing Market Intelligence? Can we know if data can't be updated or go stale?" Chosen: "Stale data: page + Guardian alert (Recommended)".
applies_to_new_node: yes — the same freshness model applies to every node-side feed and status figure.

class: non-answer stored as fresh data
what_happened: Fear & Greed never checked the HTTP status, and funding saved "unavailable" with a fresh timestamp when Kraken lacked the rate; the verifier also found manual ETF pastes accepted malformed dates (which never age) and future dates (which stay fresh).
root_cause: Responses and inputs were not validated before being stored as current.
lesson: A failed, empty or malformed fetch or input is a failure and is never stored with a fresh timestamp; dates entering the system are validated (YYYY-MM-DD, a real calendar day, not after today UTC).
tripwire: Tests for the HTTP status check and funding-without-rate as a failure; manual-paste validation (4 refusal cases + 1 accept) returns 400.
applies_to_new_node: yes — every node-side fetcher and input route.

class: incomplete upstream row parsed as real data
what_happened: At 21:36 UTC Farside listed Sep 29 with every fund blank and Total "0.0", which showed "All ETFs +0.0" and counted a 0 into the 5-session total; at 22:17 UTC the row had small funds at 0.0 while IBIT, FBTC and ARKB were still "-", and the card said "data of 2026-09-29". Three history rows written by these intermediate builds were deleted by id.
root_cause: The scraper treated a not-yet-reported session as data and blank as zero.
lesson: Scraped or upstream rows are accepted only when every required field has reported; blanks and placeholders are never zero.
tripwire: parseFarsideTable tests: a dated all-blank row is skipped; a session is taken only once IBIT, FBTC and ARKB have all reported (each red first).
applies_to_new_node: maybe — any scraped source on the new node.

class: timestamp semantics differ between sources (off-by-one day)
what_happened: A live drill refilling blocked days from Kraken showed each blockchain.info point stamped D equals Kraken's close of D-1 (it is the 00:00 UTC price), so the daily-close archive labelled every close a day late, dropped the newest complete point as "today's partial", and the Kraken seam skipped a day; the locked test had encoded the wrong assumption.
root_cause: Point-in-time prices were assumed to be that day's close without checking a second source.
lesson: Each source's timestamp semantics (point-in-time vs period close) must be established against an independent source before series are merged, and tests must use the real data shape.
tripwire: btcDailyCloses.test.ts corrected to the real shape (red 1499 != 1500); re-drill matched Kraken closes within $0-8 on 5 days and fallback MAs equal primary ones exactly (20D 80,684).
applies_to_new_node: maybe — if the new node computes MAs or returns.

class: delta computed against an arbitrarily old baseline
what_happened: The ETF issuer fallback (flowRowsFromSnapshots) compared against the last stored snapshot however old: IBIT's was from 09-15, so a 14-day asset change would have shown as one day's flow.
root_cause: Nothing checked that the baseline was the immediately previous period.
lesson: A per-period delta must be computed only against the immediately previous period; across a gap it is null, never the accumulated change presented as one period.
tripwire: Test (red first) that a flow is computed only against the previous session (the next weekday).
applies_to_new_node: maybe — any per-period figure on the new node (e.g. daily fee income, flow rates).

class: single-source metric without a labelled fallback
what_happened: MAs and rolling returns came only from blockchain.info and funding only from Kraken Futures; fallbacks were added: a persisted daily-close archive (atomic JSON, ~5,900 days) refreshed from blockchain.info with Kraken daily candles filling gaps (one fetch now serves both MAs and returns), and Deribit BTC-PERPETUAL funding labelled as a different venue.
root_cause: Each metric depended on one external service with no local history.
lesson: Each important feed must have a fallback source and, where possible, persisted local history written atomically so an outage loses nothing; the label must name the source actually used (another venue's rate is never passed off as the primary's).
tripwire: fundingRate.test.ts and btcDailyCloses tests; drills on the deployed dist: blockchain.info blocked -> "blockchain.info archive + kraken" with all 4 MAs; Kraken Futures blocked -> "deribit"; both blocked -> throws with both reasons.
owner_decision: AskUserQuestion choices (2026-09-29): "MAs + returns backup: Kraken daily candles, plus the node's own daily-close archive"; "funding: a second venue (Deribit, labelled)".
applies_to_new_node: maybe — only if market intelligence is rebuilt.

class: fixed display columns based on outdated activity
what_happened: The owner noticed GBTC barely moved; Farside's last 13 sessions showed ARKB gross 605 US$M vs GBTC 125 and BITB 72, so the fixed columns became IBIT/FBTC/ARKB, the Total became Farside's all-ETF Total, and the weekly all-ETF figure is null unless every one of the last 5 sessions has a Total. Dead ETF code (refreshEtfFlowsFromYahoo, refreshEtfFlows, parseFarsideEtfFlows, the fetch-farside route that Cloudflare always blocked, scrapeGbtc) was removed after proving no callers.
root_cause: Display choices made earlier were never revisited against current data.
lesson: Displayed selections must be chosen from measured activity and revisited, and totals must come from the source's own all-items figure, not a partial sum.
tripwire: etfFlows tests (Farside columns found by logo, Total by header); all 10 ETF sessions matched Farside scraped independently by the verifier.
owner_decision: "Need to replace GBTC as top 3 ETF, I think. There isn't much movement visible from GBTC. Looks like BITB or ARKB should be substituted." Chosen: "ARKB (Recommended)" and Total "all spot ETFs (Recommended)".
applies_to_new_node: maybe — product content; only if market intelligence is rebuilt.

class: flaky hardware at boot with no automatic, visible recovery
what_happened: After the 2026-09-29 power outage the Intel AX200 Bluetooth adapter (USB 5-1) failed its firmware load at two boots (hci0 address 00:00:00:00:00:00, DOWN; the kernel's own btusb re-register failed the same); writing 0 then 1 to the device's USB "authorized" attribute revived it. The old local fix never worked: its unit pointed at a deleted path (203/EXEC) and set -e exited before its remedy (a driver reload, which also fails).
root_cause: Intermittent firmware-load failure of the USB Bluetooth chip at boot, and a workaround that lived outside the repo, untested and silently broken.
lesson: Host-hardware recovery must be an in-repo, tested boot oneshot that waits for the device to settle before judging, touches only the affected device, retries a bounded number of times, always restores the device on exit (EXIT trap, write before log), never overrides the owner's rfkill switch, reports REVIVED / failed / unreadable visibly (unit state, a verdict file, smoke WARN since Bluetooth is not node-critical), and can be disabled with one command.
tripwire: bluetoothRevive.test.ts: 12 cases through the real script with fake sysfs and fake hciconfig (RIKURI_SYSFS, HCICONFIG), including killed mid-disconnect via timeout(1); smoke WARN line. Record status IN PROGRESS: no live run and no verifier yet, and the committed script (checked 2026-10-10) lacks the review fixes in the next entries, so it is not a port candidate as is.
owner_decision: "Bluetooth is not working at all, can't even turn it on. This is a recurring issue." then "Yes, build a boot service and reauthorize auto in rikurinode repo." (2026-09-30)
applies_to_new_node: maybe — hardware-specific (AX200 on the old x86 host); the Pi 5 and new x86 hardware differ, but the recovery-oneshot pattern applies to any flaky device.

class: detector and fixture cannot see the failure state
what_happened: The first detector found adapters only through their USB interfaces, but a de-authorized device has no interfaces in sysfs, so the "left de-authorized" state the exit trap guards against would read "no USB Bluetooth adapter — nothing to do"; the planned fake-sysfs fixture kept the interfaces and would have passed anyway.
root_cause: The test fixture modelled the device's healthy shape, not its failure shape.
lesson: Test fixtures for a recovery path must model the failure state exactly as the kernel presents it (device-level class kept, interfaces removed), and the regression must be shown failing on the old detector.
tripwire: Test "a de-authorized adapter (no interfaces left in sysfs) is still found and authorized again"; restoring the interface-only detector gives 1 failed, 11 passed.
applies_to_new_node: yes — any recovery logic in the new node needs failure-shaped fixtures.

class: self-declared device identity used as a trust gate
what_happened: Review found that treating any de-authorized Bluetooth-class device as stuck would, at boot, authorize devices a USB policy (usbguard, authorized_default=0) had deliberately left de-authorized; one Bluetooth interface marked a whole combined Wi-Fi+Bluetooth dongle for reset (possibly the node's network link, three times); a blacklisted btusb read as "no controller", causing ~99 s of resets every boot.
root_cause: USB class codes are self-declared, and the script reasoned about the whole device from one interface and from the absence of a driver.
lesson: A root recovery script must re-authorize only devices it de-authorized itself (a tmpfs marker cleared each boot), leave policy-de-authorized devices HELD, never reset a device with any non-target interface, and treat "no driver bound" as switched off, not stuck.
tripwire: All three findings accepted with tests planned; the rework was parked in the session scratchpad because another session's fix-lock refused the matching test update. A grep of the committed scripts/rikuri-bluetooth-revive.sh (2026-10-10) found no HELD, marker or NOT-reset logic.
applies_to_new_node: yes — any root hardware-recovery helper on the new node must respect USB authorization policy and multi-function devices.

class: best-effort boot unit holds the boot target
what_happened: Review nit: a oneshot after bluetooth.service would delay multi-user.target while a stuck adapter is retried, because targets add After= to the units they want unless DefaultDependencies=no.
root_cause: Default systemd ordering of target-wanted units.
lesson: Best-effort boot repair units must not hold multi-user.target: DefaultDependencies=no, a bounded TimeoutStartSec, After= the service they repair and no Wants= pulling it in.
tripwire: The committed systemd/rikuri-bluetooth-revive.service has DefaultDependencies=no and TimeoutStartSec=300 (checked 2026-10-10). Should exist: a boot-time check that multi-user.target is reached within a bound.
applies_to_new_node: yes — with automatic OS rollback on the new node, a unit that delays boot could interfere with boot health checks.

class: one global test lock shared by parallel sessions
what_happened: Another session's fix-lock (for 2026-09-30-reliability-uptime-truth.md) made every test file read-only and blocked this record's new test; later a second lock (for 2026-09-30-dashboard-measurements.md) refused the matching test update, so the reworked script was reverted to keep the other session's gate green. The dep-audit and inline-tests records also handed one lock back and forth.
root_cause: The fix-lock is a single repository-wide state file, not scoped to a change.
