lesson: Test-immutability locks must be scoped to the change (its files or record) so parallel work is not blocked, and a session must never release another session's lock; when blocked, stop the line and park the work rather than leave a red suite.
tripwire: Observed in .claude/state/fix-lock.log; not fixed. Stop-the-line applied: previous script restored (12/12 green), rework parked.
applies_to_new_node: maybe — only if the rebuild repo keeps the same guard and runs parallel sessions.

class: metric reads the wrong sensor
what_happened: The Dashboard's "Temp 60 °C" was the WiFi card's thermal zone (iwlwifi) while the CPU (k10temp Tctl) ranged 56-72 °C; with WiFi off it fell back to acpitz (20 °C). The Guardian's thermal check read the same value and so could never fire. Verifier #4 found the rewrite had dropped Raspberry Pi temperature (cpu_thermal not recognised).
root_cause: Temperature was the max of thermal zones with no check of what each zone measures.
lesson: CPU temperature must come from a CPU sensor (hwmon k10temp Tctl, zenpower, coretemp Package, Raspberry Pi cpu_thermal; else an x86_pkg_temp or cpu-thermal zone), never a WiFi or ACPI zone, with the sensor named, null when absent ("no sensor", no cap), and bands from the sensor's crit (warm = crit - 15, hot = crit - 5) or known limits (AMD 80/90 °C; Pi warm 70 / hot 80, its throttle point); the heat alert uses the same hot band.
tripwire: hostMetrics.test.ts using this machine's real file formats (never WiFi/ACPI; Pi cpu_thermal); guardianThermal.test.ts (red 4/4); live equality with hwmon temp1_input; strace showed only k10temp's temperature read.
owner_decision: "Yes, in fact, check all measurement on the Dashboard. Make sure every one of them is actually meansuring the right thing and is correctly measuring what it's suppose to." Choices: "'No sensor', no cap"; Guardian heat alert uses the "Dashboard's 'hot' band".
applies_to_new_node: yes — the Pi 5 reports cpu_thermal and the x86 node k10temp/coretemp; both must be read correctly.

class: one quantity measured by several divergent code paths
what_happened: CPU % was a 100 ms os.cpus() delta without iowait/softirq/steal (mean error 5.5 points, could read 0% on a busy node) while the Health score used load / cores; three disk code paths agreed only by accident (df /); the backup NVMe /mnt/storage at 95% appeared nowhere; swap (2.2 of 8 GiB) was not shown; the Guardian estimated free disk from a hard-coded 1.9 TB.
root_cause: Each consumer computed its own figure ad hoc.
lesson: Host metrics must come from one typed module used by every consumer: CPU from /proc/stat over all fields (idle = idle + iowait) sampled in the background every 2 s, memory and swap from /proc/meminfo, the chain disk resolved from bitcoind's datadir mount (matched by mount point, not free space), and every real data drive under /mnt or /media listed with used %, free and total; any drive over 90% caps health at Good.
tripwire: hostMetrics.test.ts; live comparison table against a 2 s /proc/stat delta, free -m, df, hwmon and docker stats (CPU within 2 points, disks equal).
owner_decision: "Every mounted drive" (any drive over 90% caps the score at Good; cost stated: a full USB stick holds the score at Good).
applies_to_new_node: yes — backup drives and the chain disk must be visible on both nodes.

class: health check passes on a proxy signal (port open, name substring, any body)
what_happened: Electrs "indexed N / N, Synced, 100%" copied bitcoind's height whenever its port was open; Control Plane read OK for any body containing "status" (so BLOCKED/HTTP 503 passed); ChromaDB's /api/v1/heartbeat answered 410 and passed; Tor was "a container name contains tor"; includes('bitcoin') matched bitcoin-testnet so a stopped mainnet bitcoind counted as running; on testnet4, mainnet electrs/mempool were judged against the testnet tip; electrs far ahead read synced and mempool ahead read behind.
root_cause: Checks tested reachability or names instead of each service's own functional state.
lesson: Each service check must judge the service's own functional state with exact container names: electrs index height from its metrics (electrs_index_height tip) within 2 blocks, with "ahead" its own state; control-plane /health status === "OK" with DEGRADED/BLOCKED/breaker reported; ChromaDB v2 heartbeat; Tor bootstrap 100% plus the SOCKS port; mempool tip within 2 of bitcoind; network-aware ("mainnet_only" on a testnet node); a check that cannot be made is unknown, never a pass.
tripwire: serviceProbes.test.ts and electrsService.test.ts (pure judges, red first); live comparison with direct probes; 19 verifier rounds. Gap: the async runners (probeTor cache, containerIp cache, probeLnd wallet_locked) have no unit tests.
applies_to_new_node: yes — electrs is expected only on the x86 full node, so the probes must know which services each node runs.

class: "synced" derived from a progress estimate
what_happened: "Synced" was verificationprogress > 99.9% and not IBD, so a stalled tip stayed "Synced" for about 50 h; the assistant's context also told it "Bitcoin Core is fully synced" from the estimate alone; bitcoind "loading block index" answered blocks 0 / headers 0.
root_cause: The estimate approaches 100% regardless of how old the tip is.
lesson: Synced must mean blocks == headers, not IBD and a tip under 2 h old; otherwise report "behind by N" or "tip N min old"; the verification % is floored (99.95% is never 100%); heights while bitcoind loads its block index are null, not 0.
tripwire: serviceProbes tests (Synced / Behind / Stale / Syncing; loading block index -> null); live against getblockchaininfo blocks = headers and time.
applies_to_new_node: yes — both the full and the pruned node.

class: aggregate score gives credit for failed or unmade checks
what_happened: The Health score read 94 "Excellent" and LND down scored 87 "Excellent": failed checks earned credit (LND error 100, others 50/80), the electrs input grepped logs that never matched, the activity input read a nonexistent log file so was always 100, three threshold sets existed, and the backup drive, temperature and tip age were ignored. Later rounds found a BLOCKED control plane, bitcoind behind, memory 95-99% and all channels inactive still reading Excellent, and a healthy new node in early sync reading red Critical.
root_cause: The score was a weighted average with partial credit, and the label was derived from the number.
lesson: A health score must give 0 for a failed check, leave an unmade check out as a named "unknown" that caps the label, cap at Critical when bitcoind or LND is not working (wallet_locked included) or the container engine misses two cycles, cap at Warning for a stale tip, show a neutral "Syncing N%" during initial sync unless something is serious, and decide "Excellent" by rule (every service and sync check passed, nothing serious, nothing unknown) with one threshold set and property-tested invariants.
tripwire: healthScoring.test.ts (red first) plus property tests: verifiers found 0 invariant failures over up to 21,589,200 scoreHealth inputs with negative controls caught; healthScoreService.test.ts for the service wiring.
owner_decision: "Honest rework (Recommended)"; later "Rule decides the label (Recommended)", "Critical (Recommended)" for Docker not answering, "Over 95% = serious (Recommended)" for memory, "Score it, no issue (Recommended)" for CPU load, "All inactive = Good at most (Recommended)" for channels, "Show 'Syncing' instead" for initial sync.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's health summary must fall when the node is in trouble.

class: stall detector fooled by trickling headers and presync
what_happened: The owner chose a neutral "Syncing" label during initial sync, but the cost he was told (that the stale-tip and behind checks would still name a stalled sync) was false, so he was asked again. The stall detector then needed four rounds: one header every ~10 min after header download reset the clock; cumulative 100-header counting let a frozen sync read grey for 30 min every ~16.7 h; header presync (Core 24+) does not move the header count; an RPC outage, then a docker miss, reset the clock.
root_cause: Progress was inferred from header changes that keep arriving while block download is frozen.
lesson: Initial-sync stall detection must count progress only as a new validated block or headers at download speed (>= 1,000 since the previous 30 s sample), treat blocks 0 and headers 0 with peers as presync, keep the clock running while bitcoind or the container engine cannot be asked, restart it on a reindex, and raise a serious issue after 30 min without progress; and every cost stated to the owner for a choice must be verified true before asking.
tripwire: trackSyncProgress tests (blocks frozen with trickling headers -> stalled at 30; a 1,030-min freeze reads 1,030; a 150-header burst is not progress; presync with, without and unreadable peers; reindex restarts) and service-wiring tests across 31 min; verifier multi-day timelines. Known limits: a dashboard restart restarts the clock (in memory).
owner_decision: "Show 'Syncing' instead"; after being told the stated cost was false and asked again, "Syncing, but serious → Warning (Recommended)".
applies_to_new_node: yes — the Pi 5 pruned node and any fresh x86 install go through initial sync.

class: synchronous shell-outs block the event loop
what_happened: All health checks ran as ~20 synchronous execSync calls every 30 s on the backend's event loop; after the rewrite a 377-386 ms stall every 60 s remained from the monitoring loop's execSync docker ps/inspect/logs (reported, not fixed), every hwmon sensor was read synchronously (~21 ms per request), and a sync statfs on a USB mount could block.
root_cause: Shell commands and slow file-system calls were made synchronously inside a single-threaded server.
lesson: Probes must be asynchronous (execFile/fetch/net, no shell) with timeouts, single-flight sharing and per-resource pending guards (async statfs with a 2 s limit; a hung drive not re-asked while pending), only the needed sensors read, and event-loop latency measured after changes.
tripwire: prefetchStatfs test and a no-NVMe/zone-read test; event-loop latency at 10 Hz over 95 s (median 2.2 ms, p99 16.3 ms); live /resources median 4.3 ms (was 21.4). The remaining monitoringLoop execSync was reported to the owner.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the cleanly rebuilt backend should have no synchronous shell-outs in the server process.

class: shared counter mutated by every caller
what_happened: The "Docker missed twice in a row -> Critical" counter was module-level and bumped by every calculateScore() caller; the AI Intelligence page recalculated on every visit, concurrently, so one slow docker plus a page visit read Critical; /api/intelligence also appended to history on each request.
root_cause: The computation was not single-flight and readers triggered recalculation.
lesson: A periodic health computation must be single-flight with per-cycle counters, and readers must get the cached latest result without triggering a recalculation.
tripwire: healthScoreService.test.ts (concurrent callers share one calculation; one slow docker + a second caller; two cycles -> Critical; latest()); live: five /api/intelligence/reliability calls left the score history unchanged (6 -> 6).
owner_decision: "Critical (Recommended)" for Docker not answering (cost stated: a docker slower than 5 s twice in a row flashes Critical).
applies_to_new_node: yes — any periodic health engine on the new node.

class: unreadable value reported as zero
what_happened: An unreadable drive's free: 0 made the Guardian raise "Disk space low: 0 GB", unreadable memory "RAM low: 0 MB", and an unreadable CPU reached the Guardian as 0 and became its baseline ("CPU at N% — normally 0%"); signalRecorder still treats an unreadable CPU as 0 (reported, not fixed).
root_cause: Missing values were defaulted to 0 in the API and parse layers.
lesson: An unreadable figure must be null end to end (API, alert parsing, baselines), and no alert or baseline may be derived from it.
tripwire: parseResources test (unreadable -> undefined); cpu:{usage:null} and {} -> undefined; diagnose.ts and heartbeat.ts raise nothing and write no baseline from it.
applies_to_new_node: yes — every metric pipeline on the new node.

class: permission error misreported as a timeout
what_happened: On testnet4 the chain lives in a Docker named volume under /var/lib/docker, which the dashboard user cannot enter, so statfs gave EACCES; the chain disk was always "unknown", the score could never be Excellent, and the log blamed "no answer in 2 s". A 10-minute cache of the chain-path fallback after one docker failure was also removed.
root_cause: The disk was read through a path the unprivileged service could not traverse, and the real error was discarded.
lesson: Disk usage for a data path must be read via its filesystem's mount point (from /proc/mounts) when the path itself is not readable, every failure must be logged with its real errno, and a fallback after a transient failure must not be cached.
tripwire: Tests (red first) for reading via the mount point and recording EACCES / timeout / pending reasons; live as the service user: volume path EACCES, via mount point / 82% = df.
applies_to_new_node: yes — container volumes on Fedora IoT may also be unreadable to an unprivileged UI service.

class: knowledge chunks exceed the embedder's token window
what_happened: The Health score section was 751 tokens, past the embedder's 512-token window, so the owner's new choices were truncated away; corrections files without ## headings became single chunks with everything after the first lines unretrievable; the doc watcher missed new files; two glossary.md files collide under one Chroma source name; the navigation guide has a 915-token chunk.
root_cause: Docs were chunked by heading without measuring tokens against the embedder.
lesson: Every knowledge chunk must fit the embedder's window measured with its own tokenizer, each correction must have its own heading, source names must be unique, and ingestion must be verified (new files indexed; owner-style questions answered in the top 3).
tripwire: Chunk sizes measured with the :8082 tokenizer each round (largest 474 at close); owner-question retrieval checks per round. The 915-token chunk and the glossary collision were reported, not fixed.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant will use retrieval too.

class: assistant tools read a different status path than the API
what_happened: The assistant had no tool that reads the Health score, its electrs tool read keys /api/electrs/status never had (so it always said electrs is down), and dashboardKnowledgeService told it "Bitcoin Core is fully synced" from the progress estimate alone; docs that said "ask the assistant" had to be withdrawn.
root_cause: The assistant's context was built by separate code from the node's status API.
lesson: The assistant must read node status through the same API and rules the page uses, and its tools must be contract-tested against real endpoint responses.
tripwire: Carried to 2026-09-30-dashboard-page-truth.md as R6b/R6d (outside this batch). Should exist: contract tests between assistant tools and API shapes.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant must see the same truth as the page.

class: consumer not updated with an API shape change
what_happened: The new {ok, state} service shape made the infra bar (Control Plane / ChromaDB / Tor / Redis) show all four down, and the Health card computed its own label (80/60/40), so the API's 89 "good" read "Excellent" and it showed 0 before the first score.
root_cause: The frontend kept its own field names and thresholds instead of the backend's.
lesson: The page must render the backend's status label and fields from shared types, show "—" before the first value and "stale" past its limit, and an API shape change must be checked against every consumer before deploy.
tripwire: InfraStatusBar.test.tsx (red 4 of 5), healthDisplay.test.ts (red 3 of 3); frontend types in dashboard/frontend/src/types/api.ts aligned with the API; headless render at 1920 px.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the rebuilt UI must share types with the backend.

class: recurring errors logged but never surfaced
what_happened: Verifiers found errors repeating unnoticed: "Failed to refresh Bitcoin wallet … toFixed" (3,183 since Sep 28, ~1,440 a day), "Post-IBD optimization failed" with an empty message at every start (a .js require of a .ts module), an lnd release 404, and the dashboard rewriting a tracked RAG file at every start; 2026-09-28-runtime-dependency-vulnerabilities.md also noted rikuri-fingerprint.service failed (start-limit-hit) unchecked by smoke and a refused sudo call every 30 s.
root_cause: No monitor counts repeating error lines or failed units.
lesson: The node must count recurring error log lines and failed units and surface them as health issues, and services must never write into the tracked source tree at runtime.
tripwire: Reported to the owner, not fixed. Should exist: a log-rate monitor and a failed-unit check in smoke and health.
applies_to_new_node: yes — Law 1 (nothing fails silently) for the new node.

class: consumer reads a field the producer never sends
what_happened: The Dashboard's mempool count read `btcData.mempool_size`, a field `/api/bitcoin/blockchain` never sends, so it always showed "— txs" (the mempool held 66,164 transactions at the time); the frontend type `BlockchainInfo.mempool_size` even declared the non-existent field.
root_cause: The page's type declared a field the API never had, and no test drove the page with the API's real response shape.
lesson: Every figure the node displays must be bound to a field the producing API actually returns, checked by a contract test built from the producer's real response; a field that is always absent must fail a test, not render a dash forever.
tripwire: Dashboard render test with every data hook mocked in the real API shapes, read as the owner would (pageRound4Fixes.test.tsx); headless render where each figure is compared with its API field at the same moment (mempool count vs getmempoolinfo.size).
owner_decision: Yes, in fact, check all measurement on the Dashboard. Make sure every one of them is actually meansuring the right thing and is correctly measuring what it's suppose to.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the rebuilt backend and UI keep the same producer/consumer seam; a contract test per displayed field prevents permanently dead figures.

class: unknown coerced to zero (and zero coerced to unknown)
what_happened: `connections || '—'` hid a real 0 peers while `|| 0` and `parseFloat(null) || 0` turned unknown peers, sync % and LND channels into 0; the Electrs card assumed 100% when no tip height was known and drew "Indexed 0 / N · 0%" under a stopped container; `/api/status/disk` returned 0 for an unreadable disk. Round 6's verifier still found unknowns drawn as 0 on the service cards (I1).
root_cause: Falsy coalescing (`||`, `?? 0`, `?? 100`) was used as the default everywhere, so no layer kept null distinct from 0.
lesson: The node must carry unknown as an explicit null from probe to API to UI and assistant; the UI shows "—" in a neutral colour for unknown and "0" for a real zero, and no layer may default an unreadable figure to 0, 100% or a healthy state.
tripwire: Per-figure tests with null fixtures and real zeros (pageRound6.test.tsx failed with "expected '0' to be '—'"); mutations reintroducing `|| 0` or `${electrs.pct ?? 100}%` must turn tests red (pageRound4Guards C6); suggested: a ratchet on `|| 0` in display code.
applies_to_new_node: yes — any rebuilt UI/backend faces the same null-vs-zero seam; cheapest to design in from the start.

class: estimate or guess presented as a measurement
what_happened: The Bitcoin card showed a sync "ETA" that was simply the remaining fraction × 48 hours; the chain bar showed "mainnet" when the chain field was missing; the builder's own test expected "Reindexing" for a partial sync although nothing bitcoind reports tells a reindex from a first sync.
root_cause: Placeholder heuristics were written as if they were readings, with nothing marking them as not measured.
lesson: The node must never display a number or label it did not measure; what it cannot know is shown as unknown, and any estimate must be labelled as an estimate with its method.
tripwire: Tests pinning "—" for a missing chain and "IBD"/"Syncing" rather than "Reindexing"; review rule that every displayed figure names its source field.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the same temptation exists for sync ETAs on the slow Pi 5 pruned node.

class: one fact computed by divergent rules on different surfaces
what_happened: The page used the node's sync rule (tip age with a 2 h stale line, blocks behind), but the assistant's knowledge service called Bitcoin Core "fully synced" when verificationprogress exceeded 99.99%, and the rewritten Bitcoin Core tool first took sync from the IBD flag alone, so a 3-hour-stale tip or a node 5 blocks behind read "HEALTHY · Sync: synced" to the assistant; a missing block time was taken as "now" ("synced, 0 min old").
root_cause: Each consumer re-derived "synced" from a different bitcoind field instead of calling one canonical function.
lesson: The node must compute sync state once (Synced / Syncing N% / Behind N / Stale tip N min, from block time or else median time plus both heights; "could not be worked out" when either is missing) and every surface — page, health score, alerts, assistant — must consume that single result.
tripwire: Per-consumer tests for a stale tip (150 min vs the 2 h line, with 95 min pinned as synced) and for N blocks behind; mutations "stale as synced", "no block time → now", "median preferred" must fail (assistantRound5Fixes*.test.ts, assistantRound9.test.ts V5).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the x86 full node and the Pi 5 pruned node both need one sync-state definition shared by UI, alerts and the assistant.

class: same metric measured differently by different consumers
what_happened: The assistant's CPU context was load average ÷ cores while the page used CPU % from hostMetrics; `os.freemem()` counted file cache as used; `/api/status/disk` ran `df` on `/data` or `/` instead of the chain disk; the page's temperature bands were hard-coded 50/70 °C while the sensor's own bands were 80/90; swap and extra drives (one at 95%) were not shown; a drive at exactly 80% had a Health issue (`>= 80`) but no amber colour.
root_cause: Metrics and thresholds were re-implemented per consumer instead of read from one host-metrics source with one band table.
lesson: The node must have one host-metrics source (CPU %, memory with cache counted as free, swap, every data drive by mount with free GB, sensor temperature with the sensor's own bands) and one threshold table used by UI, health score, alerts and assistant, with the boundary values tested.
tripwire: Boundary tests at 79/80/90/91% for drives and "No swap"; live check that `/api/status/disk` equals `/api/status/resources` disk.
applies_to_new_node: yes — both machines report host metrics; the Pi's thermal and disk profile differ, so bands must come from the platform/sensor, not constants.

class: container running reported as service operational
what_happened: The Tor and Mempool service cards said "Operational" whenever the container ran; the assistant's `refreshServiceHealth` called a running container "healthy"; the Services header counted containers ("N of M running") while the top card counted 8 health checks ("8/8"), unlabelled, so they disagreed; Tor's real probe state "bootstrapping 45%" first rendered as red "Not working".
root_cause: Container liveness was used as the health signal, and two different counts shared one label.
lesson: The node must call a service working only from a functional check (Tor bootstrapped, mempool not behind, onion answering), label "containers running" separately from "checks passing", and show every probe state (connecting N%, not answering, mainnet only, unknown) instead of collapsing to up/down.
tripwire: Tests of the status mapper against every state the backend probes actually send (`checkStatus` vs `probeTor`), a test that the header reads "N of M containers running" (pageRound7Dashboard.test.tsx).
applies_to_new_node: yes — Law 4 (absence of success): liveness alone must never be reported as health on the new node.

class: planned owner stop reported as a critical failure
what_happened: While the owner had stopped the node, the Health card read "29 Critical"; after a testnet4 Stop (which runs `compose down`, removing the containers) the new testnet card would have said "Not installed", which is false.
root_cause: The health score and cards had no notion of an owner-requested stop, and a removed container was read as absent software.
lesson: The node must treat an owner stop as a first-class state: the health view shows "Stopped by you since <time>" with no score, still surfaces real faults in what keeps running, keeps stopped periods out of the score history, and shows "Not running" (reason unknown) rather than guessing "not installed".
tripwire: healthOwnerStop.test.ts, healthScoreOwnerStopLoop.test.ts (drives the real calculateScore with probes and the stop marker mocked), healthScoreOwnerStopWiring.test.ts, testnetOwnerStopApi.test.ts.
owner_decision: 'Stopped by you' (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node also has owner stops and test networks that are deliberately switched off.

class: UI content silently clipped or style silently missing
what_happened: Reliability rows were cut off at 1,400 and 1,920 px (`nowrap` inside an `overflow-x: hidden` page); later every service card was cut at 320–390 px by a `nowrap` status or RAM share; `var(--border-color)` was used 243 times in 27 files but defined by no theme, so those borders were never drawn; the sidebar had no phone layout.
root_cause: The page clips sideways overflow, and the jsdom tests compute no layout and never check that CSS variables exist.
lesson: The node's UI must be checked by real headless renders at phone, tablet and desktop widths (no element past the edge, no raw text key) and by a test that every CSS variable used is defined by every theme.
tripwire: Headless Chrome renders at 320/360/390/768/1,400/1,920 px measuring card edges; themeBorders.test.ts; the record states that tests reading CSS as text cannot catch cascade or layout, so renders are the check.
owner_decision: Borders: "Turn them on (Recommended)"; phone menu: "Yes, in its own record (Recommended)"
applies_to_new_node: yes — the owner reads the node from a phone; layout checks belong in CI.

class: deleting a file assumed private that had global effects
what_happened: Round 7 deleted `RestartConfirmDialog.css` with its dead component, but the app bundles all CSS globally and the file's `.modal-overlay`, `.modal-close`, `.btn-secondary`, `.btn-danger` rules styled 31 components: buttons lost `flex: 1` and `.btn-danger` its hover colour. Six page screenshots still matched because modals and hover were not rendered.
root_cause: "No other user" was proven for the component by grep, not for the stylesheet's selectors, which are global.
lesson: Before deleting or moving a stylesheet or any globally registered asset, the node's build must prove each selector unused, and the built CSS bundle must be diffed rule by rule before and after.
tripwire: Rule-by-rule comparison of the built CSS bundle (5,441 vs 5,429 top-level rules, only dialog-only rules removed) and a declaration-pinning test for the restored sharedModal.css (pageRound9.test.tsx).
applies_to_new_node: maybe — applies if the new UI bundles global CSS; scoped/module styles remove most of this class.

class: missing translation keys render as raw keys
what_happened: QuickOpenChannelModal.tsx used 8 text keys (e.g. `lightning.channelOpeningSuccess`, `lightning.fundsReturnTo`) that existed in no locale, ChannelSearchTab showed `lightning.tooManyPending` and `lightning.noUpfrontShutdown` raw on channel-open errors, and `wallets.nodeUnreachableTitle/Body` existed in English only; an English-only wording test also let the Spanish "SIEMPRE" overclaim through.
root_cause: Nothing checked that every key the code uses exists in every shipped locale.
lesson: The node's build must fail when any text key used by the code is missing from any shipped locale, and wording/safety tests must run in every locale, not only English.
tripwire: Script check that all used keys exist in all 5 locales (e.g. "All 71 dashboard.* keys the code uses exist in every locale"); per-locale wording check in coldWalletWording.test.ts.
applies_to_new_node: yes — if the new UI is multilingual; raw keys on a channel-open error leave the owner blind at a money step.

class: UI overclaims where funds go
what_happened: Cold-wallet texts in 5 languages said channel funds "ALWAYS return to your hardware wallet", the channel-open success screen said "Funds will return to: …", and route replies said a channel "will automatically close to your cold wallet". LND's upfront-shutdown address is paid only by a cooperative close; a force close pays this node's on-chain wallet after its timelock (up to about 2 weeks).
root_cause: The wording described the cooperative happy path as a guarantee.
lesson: Every statement the node makes about where funds go must match the protocol: the cold (upfront-shutdown) address is paid only by a cooperative close of a channel opened while it was set, peer accepting; a force close pays the node's on-chain wallet after the timelock, and recovering it needs this node or its seed plus channel backup.
tripwire: coldWalletWording.test.ts (per-locale "always" words, frontend), coldWalletReplies.test.ts and coldWalletRouteWording.test.ts (backend replies and the route warning).
owner_decision: correct the language if force closes don't return funds to hardwallet
applies_to_new_node: yes — any cold-wallet / upfront-shutdown feature on the new node must state the force-close path.

class: consumer reads a field the producer never sends
what_happened: The assistant's Electrs tool read `running/synced/tipHeight/bitcoinConnected`, keys `/api/electrs/status` never had, so it always told the model Electrs was "UNHEALTHY / down / cannot connect to Bitcoin Core"; the Bitcoin Core tool read `usedPercent/free` (always "0% used, 0 GB free") and status keys `/api/bitcoin/status` never sends, so a synced node with 19 peers read "UNHEALTHY / Sync: down (0.00%) / Blocks: 0 / 0 / Peers: 0".
root_cause: Tool adapters were written against an imagined response shape and never tested against the real route.
lesson: Every assistant tool must be tested against the real route's response (route exercised, inputs mocked below it), and the assistant's facts about the node must come from the same canonical services as the page.
tripwire: assistantWiring.test.ts (real refreshes, both tools and the disk route via supertest); live read-only run of each tool's buildAIContext() against the API, compared with the API.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant will consume node APIs through tools; a contract test per tool is mandatory.

class: unreadable status classified as down or healthy
what_happened: The new Electrs mapping said "HEALTHY" for `unknown` (metrics not answering, or ahead of bitcoind) and `waiting`, and "down" for `error` (status unreadable); both tools called a non-2xx or a loading bitcoind DOWN and advised `docker restart`; LND's "Chain sync" read "Syncing…" in the warning colour when LND's state was unknown (wallet locked) or the container stopped.
root_cause: The status mappers had two outcomes for a question with at least four (healthy, degraded, down, unknown) and ignored the route's own `health` field.
lesson: The node's status model must keep healthy / degraded / down / unknown distinct; "could not be read" is unknown, never down, is drawn neutral, and must not trigger restart advice or self-healing.
tripwire: Tests for every state the route can send (unknown, waiting, error, down, mainnet_only, ahead), asserting status and absence of restart advice (assistantRound5Fixes2.test.ts); pageRound7.test.tsx for the neutral LND/sync-% rendering.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the same four-state model is needed before any self-healing acts on a status.

class: remediation advice contradicts the node's configuration
what_happened: Round 5 woke the Bitcoin Core tool's own 85/95% disk checks, which at 95% advised "Enable blockchain pruning" — impossible here because the node runs `-txindex=1` and bitcoind refuses txindex on a pruned chain — and its bands contradicted the owner's 80/90 drive bands; afterwards any note (80–90% disk, a mempool over 90% of maxmempool) made Bitcoin Core DEGRADED to the assistant.
root_cause: The tool carried generic advice and private thresholds instead of reading the node's configuration and the shared severity rules.
lesson: Remediation advice must be generated from the node's actual configuration (never suggest pruning on a txindex full node; never suggest txindex-dependent fixes on a pruned node) and use the same bands and severity semantics as the health score: a note is listed with its advice but does not degrade status; a note beside a real problem does not hide it.
tripwire: assistantRound7/8/9.test.ts: 96/91 → high, 90/85/80 → note, 79 → none, never "prun" in the diagnosis; a note beside a 3 h stale tip still DEGRADED; mutation runs 18 of 18 and 15 of 16 red.
owner_decision: "Note doesn't degrade (Recommended)" (disk note); "Same rule (Recommended)" (mempool note)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new design runs a full node (x86) and a pruned node (Pi 5); advice keyed to one configuration will be wrong on the other.

class: fixing instances by name instead of the structural cause
what_happened: Rounds 7–9 copied each issue's advice into the assistant's top-level recommendations one issue at a time (disk, then mempool); round 9's verifier found the advice for a stale tip or a node behind never reached the assistant, because `buildAIContext` printed issue descriptions and top-level recommendations but not per-issue advice.
root_cause: The context builder dropped per-issue advice structurally, and each fix patched one named issue.
lesson: When a defect recurs across siblings, the node must be fixed at the structure (every issue printed with its own advice, exactly once) and tested with multi-issue fixtures, not patched issue by issue.
tripwire: assistantRound10/11.test.ts: every issue's advice reaches the context, none printed twice, both advices in a two-issue fixture; mutations "advice for the first issue only" and "copied to the list again" red.
applies_to_new_node: yes — applies to any generated context or report on the new node.

class: assistant knowledge names controls that do not exist
what_happened: The tools advised "Restart Electrs" and "Start it from the Dashboard (Start All)" though there is no Electrs-only restart and Start All lives in Settings → Node Management; `container-management.md` claimed card restart buttons, "per-service controls are not offered", testnet4 Stop in Settings → Network (it is Node Policy), and that the assistant restarts services (its `restartService` was registered nowhere); it took rounds 9–12 to make every sentence true, and older closed claims ("These are the ONLY compose files") remain as debt.
root_cause: Guides and advice strings were written from memory of the UI rather than checked against the code that renders each control.
lesson: Every control the assistant or a guide names must be checked against the code that renders it (file and label), the assistant's stated capabilities must match its actually registered tools, and closed lists ("the only ways") must be avoided or verified exhaustively.
tripwire: assistantRound12.test.ts pins advice to the real control names; the verifier checked each doc sentence against code; suggested: a knowledge lint resolving each named control to a UI label.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant must never tell the owner to use a control that does not exist or that it cannot invoke.

class: threshold compared against the wrong metric and unit
what_happened: The Bitcoin Core tool compared the mempool's serialized `bytes` (25.6 MB) with the 300 MB limit that applies to `usage` (147.6 MB) and labelled MiB as MB; the next fix compared usage with a fixed 300 MB, which never fires at the default and would call a normal mempool "high" under a raised `maxmempool`.
root_cause: The check used the wrong getmempoolinfo field and a hard-coded limit instead of the node's own `maxmempool`.
lesson: Mempool fullness must be `usage` divided by the node's own reported `maxmempool` (both from getmempoolinfo), in consistent units; never hard-code a limit the node reports.
tripwire: Tests with usage/maxmempool fixtures at exactly 90% and just over (X8 boundary); mutation "fixed 300 MB" must fail (assistantRound5Fixes3.test.ts, assistantRound9.test.ts).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the Pi 5 pruned node will likely run a smaller maxmempool, where a fixed limit is wrong.

class: RPC field change breaks a consumer silently
what_happened: `Failed to refresh Bitcoin wallet: … reading 'toFixed'` was logged about once a minute (2,533 times since 2026-10-02, seen since at least 2026-09-28), so the assistant's wallet fact never refreshed; the fix reads balances from `getbalances` when `getwalletinfo` has none (Bitcoin Core 31).
root_cause: Code read balance fields from `getwalletinfo` that this Bitcoin Core version no longer returns, and the error only reached the log.
lesson: The node must read balances from `getbalances`, test every RPC adapter against the bitcoind version it ships, and treat a missing field as "could not be read" rather than throwing.
tripwire: assistantRound5Fixes2.test.ts (wallet from getbalances; balances unreadable → "could not be read"); suggested: version-pinned RPC fixtures refreshed at each bitcoind upgrade.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node will track current Bitcoin Core releases, where RPC fields keep being deprecated.

class: recurring error logged but never surfaced
what_happened: Two errors ran for days unnoticed until verifiers tripped over them: the wallet `toFixed` error (about 60 an hour) and `Post-IBD optimization failed: Cannot find module '../dashboard/backend/src/services/hardwareDetector'` on every backend start (100 times since 2026-09-25).
root_cause: Errors went to the journal only; nothing counted repeated errors or turned them into a finding.
lesson: The node must count recurring errors per source and raise a health finding when one repeats, so a log line is never the only place a failure lives.
tripwire: Suggested: a journal error-signature monitor that raises a finding or fails smoke on any repeating ERROR (the record only reported them to the owner).
applies_to_new_node: yes — Law 1 (nothing fails silently) applies directly to the new backend's logs.

class: reverse-proxy timeout shorter than the operation it fronts
what_happened: nginx `ryzen.conf` gave `/api` a 60 s `proxy_read_timeout` while a testnet4 stop/start route could take 540/420 s, so the browser saw an error while the backend completed; the same site had no `/socket.io/` location, so the page's WebSocket fell through to index.html and failed 8 times per page load. Installing the fixed config still needed a manual owner sudo step.
root_cause: Proxy configuration was neither derived from nor tested against the routes' timeouts and the app's transports, and the deployed copy could differ from the repo's.
lesson: Long operations must run as background jobs with a status endpoint; any reverse-proxy timeout must exceed the longest route it fronts, every transport the app uses must have a location, and the deployed proxy config must be the tested one.
tripwire: nginxApiTimeout.test.ts (red on a 60 s `/api` timeout); suggested: a check that the installed site config equals the repo copy.
applies_to_new_node: yes — whatever proxy fronts the new node's API needs the same timeout and transport checks.

class: process guard silently not covering the repository being changed
what_happened: Session a9a3c3c8 started in /home/junc/Rikuri-PI, so its PreToolUse hook was that repo's guard.py rooted at Rikuri-PI: rikurinode edits got no fix-lock denies, protected-path asks or relaxed-ask log on 2026-10-05/06, and locks were followed by hand. The record also logs a test written inside another session's lock window and a lock released in the same command as the fix and test run, with two tests still red.
root_cause: The guard resolves its root from its own location, so a session started elsewhere was unguarded, and lock calls bundled with edits ran before results were seen.
lesson: Development guardrails for the node must fail closed: a session editing a repository whose guard is not active must be refused or warned, and a lock release must be its own step after an observed green run.
tripwire: The owner's chosen fix: a second PreToolUse hook running rikurinode's guard.py from Rikuri-PI's settings; an empty guard-relaxed.log on an active work day as a signal; verifiers auditing lock windows from fix-lock.log and file mtimes.
owner_decision: Add rikurinode's guard here (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node will be built by AI sessions spanning more than one repository.

class: tests pass without constraining behaviour
what_happened: Round 4's verifier found 30 of 79 mutations surviving (14 of 16 in the Dashboard wiring, whose guards only checked that calls exist); one test pinned a Tor state shape the backend never sends; a `beforeAll` render left later tests reading an empty page; CSS-as-text guards passed while specificity undid the fix; mutation runs were first done in place on the live shared source tree.
root_cause: Tests were written to pass on the new code rather than shown to fail against plausible wrong code.
lesson: Every guard test for the node must be shown to fail against a mutation of the behaviour it guards, run on a scratch copy (never the live tree), with fixtures built from the producer's real outputs.
tripwire: Per-round mutation runs on a scratch worktree (mutN.py / mutN.out), each file restored and hash-checked; survivors listed and either killed or recorded as equivalent with a reason.
applies_to_new_node: yes — cheap insurance for an AI-written codebase.

class: quality gate silently checks nothing
what_happened: Frontend `eslint.config.js` matched only `**/*.{js,jsx}`, so the whole TypeScript app was outside `npm run lint`, and every round's "frontend lint 0" proved nothing for a `.ts`/`.tsx` change.
root_cause: The linter's file globs were never checked against the language the app is written in.
lesson: Each gate step for the node must assert it actually examined the files it claims to cover (non-zero file counts per language), so a misconfigured gate fails instead of passing empty.
tripwire: Suggested: a gate check that the linter's ts/tsx file count is > 0; recorded as an owner-owned skipped item.
applies_to_new_node: yes — applies to every gate the new repo adds.

class: work built on a stale base or deployed from a shared dirty tree
what_happened: HEAD moved three times while this record's scratch tree was verified, so committing it would have reverted other commits; separately another session built the backend from the shared working tree after an OS release upgrade, so this record's unverified third fix ran live from about 20:30 PDT on 2026-10-03.
root_cause: Several sessions shared one working tree and deployed whatever was in it, and change sets were prepared on trees that did not track HEAD.
lesson: The node must be built and deployed only from a committed, verified revision, and a change set must be rebuilt on the current HEAD at commit time.
tripwire: Deploy step that refuses a dirty tree and records the deployed commit; verifier checks the running artifact is byte-identical to a fresh build of that commit.
applies_to_new_node: yes — image-based deploys make this natural: build images only from tagged commits.

class: upgrade reported complete without checking the service runs
what_happened: The Upgrades page said electrs v0.12.0 "Upgrade complete ✓" while the container crash-looped (`unknown argument '--daemon-p2p-addr'`) and the monitoring loop escalated it; the upgrade's test was only `--help`, and upgrading electrs also recreated bitcoind and tor. Another session rolled it back to v0.11.1.
root_cause: The success check exercised the binary, not the running service with the node's real configuration, and the upgrade recreated unrelated containers.
lesson: An upgrade must be declared complete only after the upgraded service is running healthy with the node's real configuration (and rolled back automatically otherwise), and upgrading one service must not recreate others.
tripwire: Post-upgrade health gate on the real service (not `--help`); check that untouched containers keep their IDs.
applies_to_new_node: yes — image updates with automatic rollback need exactly this health gate to decide rollback.

class: two orchestrators bring the stack up at once
what_happened: After the owner's OS upgrade, `rikuri-stack.service` restarted at 13:00:55 and ran its own `compose up` beside the upgrade runner's (13:01:03), recreating containers the runner had just started; `rikuri-testnet-stack` timed out on stop; and the ~10 minutes with the stack down counted as downtime (bitcoin 98.48% → 98.46%) because an owner-started upgrade is not "stopped by you".
root_cause: Two components each owned bring-up after the upgrade, with no lock between them and no planned-maintenance marker for upgrades.
lesson: Exactly one component may bring the stack up after an upgrade or boot, others must wait on it, and an owner-started upgrade must be recorded as planned maintenance distinct from an outage (to be exposed as an owner choice).
tripwire: Suggested: a bring-up lock checked by every path and a journal check that a bring-up never recreates containers it just started; uptime test for an upgrade window.
applies_to_new_node: yes — Fedora IoT updates with reboot/rollback make the post-update bring-up path a single point that must be owned once.

class: knowledge store out of step with deployed code
what_happened: `rag:build` ran at 10:21:37, before the 10:23:37 correction, so the file store kept a false ETA reason until the verifier found it; later the doc-watcher indexed rounds 9–12 text on write while the live backend still ran the 19:57 build, so the guide described behaviour the running tools did not have.
root_cause: Knowledge indexing was triggered by file writes and manual builds, not tied to the code deploy.
lesson: The node's assistant knowledge must be indexed as part of the same deploy as the code it describes, after the last edit, and verified by querying for the new text and for zero chunks of the old.
tripwire: Post-deploy query check ("the new text found, 0 chunks of the old"); suggested: stamp the index with the deployed commit.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant's knowledge must match the image actually running.

class: auth wrapper incompatible with the deployment's auth mode makes controls dead
what_happened: Safe Shutdown, Start All and Restart All were all dead: `NodeControl.tsx` sent through `fetchWithAuth`, which throws "Not authenticated" without a login token, and this node runs loginless, so every press failed in the browser with "Failed to communicate with backend" and nothing was sent; the dashboard log had no "[System] Initiating…" line in 14 days.
root_cause: The buttons used a token-only fetch wrapper that no test exercised in the node's actual (loginless plus step-up) auth mode.
lesson: Every control must be exercised end to end in a real browser in the auth mode the node actually runs, up to the step-up prompt; a cancelled or wrong password must say "nothing was changed", never a backend failure or a logout.
tripwire: Headless-browser check that each button sends its POST and raises "Confirm it's you"; NodeControl tests red against the old component (8/8); unauthenticated POST /api/system/shutdown → 401 step_up_required and nothing stops.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new UI will also mix auth modes and step-up for money actions.

class: stop timeout overrides the daemon's own shutdown grace
what_happened: `stopInOrder` ran `docker stop -t 15`, overriding the compose `stop_grace_period: 90s` of bitcoind and LND (StopTimeout=90), so Docker would SIGKILL both money daemons after 15 s; the dead buttons had hidden it.
root_cause: A hard-coded short `-t` replaced each container's configured stop timeout.
lesson: The node must stop bitcoind and LND with their own full grace period (no override) and a command timeout longer than that grace, and read every exit code: 137 (killed) means the shutdown was not safe.
tripwire: nodePower.test.ts (no `-t`, exit codes read); live: all 11 containers exit 0, none OOM-killed (docker events with exit codes).
applies_to_new_node: yes — under podman/systemd on Fedora IoT the same applies to TimeoutStopSec and `podman stop -t`.

class: success claim not derived from the verified end state
what_happened: The page said "Safe to disconnect power" while the testnet pair (`bitcoin-testnet`, `lnd-testnet`) and `rikuri-tapd` kept running; the stop list also named `control-plane` containers that do not exist (it is a systemd service).
root_cause: The message followed the stop list rather than being computed from which data services actually stopped, and how.
lesson: The node may say it is safe to cut power only when every service holding chain or channel data (every bitcoind, every LND, tapd) has stopped with a clean exit; otherwise it must name what is still running or was killed.
tripwire: nodePower.test.ts for safeToPowerOff with a running or killed data service; live: `safeToPowerOff: true` only after all 11 containers exited 0 and tapd was inactive.
owner_decision: Everything with data (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — both the x86 and the Pi need a truthful 'safe to unplug'.

class: hold implemented per path misses other actors
what_happened: The owner's stop first un-stopped itself (the maintenance flag had no TTL and readers defaulted to 45 min, after which self-healing restarted LND). After a boot-scoped owner-stop marker was added, the 5-minute Guardian heartbeat still proposed restarts and the control plane restarted tor; then the 30-minute Guardian loop sent 16 restart proposals, a diagnosis runbook (RB-TAPD-ENABLE-START-01) ran, the control-plane anomaly scanner sent 5 "wallet_missing" emails and the dashboard bell raised 30 "is down" alerts during the stop.
root_cause: The hold was added to the monitoring loop and diagnosis trigger only, while at least five other actors (heartbeat, Guardian loop and its LLM actions, DRB, the Rust anomaly scanner, the bell) could restart or alert without asking it.
lesson: The node must have one owner-stop state (written before stopping, scoped to the boot, cleared only by Start All or the next boot) that every actor able to restart a service or send an alert queries before acting; those actors must be enumerated and each covered by a test, while network, nginx, sshd and system findings stay active so the owner can always reach Start.
tripwire: guardianHoldAllPaths.test.ts, heartbeatOwnerStop.test.ts, bellOwnerStop.test.ts, the Rust test that the anomaly loop scans only through the owner-stop hold (with a real mutation check), and a live audit that every notification during a stop came from a held path (57 checked).
owner_decision: Until I press Start All (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node has self-healing, alerts and a sandboxed assistant; one central stop state they all consult is essential.

class: second bring-up path diverges from the boot path
what_happened: Start/Restart ran `docker compose … up -d` directly instead of `scripts/rikuri-stack-compose.sh`: no RAM-scaled memory limits (the dashboard had 0 `*_MEMORY_LIMIT` variables while bitcoin ran at 18,038,652,928 bytes vs the 20G compose default, so compose would recreate the containers), no compose lock, no post-up health gate, the operating network's files instead of mainnet's, and never the testnet stack or tapd.
root_cause: The UI's start path re-implemented bring-up instead of calling the one used at boot.
lesson: Start All must be the boot bring-up (same script, environment, lock and health gate); if the generated environment such as memory limits is missing it must refuse rather than recreate the money containers at defaults, and a start must keep container IDs (started, not recreated).
tripwire: nodePower tests for the refusal without /run/rikuri/memory-limits.env; live check that all container IDs and memory limits are unchanged after Start All; a compose dry-run / config-hash check before any live test.
applies_to_new_node: yes — on Fedora IoT the boot bring-up (systemd/quadlet) must also be the only path the UI uses.

class: long-running operation executed inside one HTTP request
what_happened: The power operations ran inside the HTTP request while the LAN nginx site allowed 60 s, and a full stop waits up to ~90 s per bitcoind and LND.
root_cause: Multi-minute work was coupled to a request's lifetime.
lesson: Node power operations must run as one background operation at a time (202 with the operation, 409 if one is running) with a status endpoint the page polls step by step, and the last result should survive a backend restart.
tripwire: Route tests for 202/409 and GET /api/system/operation; stated gap: the last result is forgotten when the dashboard restarts (it is in the journal).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the same pattern fits every long node operation (upgrades, backups, restores).

class: dependency start-order race
what_happened: Restart All failed with "dependency failed to start: container bitcoin is unhealthy": bitcoind started before tor, resolved `proxy=tor:9050` once at start-up and exited ("Invalid -proxy address or hostname: 'tor:9050'"), Docker restarted it after compose had given up, and its cookie was written twice so the cookie cascade restarted electrs, LND and mempool twice. Verification added that after a power loss dockerd restarts containers without honouring `depends_on`.
root_cause: `bitcoin` (and `bitcoin-knots`) had no `depends_on: tor`, and bitcoind resolves its proxy hostname only once at start.
lesson: Every service that routes through Tor must be ordered after Tor in every start path — boot, UI start, watchdog and post-crash auto-restart — and should wait for Tor rather than exit when it is not resolvable yet.
tripwire: composeStartOrder.test.ts: every service whose command routes through tor:9050 waits for tor (red 3/3 before the fix); suggested equivalent for systemd units (After=/Requires=) on the new node. "Restart All does both" was not re-exercised after the fix.
owner_decision: Bitcoin waits for tor to start (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — quadlet/systemd units need the same ordering, and the post-crash restart path must respect it too.

class: silent fallback reported as success
what_happened: `lnd-start.sh` checked tor's control port once (`nc -z tor 9051`) and, when it failed, started LND without its Tor onion; this happened at the 2026-09-30 boot, at Start All (via the cascade) and in Restart All's first cascade, and only an accidental second cascade restored it — the record had first said "no harm was seen".
root_cause: A single readiness probe with a silent degrade path and no monitor for the advertised onion.
lesson: LND must wait for Tor's control port for a bounded time (2 minutes) before starting; if it still starts without its onion the node must raise a high alert, and a monitor must check that LND's onion actually answers through Tor, not only that getinfo lists it.
tripwire: lndTorWait.test.ts (runs the marked wait block in sh with stub nc/sleep), lndOnionMissing.test.ts (no onion for 10 min → lnd_onion_missing, high), lndOnionReach.test.ts (two failed SOCKS probes → lnd_onion_unreachable, alert-only).
owner_decision: "Wait for tor, then alert (Recommended)"; after a tor restart: "Alert you to restart LND (Recommended)"
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node will also advertise LND over Tor; a silently clearnet-only or unreachable node defeats the privacy design.

class: recovery verified against the degraded state instead of the expected state
what_happened: A tor restart during the owner's stop ran `tor-start.sh`, which skipped every hidden service whose container was not resolvable ("Skipping bitcoin (container not resolvable after 90s)"), so tor served only the dashboard's onion; Start All did not restart tor; the canary fired `tor_onion_unreachable`, and runbook `RB-TOR-ONION-RECOVER-01` reported "completed 1/1 steps" yet fixed nothing because it probed only the onions tor still listed. The recovery script's `--missing` mode could also start a stopped tor.
root_cause: Recovery derived its target set from tor's current config rather than from what should be published, and its start step ran in every mode.
lesson: Tor recovery must compute the expected hidden-service set from what should be running, count any missing one as a failure, repair at bring-up (restart tor, then LND whose onion depends on it), probe each onion through SOCKS, and never start services during an owner stop.
tripwire: torRecoverMissing.test.ts (fake docker on PATH over a temp copy of tor's folder: --missing, --check, --repair-after-up, a stopped tor never started; one unexplained failure under full-suite load is recorded), nodePowerTorOnions.test.ts, stackUpRepairsOnions.test.ts (text match).
owner_decision: "Restart tor now (Recommended)"; at Start All: "Repair: restart tor, then LND (Recommended)"
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node publishes several onions; recovery must check the full expected set.

class: secondary orchestrator acts on a side-effect signal and races the primary
what_happened: The control plane's cookie cascade (`control-plane/src/cascade.rs`) started electrs and LND as soon as bitcoind's cookie appeared — 5–8 s after bitcoind, about 25 s before compose's `service_healthy` gate — so LND came up without its onion, and when bitcoind restarted within one start the cascade ran twice.
root_cause: Restarts were triggered by a credential file appearing, independently of compose's health-gated ordering.
lesson: Only one orchestrator may own start ordering; dependants restart when the dependency is healthy (debounced), never merely because a credential file changed, and credential rotation must be explicit.
tripwire: Suggested: journal check that dependants start after bitcoind is healthy and a test that one cookie rewrite causes at most one dependant restart (the record reported the cascade to the owner rather than fixing it).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node should have one supervisor for ordering and one credential hand-off.

class: editing a running shell script in place
what_happened: To apply the tested LND start-script change: PID 1 sits in `wait` and reads the rest of the file when LND exits, so the file could be written only while LND was stopped; the session's `docker stop lnd` was refused by the permission check, so it waited for the owner's Safe Shutdown, then wrote the tested copy in place (same inode, `cmp` identical, `sh -n` OK).
root_cause: A shell reads its script incrementally, so an in-place edit changes what a running PID 1 executes next (the 2026-09-25 lesson).
lesson: The node must never modify a script a running process is executing; ship scripts immutably (new file plus restart, or an image update) and develop on a copy.
tripwire: Deploy procedure that replaces start scripts only while the service is stopped, with `sh -n` and `cmp` against the tested copy.
applies_to_new_node: maybe — read-only Fedora IoT images remove most of this class, but any writable start script keeps it.

class: secret read into an agent transcript
what_happened: While looking for LND's tor settings, a session command printed LND's tor control password (`tor.password` in `lnd.conf`) into its tool output; it was not shown in the owner's chat but is in the session transcript, and rotation (three places) was left to the owner.
root_cause: A config file mixing ordinary settings with a secret was read whole, and the guard classifies secret files by name, not content.
lesson: Secrets must live in dedicated secret files, never inline in general config that operators or agents read, and agent tooling must redact secret-looking keys when reading config.
tripwire: Suggested: a guard rule treating config files with embedded credentials as secret or redacting on read, and a CI check that non-secret config files contain no password/token keys.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node keeps an AI assistant and AI-built development; secrets must be separated by file.

class: substring identity match picks the wrong entity
what_happened: Bitcoin showed 83.38% and LND 83.92% uptime with an MTTR of ~58 s: the uptime poller matched containers with `name.contains(svc)`, so "bitcoin" also matched `bitcoin-testnet` and "lnd" matched `lnd-testnet`, and `find` over a HashMap picked either at random per poll; while the testnet pair was stopped, half the polls read the stopped container (outage lengths formed a geometric series, ratio 0.48). Real mainnet uptime was ≈99.92–99.93%, and the flapping went back to June.
root_cause: Components were identified by substring over an unordered map.
lesson: The node must identify services by exact name (or an explicit alias list such as bitcoin|bitcoin-knots), never by substring, and never let a testnet or sibling instance stand in for the mainnet one.
tripwire: Pure-function unit test with `bitcoin` Up and `bitcoin-testnet` Exited in the same map that must read Up; siblings to sweep: `service_monitor.rs:637` and the page's `includes('mempool')` grouping.
owner_decision: Yes, in fact, check all measurement on the Dashboard. Make sure every one of them is actually meansuring the right thing and is correctly measuring what it's suppose to.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node runs mainnet plus test networks across two machines; exact identity is mandatory.

class: absence of samples extrapolated as the last known state
what_happened: Machine-off time counted as UP: the 2026-09-29 crash (10 h 27 m, −1.45 points) had no row because the poller extended the last state forever; there was no last-sample time, so a dead poller was invisible; "unmeasured" intervals were later stored but never used while the docs said such time was "not measured"; the page section vanished silently on 401/502 and drew a missing % as a red 0.00%.
root_cause: The poller recorded transitions only, with no heartbeat to tell a gap from continuous state.
lesson: Every monitor must write a heartbeat (last sample time); on restart the node must classify the gap — machine off (the system booted after the last sample) or unmeasured (machine on, poller not sampling) — and expose `stale` when no sample has arrived for a few polls; an unavailable section says so instead of vanishing.
tripwire: Rust tests of classify_gap and gap recording; API fields `last_sample_ts` and `stale`; a 900,000-case fuzz of timelines against an independent per-second model; ReliabilityPanel tests for the unavailable card and "—".
owner_decision: Count it as downtime (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the Pi and the x86 will both lose power or crash; a heartbeat-based gap rule is required for honest uptime.
port_candidate: control-plane/src/uptime.rs (classify_gap, summarize_with, with its inline tests)

class: availability metric conflates planned, machine-off and service downtime
what_happened: Once machine-off counted, one 10.5 h crash dominated MTTR (bitcoin 60 min, LND 83 min); an owner Stop All or testnet4 switch-off counted as downtime; a power-off after Safe Shutdown counted as downtime although the docs said it did not; start-up after Start All (3–4 min waiting for bitcoind) was recorded as an outage.
root_cause: One "down" status covered every reason a service was not running, and the rules had not been put to the owner as choices.
lesson: The node's uptime model must keep distinct states — up, own outage, stopped by the owner, machine off, unmeasured — with owner-chosen rules: MTTR and the incident count use only the service's own outages; stopped and unmeasured time leave the window; start-up after Start All or a planned power-on stays "stopped" until first up, capped at 15 min; after a crash, a service still down 15 min after measuring resumes is its own outage.
tripwire: Inline Rust tests for each rule and boundary (+899/+900/+901 s); fuzzed timelines against a per-second model (240,000 and 192,000 cases); live /api/uptime compared with a recomputation from a DB copy on every field.
owner_decision: "Services only (Recommended)" (MTTR); "Show as 'stopped by you' (Recommended)"; "No: 'stopped by you' (Recommended)" (power-off after Safe Shutdown); "Stopped until up, 15-min cap (Recommended)"; "15-min rule, like Start All (Recommended)" (slow start after a crash); "Keep 'stopped by you' (Recommended)" (testnet4 stopped, then a reboot)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the same states and choices apply to both machines of the new node.
port_candidate: control-plane/src/uptime.rs (summarize_with and Exclusions, with its inline tests)

class: intent marker written after the action it labels
what_happened: The testnet4 Stop wrote its "stopped by you" marker only after `compose down` returned (up to 90 s), so a 30 s poll could see the pair gone with no marker and record a real outage; the routes' timeouts (stop 60 s, start 120 s) were also shorter than compose's worst case (90 s grace per container, a 300 s lock wait), so a slow stop cleared the marker and a slow start kept it.
root_cause: The marker followed the action instead of preceding it, and wrapper timeouts were shorter than the work they wrapped.
lesson: The node must record an intent (planned stop, maintenance) before starting the action and remove it if the action fails, and every wrapper timeout must exceed the worst case of what it wraps (lock wait plus stop graces).
tripwire: testnetOwnerStop.test.ts (marker written before down, removed on failure; red first); timeouts sized as 300 s lock + 2 × 90 s grace + margin = 540 s, with the reasoning in a code comment.
applies_to_new_node: yes — every planned stop on the new node needs the marker-first ordering.

class: boundary error at a sliding-window edge
what_happened: A crash interval that ended in the 15 minutes before `window_start` was not fetched (`end_ts > window_start`), so the in-window start-up would have counted as a full outage on the live history around 2026-10-30 (bitcoin 2 incidents and MTTR 108 s instead of 1 and 60 s); separately, a component measured for under 30 days was summarised over a fixed 30-day window assuming Up before its first event, so tapd showed "100.00%" under "30-day".
root_cause: Window queries ignored state that began before the window and the component's own measured_since.
lesson: Windowed metrics must fetch the intervals that affect the window even when they end just before it (by the largest grace), judge the first segment by when it really began, and use max(now − window, measured_since) with the span reported.
tripwire: Inline tests a_crash_start_up_cut_by_the_window_start_is_still_not_an_outage, the_store_sees_a_crash_that_ended_just_before_the_window, a_component_measured_for_less_than_the_window_is_summarised_over_its_measured_time; a 192,000-case fuzz that fails the old logic on 7,253 of 25,000.
applies_to_new_node: yes — every rolling-window figure on the new node has the same edge.

class: errors swallowed into plausible defaults
what_happened: In the uptime service, failed interval, heartbeat and transition writes logged at debug or not at all; an unreadable or malformed owner-stop marker read as "no stop"; a failed summary row was simply absent from the JSON; the single-component handler answered 404 "not measured" on a DB error and `uptime_pct: 100` for a component never measured; an invalid UPTIME_POLL_SECS silently became 30; the backend's `currentBootId()` fell back to 'unknown-boot' silently.
root_cause: Error branches returned the most convenient default instead of reporting.
lesson: Every failure path in a measurement must be visible: warn once until it recovers (not every poll), answer 500 rather than a plausible value, list rows that could not be computed (`missing`), answer 404 for unknown components, and never read an unreadable marker as "no stop" without saying so.
tripwire: API `missing` array checked live; 404 test for unknown components; the record notes the log-only warning paths have no unit tests (checked by reading).
applies_to_new_node: yes — Law 1 applies to every new monitor.

class: history repair without labelled provenance
what_happened: The coin-flip history (bitcoin 25,024 rows, LND 25,040 rows) was replaced by electrs's co-incident real transitions and the crash gap added as machine-off, after a backup and dry run, with the exact SQL recorded and note rows labelling the rebuild; the backup `data/uptime.db.bak-…` was not git-ignored, so `git add -A` would have committed a 3 MB SQLite DB.
root_cause: Months of history were corrupted by the matching bug, and the repair's artefacts were outside .gitignore.
lesson: Repairs of recorded history must be backed up, dry-run, reversible, recorded with their exact SQL and labelled in the data itself ("reconstructed, not measured", shown with the figures); backup artefacts must be ignored by version control.
tripwire: `git check-ignore` on the backup pattern; integrity_check on both DBs; API recomputed from the DB copy (50,064 rows deleted, 56 inserted, 0 changed).
owner_decision: Rebuild, labelled (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: maybe — the new node starts with fresh history, but any later repair of uptime or ledger data needs this procedure.

class: deploy not verified by running-artifact identity
what_happened: `cp` over the running control-plane binary failed with "Text file busy" (nothing restarted), so staging became copy to `.new` plus `mv -f`. In the power-buttons record a chained `cp … && restart` failed at the copy, the session misread it and then restarted the service onto the OLD binary; the old binary was afterwards saved from /proc/<pid>/exe as a rollback copy.
root_cause: In-place overwrite of a running executable, and success judged by the restart command rather than by what is running.
lesson: The node must stage new binaries by atomic rename, keep the previous one for rollback, and verify after restart that the running executable equals the built artifact (`cmp /proc/<pid>/exe`) with no source newer than the build.
tripwire: Post-deploy `cmp /proc/<pid>/exe target/release/control-plane` and a no-src-newer check (the repo's deploy rule).
applies_to_new_node: maybe — image updates with automatic rollback replace binary copying, but 'running artifact = verified artifact' still has to be checked after each update.

class: process guard blind to alternate write paths
what_happened: Uptime code beside Rust inline tests was written through `python3` scripts while the fix-lock was on; the guard cannot see such writes, so the lock could not have stopped a test edit. An unquoted shell heredoc used to write the record executed its backticked spans as commands (nothing changed; ImageMagick's `import` failed for lack of a display).
root_cause: The guard inspects only certain tool calls, and shell heredocs interpolate backticks.
lesson: Guardrails for AI-built node code must cover every write path or forbid the ones they cannot see, and generated text must be written with quoted heredocs or file-write tools, never through an interpolating shell.
tripwire: Edit-tool-only rule for code under a lock; verifier compares the test module with its pre-lock text; quoted heredocs only after the incident.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new repo's guard (shared guard.py) has the same blind spot.

class: silent truncation of context fed to the model
what_happened: `formatCardsForPrompt(matches, 1500)` hard-cut the reliability concept card (2,272 characters) to 1,484, ending "…until each service is first up, fo…", and because the slim path skips the document search whenever a card matches, the model never saw the 15-minute cap, Restart All, the Knots exception or "not measured" — the cut sentence read as the opposite of the owner's rule. 17 of 68 cards exceeded the budget; later 13 of 36 reliability questions reached the model with neither card nor guide.
root_cause: A fixed byte budget truncated content mid-sentence without any signal, and the fast path skipped retrieval.
lesson: The node's assistant must never silently truncate a knowledge item: each item must fit its budget whole (enforced by a test), the prompt must record which items actually reached the model, and a fast path without a matching item must fall back to document search.
tripwire: conceptCardBudget.test.ts: each card reaches the model whole through the real formatter, with a KNOWN_OVER_BUDGET debt list that may only shrink; an offline 36-question harness through the real slim gate and classifier.
owner_decision: "Shorten cards to fit (Recommended)"; then "Search docs when no card (Recommended)"
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant will run a small local model with a tight context; silent truncation is its default failure mode.

class: retrieval ranking biased by lexical artefacts and never measured
what_happened: For 3 of the 13 failing questions a card was attached but the wrong one (2 lost to a worse card filling the budget, 1 ranked third below the top-2 cut). Offline analysis found four word-matching biases — substring keyword matches ("back"→"backup"), common words weighted like key ones, uncapped keyword hits, a reward for longer cards; the `/dashboard` page boost never fired because the Dashboard route is `/`; `conceptCardsUsed` listed cards the budget had dropped.
root_cause: Keyword scoring was hand-tuned without a labelled evaluation set, and telemetry reported intent rather than what reached the model.
lesson: The assistant's retrieval must be evaluated on a labelled question set (top-1/top-2/none accuracy before and after every change), match whole words with term weighting, and its telemetry must list only the items actually included in the prompt.
tripwire: Labelled set of 242 questions run offline with the real card functions (troubleshoot mode top-1 24.0% as the baseline); cardRanking tests with accuracy floors.
owner_decision: "We can increase the context window to 3000 bytes, if needed to fit the 2 relevant cars.  If better match is not ranked first, what does that mean?  Our ranking is wrong or is using some other criteria than match?" — then chose "Fix the word-matching (Recommended)"
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new assistant's retrieval needs an evaluation set from day one.

class: knowledge chunk exceeds the embedding window or lacks retrievable shape
what_happened: "What does MTTR mean?" did not retrieve the guide until a question-shaped section was added; the corrections file had no `##` headings, so it was one chunk that the 512-token embedding truncates; several owner phrasings found no answering section until sections were split and retitled.
root_cause: Documents were written as prose rather than as sections sized and phrased for the retriever.
lesson: Knowledge for the node's assistant must be sectioned under question-shaped headings, each section within the embedding limit (target ≤ 450 tokens, never over 512), with retrieval checked against the owner's real phrasings after each edit.
tripwire: Per-section token counts via the embedding server's /tokenize (none over 512); a top-3 retrieval table for named owner questions.
applies_to_new_node: yes — same retriever constraints for the new assistant.

class: health check conflates catching up with down
what_happened: Knots's healthcheck (`docker-compose.knots.yml:146`) requires `initialblockdownload: false`, so bitcoin reads as down for a whole first sync and whenever its tip is over about a day old; LND, electrs and mempool can read down too — restarted `--no-deps` during an engine switch, or restarted at once by Docker after a crash.
root_cause: One health check answered both "is the process serving" and "is it caught up".
lesson: The node's bitcoind health must separate "running and serving RPC" from "caught up" (IBD/syncing), so a node catching up after being off is reported as syncing, not as an outage, and dependants' readiness is defined accordingly.
tripwire: Suggested: health-state tests for catch-up after a long offline period (the record documented the limitation in the guides rather than changing the check).
applies_to_new_node: yes — a Pi 5 pruned node that was off for days will be catching up; that must not read as an outage.

class: evidence written from memory instead of from logs
what_happened: Four verification rounds in a row (#9–#12) caught an estimated time in this record; counts ("7 stretches", "14 transitions") and a claimed HTTP 200 from a command that printed only the body were also wrong.
root_cause: Times and counts were written from recollection instead of read from a log, transcript or file mtime.
lesson: Every time, count and status in a record or report about the node must be read from a log, transcript, mtime or command output, and re-checked on the final text before it is quoted.
tripwire: CLAUDE.md rule added: "Times in a build record come from a log, the transcript or a file's mtime, never from memory"; verifiers recheck each quoted number.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new repo's build records follow the same procedure.

class: backup path never exercised end to end
what_happened: The channel.db backup had never succeeded on this node: 186 `skipped_no_key` (2026-04-30 → 06-02), 2 `stop_failed` and 3 `read_failed` on 06-02 (an old read path, since fixed), then 450 `skipped_no_channels`; the first channel the owner opens will be the first real run of stop → copy → encrypt → write → restart.
root_cause: Skips were recorded as normal outcomes, no rehearsal exercised the full path, and nothing checked for a last success.
lesson: Every backup the node relies on must have last-success evidence and an alert when it has never succeeded or keeps skipping, and a new backup path must be rehearsed end to end (e.g. on a test-network LND) before it is relied on.
tripwire: Suggested: a health check on the backups table — time since the last `success` per backup kind, skip reasons counted; the record offered the owner a testnet4 rehearsal.
applies_to_new_node: yes — Law 4 (absence of success) for every backup on both machines.

class: unbounded backup retention
what_happened: Nothing ever deleted a channel.db copy: each run wrote a new `channeldb-<time>-<hash>.aes` of about 229 MB to two folders on the main disk.
root_cause: The backup writer had no retention step.
lesson: Every backup writer must prune to an explicit retention count after a successful write, touching only its own file pattern, with the count configurable and pruning failures reported.
tripwire: Inline Rust tests `files_to_prune` (only `channeldb-*.aes`, newest N kept) and `keep_count_from` (default 4, range 1–96, RIKURI_CHANNELDB_KEEP).
owner_decision: Newest 4 (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the Pi has the least storage; unbounded copies would fill it first.
