port_candidate: control-plane/src/backup/channeldb.rs (files_to_prune, keep_count_from, ChangeWatch, with its inline tests)

class: backup cadence not tied to state changes
what_happened: The SCB (`channel.backup`) was already copied within 30 s of any channel open, close or pending change and mirrored to both backup drives, but the full channel.db was copied only every 6 h (stopping LND about a minute each time); a watcher now reads the open channel points every 60 s, waits for 2 minutes without change and runs one backup at least 10 minutes after the previous one, with every existing gate.
root_cause: The full-database backup ran on a timer only.
lesson: The node must back up channel state on every channel open or close — the SCB immediately, any full-DB copy debounced and rate-limited because it pauses LND — keep the SCB as the fund-recovery file, and state that an old channel.db must not be restored because it can trigger a penalty that loses a channel's funds.
tripwire: Inline tests of ChangeWatch (first reading is a baseline, 120 s settle, ≥600 s apart, a failed reading changes nothing); live log "watching for channel opens/closes".
owner_decision: "2. channel backup should be made when ever there's changes to its state so 15 min should be right ( also open and close channels)." Choice: "Also channel.db after open/close"
applies_to_new_node: maybe — SCB-on-change applies as is; whether the new node stops LND to copy channel.db should be revisited as an owner choice.

class: UI states a policy the code does not implement
what_happened: Settings → Backup → Recommended said channel.db was backed up "Every 15 min / Keeps last 24 hours (96 copies)" and config files "On configuration changes"; the code did every 6 h and hourly.
root_cause: The text was hand-written apart from the scheduler's constants.
lesson: Schedules and retention shown to the owner must be rendered from the same constants the scheduler uses, or tested against them, never hand-written.
tripwire: backupWording.test.ts pins the displayed cadence; suggested: derive the text from the scheduler configuration.
applies_to_new_node: yes — backup promises shown to the owner are part of the recovery guarantee.

class: monitor silent on its own failure and noisy on planned maintenance
what_happened: A failed reading of the open channels was silent, so a channel change would not be backed up; once a warning was added it would have fired at every 6-hourly backup because the backup itself stops LND, so the watcher now skips its reading while a backup holds the backup lock.
root_cause: The watcher did not report its own failure and did not know about the system's planned interruptions.
lesson: Each watcher must say once when it cannot observe and once when it recovers, and must suppress readings during the node's own planned interruptions, keyed to the same lock, so warnings stay meaningful.
tripwire: Rust test backup_in_progress_follows_the_backup_lock and `observe_failed()` returning true on the first failure; stated gap: the watcher's call to `backup_in_progress()` is untested.
applies_to_new_node: yes — applies to every watcher on the new node.

class: wrapper does not forward SIGTERM so the daemon is SIGKILLed
what_happened: On 2026-06-02 three backup runs stopped LND with 60–61 s of downtime each, equal to the stop grace — probably Docker's SIGKILL, because LND's wrapper did not forward SIGTERM until the 2026-09-25 fix (the record marks this as inferred, not proven).
root_cause: (Inferred by the record) the container's PID 1 wrapper script did not pass SIGTERM on to LND.
lesson: A wrapper that launches LND or bitcoind must forward SIGTERM and pass on the daemon's exit status, and every stop must be checked for a clean exit rather than a grace-period kill.
tripwire: lndStartScript.test.ts ("TERM to the wrapper is passed to LND", "LND's own exit status is passed on") — noted elsewhere in this batch as timing-flaky under full-suite load.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node will also wrap daemons in containers or units; signal forwarding is required for clean stops.

class: running only the tests you think are affected
what_happened: Adding the word "after" to one concept card turned the backend suite red: the fallback ranking weights words by rarity across all cards, so an unrelated fixture question lost its card (0.2159 against a 21.8% floor); the session had run only the card tests after the edit.
root_cause: A content edit changed corpus-wide statistics, and the full suite was not rerun.
lesson: Any change to the node's knowledge content or code must be followed by the full gate, not a hand-picked subset, because corpus-wide statistics couple unrelated items.
tripwire: Full jest before claiming green; cardRanking accuracy-floor tests.
applies_to_new_node: yes — same coupling in any retrieval corpus.

class: unreachable UI code duplicating live controls
what_happened: `SecuritySettings.tsx` held an "AI" tab (emergency stop, spending limits, approval mode) and a "Security guide" tab that could never be shown because the tabs list held only `auth`; its state, effect and `fetchAIControls` existed only for them while the live controls were in AI Settings. 227 lines, 12 icon imports, 7 CSS blocks and a leftover `EmergencyStopButton` import were removed.
root_cause: Controls were moved to a new page without deleting the old copy.
lesson: Safety controls (emergency stop, spending limits) must exist in exactly one place; moved code is deleted in the same change and proven unreachable by a render test.
tripwire: securitySettingsDeadTabs.test.ts (fails while the branches exist); jsdom render shows one tab and only the two auth fetches.
owner_decision: 3. Dead code should be cleaned up if not needed.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new UI should never carry a second, stale copy of a safety control.

class: parallel tests race on process-global state
what_happened: `watchonly::writes_gate_recognises_truthy_values` failed 2 of 5 full-suite runs and 20 of 30 runs of the module alone: several tests set and restore `RIKURI_WATCHONLY_WRITES_ENABLED` with no lock, and Rust runs tests in parallel threads sharing one environment; a second family (`RIKURI_DASHBOARD_URL`) failed 1 of 20 full runs.
root_cause: Tests mutated the process environment concurrently.
lesson: Node code must take configuration as explicit parameters so tests do not mutate process-global state; where env access is unavoidable a module-wide lock must serialise set → run → restore.
tripwire: Repeated-run measurement (20/30 → 0/30; 1/20 → 0/20); the record states this guard is statistical, not a deterministic test.
owner_decision: 5. Clean the flaky Rust test. If not needed then delete/clean.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new Rust code should be designed with injected config from the start.

class: test reaches live system
what_happened: `dashboard_internal::tests::internal_calls_use_the_token_and_the_machine_routes` failed with a 401 from the real dashboard: while another test had removed `RIKURI_DASHBOARD_URL`, the code fell back to its default URL, the live dashboard on the node machine.
root_cause: Production default endpoints applied inside tests whenever the override was absent.
lesson: A test must never be able to reach a live node service: test builds must have no production default endpoints (fail closed when unset), and test runs on a node machine must be isolated from its live services.
tripwire: Test-only `DASHBOARD_URL_ENV_LOCK` in the old repo; suggested: a network-isolated test runner and a test configuration with no default URLs.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's tests will run on or beside live mainnet services.

class: ratcheted debt list for a size budget
what_happened: All 16 remaining over-budget concept cards were rewritten to fit (lines 1,408–1,474 of the 1,485 limit), each checked against the code, and `KNOWN_OVER_BUDGET` was emptied, so the gate now holds all 69 cards; the card with the most owner choices (3,022 characters) fit at 1,463 without a split.
root_cause: Card length had never been gated, so cards grew past what the prompt builder could carry.
lesson: Every piece of assistant knowledge with a context budget must be gated by a test that fails when any item would be cut, with existing debt listed explicitly and allowed only to shrink.
tripwire: conceptCardBudget.test.ts (each card fits alone through the real formatter; the debt list empty; worst pair 2,962 ≤ 3,000).
owner_decision: Shorten cards to fit (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the same gate belongs on the new assistant's knowledge.

class: assistant knowledge drifts from code
what_happened: Rewriting the cards found false statements in them: Loop called an "off-chain swap" (the page says on-chain), "closing ALL channels sweeps to the cold wallet", "wallets and channels live in Docker volumes" (host folders), "Strict on Core and Knots identical" (Knots also writes `rejectparasites=0`), a July budget design, seven stale Settings statements. The verifier then found the same false statements still live in the guides after the record said they were fixed, and "Does a force close send my funds to my cold wallet?" got no answer.
root_cause: Knowledge was written once and never re-verified against the code; fixes landed in one store (cards) and not its siblings (guides).
lesson: Each assistant knowledge claim about the node must be verified against code with file:line evidence, re-reviewed when that code changes (last_reviewed), fixed in every store that carries it, and money-safety facts such as where a force close pays must be answerable.
tripwire: Grep for each known-false phrase across cards, guides and the index; live queries for the safety questions after reload ("Where do my funds go after a force close?" carries the fact).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new assistant's knowledge will drift the same way unless tied to code review.

class: background ingestion failure silent
what_happened: The doc-watcher's automatic ingest of all six edited guides failed (`ChromaConnectionError`: chromadb had been stopped by the owner's Safe Shutdown), and the record did not say so until the verifier found it in the journal.
root_cause: Ingest failures reached only the journal, and nothing checked the index against the files.
lesson: The node's knowledge indexer must report a failed ingest as a visible health finding and verify index freshness (indexed count equals expected) after every change.
tripwire: Post-change check "Chroma N = indexed" plus a query for the new text; suggested: an indexer health finding on failure.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new assistant's index will also be offline whenever its store is stopped.

class: scheduled report routed by severity to a channel with no receiver
what_happened: The daily digest ran every day at 06:00 and logged "Daily digest sent", but it was sent at GREEN → LOW severity, LOW is routed to the dashboard bell only, and the bell delivered it to "0 client(s)" — it had never reached Telegram; the weekly reflection was titled "[YELLOW] Node Guardian", which did not say what it was.
root_cause: Scheduled reports reused alert-severity routing, and "sent" meant handed to the router, not delivered.
lesson: Scheduled reports must have explicit channels and a descriptive title, and the node may log "sent" only when at least one owner-facing channel confirmed delivery; while the owner has stopped the node a summary says so, with no LLM call and no list of stopped services.
tripwire: guardianSummaries.test.ts, guardianWeeklyRoute.test.ts; acceptance by the notification-history entry "Daily digest — Node Guardian" with `channels.telegram.success: true` (seen live on 2026-10-03).
owner_decision: Fix the guardian's daily telegram summary (is this sent to Telegram, I don't think I've been receiving any daily summary. Used to receive weekly summary from Groq, but not anymore).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's reports must prove delivery, not dispatch.

class: behaviour-changing default introduced without exposing it
what_happened: While making the weekly reflection's channels explicit, the session narrowed them to Telegram, email and the bell, silently dropping Push and Discord that its HIGH route had always used; later it told the owner the alert hold lasted "up to 45 minutes" when an engine-switch post-flight renews the flag for up to 6 h.
root_cause: Implementation choices changed behaviour beyond the owner's request, and their costs were estimated rather than read from the code.
lesson: Any change to who is notified, or for how long alerts are held, must be exactly the owner's request or put to him as an explicit, costed choice, with the cost read from the code.
tripwire: Verifier review for unrequested behaviour changes; guardianWeeklyRoute.test.ts pins the weekly route to the HIGH route.
applies_to_new_node: yes — 'a choice not exposed is not a choice' applies to every default on the new node.

class: a broad suppression flag silences safety monitors
what_happened: To stop false "is down" alerts during Start All / Restart All, `isInMaintenance()` was made to read the timed maintenance flag; that also paused the node monitors it gates (force closes, fund movements, fees, mempool, peers) during Start All, Restart All, an engine switch, its post-flight (renewed up to 6 h) and relay-setting applies. It was narrowed to hold only the external "is down" alert, only for `owner_start`/`owner_restart`, at most 25/40 min.
root_cause: One maintenance boolean gated both alert delivery and safety monitoring, and was set by more operations than the one the owner meant.
lesson: Alert suppression on the node must be scoped by alert type, reason and a bounded window, and must never pause safety monitors such as force-close and fund-movement detection.
tripwire: healthMaintenanceFlag.test.ts (the flag holds the alert and does NOT make isInMaintenance true), healthHeldAlertsFlow.test.ts (the reasons that do and do not hold); mutation "any flag holds" → 3 red.
owner_decision: Restart All health services should read the flag, right?
applies_to_new_node: yes — money-safety monitors must keep running through every maintenance window on the new node.

class: edge-triggered alert suppressed during a window is lost
what_happened: Alerts fire only on a change to "down", so an alert held during Restart All was dropped, not delayed; and a held "down" consumed the 5-minute cooldown, so a service that came back inside the window and then really crashed within 5 minutes got 0 alerts.
root_cause: Suppression discarded the edge event and still consumed throttle state.
lesson: A held alert must be kept per service and sent when the window ends if the condition still holds; a held alert that is dropped must free its cooldown and be logged.
tripwire: healthHeldAlerts.test.ts, healthHeldAlertsFlow.test.ts (down during Restart All → held → window ends, still down → sent once), healthHeldAlertsEdges.test.ts (planned down, back up, real crash within 5 min → 1 send); stated gaps: the window check in releaseHeldAlerts has no biting test, and the held map lives in memory.
applies_to_new_node: yes — any alert hold on the new node must delay, not drop.

class: unconfigured channels counted as delivery failures
what_happened: Push was not set up yet was attempted and counted as failing every send for at least 10 days (0 delivered); disabled Discord and SMS were still attempted and counted as failures; Telegram had 21 real failures 2026-09-25 → 10-02 (DNS EAI_AGAIN, a TLS name error) in the same tally — the "9" first quoted was only the 200-record history window.
root_cause: Channel configuration state was not distinguished from delivery failure.
lesson: The node must not attempt or count disabled or unconfigured channels, and must track real delivery failures per channel with an alert when the owner's primary channel keeps failing.
tripwire: Suggested: per-channel delivery stats excluding disabled channels, with a finding on repeated primary-channel failure (flagged to the owner, not changed in this record).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the owner relies on Telegram/email from the new node; real failures must not hide in noise.

class: alternate configuration never parsed by any gate (rots while inactive)
what_happened: The Knots compose overlay carried six '#' comment lines inside a `command: |` literal block, so compose refused to parse it ('invalid command line string') and the lines would also have reached bitcoind as stray arguments. Switching the engine to Knots was broken from 2026-09-20 to 2026-10-02 without anyone noticing, because the node ran Core.
root_cause: In a YAML literal block '#' lines are part of the command string, and no test or CI step ever parsed the inactive Knots overlay.
lesson: The node must parse and validate every alternate configuration it can switch to (other engine, other network, pruned vs full profile) in CI, not only the active one, and start commands must never contain comment lines.
tripwire: dashboard/backend/src/tests/composeCommandBlocks.test.ts walks every docker-compose*.yml in the repo (skipping node_modules, .git, data, dist, target) and fails on any '#' line inside a command block; it pins all 14 Knots start options. Plus `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.knots.yml config` must exit 0.
owner_decision: Fix now, with a test (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node has inactive variants (Core/Knots, x86 full vs Pi 5 pruned profiles) that rot unless every variant is rendered and parsed in CI

class: policy setting with two sources of truth
what_happened: Relay-policy flags had been taken off the start commands on 2026-09-20 so the owner's relay posture lives in bitcoin.conf only; verification found the Knots test checked only 6 of 14 options and did not assert the absence of relay flags that its title promised.
root_cause: The rule 'relay policy is not passed on the command line' existed only as a comment, not as an assertion.
lesson: The node must keep the owner's relay policy (datacarrier, permitbaremultisig, rejectparasites, rejecttokens and similar) in exactly one place, bitcoin.conf, and a test must fail if any start command carries a relay-policy flag.
tripwire: composeCommandBlocks.test.ts asserts none of datacarrier, permitbaremultisig, rejectparasites, rejecttokens is in the bitcoin-knots command; mutation check: a planted -datacarrier=0 line is caught.
applies_to_new_node: yes — relay posture is an owner choice on both nodes and needs one source

class: identity keyed on a non-unique attribute (basename collision overwrites)
what_happened: The live Chroma knowledge store held 1,530 chunks though 1,593 were indexed: three guides named glossary.md in different folders overwrote each other, so the Bitcoin (34 chunks) and Lightning (29) glossaries were missing from what the assistant could retrieve.
root_cause: Chunk ids (`<file name>_chunk_<n>`) and the delete-before-reindex both keyed on the file name alone, not the path.
lesson: The assistant's knowledge index must key every document on a unique identity (full path, or names enforced unique), and indexed vs stored counts must be compared after each ingest.
tripwire: docNamesUnique.test.ts fails if two .md files under the ingest roots (docs/rag, docs/knowledge) share a name; live check: 'Indexed N documents (M chunks)' equals the collection count (1,603 = 1,603).
owner_decision: 1. Make the 2 glossaries if that's what's needed.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant will retrieve from node guides; silent loss of guides degrades answers without any error

class: derived index never removes deleted sources (stale data served)
what_happened: When a guide was deleted or renamed, the doc watcher only logged 'Deleted: … (re-index to remove)'; its chunks stayed in the store and kept being served to the assistant.
root_cause: The watcher handled add/change but had no remove path, and nothing reconciled the store with the files on disk.
lesson: Any derived index (RAG store, search index, cache) must remove entries when their source is deleted and must reconcile against the source of truth.
tripwire: ragService.removeDocument on unlink; pure `staleSources(indexed, onDisk)` with ragSources.test.ts; `doc-watcher --once` prunes sources no longer present under docs/.
applies_to_new_node: yes — same class for any assistant knowledge store or derived index

class: destructive reconcile on a partial view (unreadable listing treated as empty)
what_happened: Verifier round 1 found the new prune could run on a partial view of the disk: walkMarkdown returned [] for a missing or unreadable folder, so existing guides would look deleted and be swept from the store.
root_cause: A listing error was indistinguishable from an empty listing, and the prune trusted it.
lesson: A reconcile or prune step must refuse to delete anything unless its view of the source is complete (every folder read, non-empty result), and must say that it refused.
tripwire: `safeToSweep(onDisk, walkErrors)` with ragSweepSafety.test.ts; pruneStale refuses and logs otherwise. Stated gap: walkMarkdown's error count and the pruneStale wiring have no test.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the same rule governs backup rotation, snapshot pruning and any cleanup that deletes by absence

class: fix deployed but the running process still runs the old code
what_happened: The doc-watcher fix was built, but the running rikuri-doc-watcher service (started 2026-09-30) kept the old code until the owner restarted it, because the restart needed his sudo password; until then a guide deleted meanwhile would stay in the store until the next manual run.
root_cause: The deploy path could not restart that host service, and nothing reported which processes still ran old code.
lesson: Every deploy must restart (or explicitly report) each process whose code changed, and a check must compare the running binary or code with the deployed one.
tripwire: Manual owner restart (active since 2026-10-03 06:43:55). Related checks in this batch: `cmp /proc/<pid>/exe` against the built binary (electrs-0.12 record) and smoke's '(deleted)' exe warning (native-modules record).
applies_to_new_node: yes — image deploys on Fedora IoT reboot into new code, but services updated outside the image still need this

class: fast path skips retrieval when nothing matched (ungrounded answer)
what_happened: On a confident classification the assistant took the slim path, which skipped the document search even when no concept card matched; an offline run of the real classifier showed 13 of 36 uptime questions reaching the local model with neither a card nor the docs. After the switch to blended ranking, a card nearly always cleared the bar, so the doc search almost never ran and weak matches (top score below 0.45, right about half the time) got two unrelated cards and no docs.
root_cause: The fast-path gate keyed on intent confidence, not on whether any knowledge was attached or how strong the match was.
lesson: The assistant must not send a question to the model without grounding when retrieval could supply it: no card, or a weak best match, must trigger the document search, and a failed search must be logged and stated, never silently empty.
tripwire: slimKnowledge.test.ts ('the weak bar is 0.45', 'below the weak bar → the card stays, and the docs are added', 'a strong card match → no document search', failed search → docSearch 'failed' logged and the answer proceeds); 14-question acceptance harness with the real classifier (14/14).
owner_decision: Search docs when no card (Recommended); later: Card + docs when weak (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant should ground answers in the node's own guides

class: context budget silently drops the relevant item; telemetry reports items not delivered
what_happened: A worse-matching card ranked first filled the 1,500-byte slim card budget, so the right second card was silently dropped; the log field conceptCardsUsed still listed cards the budget dropped, and a maxTotalBytes option passed by both callers was ignored by findRelevantCards.
root_cause: formatCardsForPrompt dropped any later card that did not fit without saying so, telemetry came from the ranked list rather than the assembled prompt, and an unused option looked like a working knob.
lesson: Prompt assembly must size budgets so the intended top-k fits, report exactly what reached the model, and carry no configuration option that is accepted but ignored.
tripwire: conceptCardBudget.test.ts checks each card against a per-card limit (1,500) separate from the total (3,000); an R7 test requires conceptCardsUsed to list only cards actually in the block; maxTotalBytes removed from the options and both callers.
owner_decision: We can increase the context window to 3000 bytes, if needed to fit the 2 relevant cars.
applies_to_new_node: yes — any assistant prompt builder with byte or token budgets

class: retrieval ranking tuned without a labelled, held-out evaluation
what_happened: Card ranking was literal word overlap with four biases (substring matches like 'back' in 'backup', common words weighted like rare ones, uncapped keyword hits, longer summaries winning); the right card ranked third for an owner question, and an old test even required a decoy that matched only through the 'score'/'core' substring bias. Fixing the word rules alone reached 56%/52% top-1 (tuned/held-out); a 50/50 blend of word score and local-embedding meaning reached 72.4%/87.4% tuned and 68.1%/82.6% held-out (top-1/top-2).
root_cause: Ranking was never measured against labelled questions, so its biases (and a test that encoded one) went unnoticed.
lesson: Assistant retrieval and ranking must be judged on a labelled question set with a held-out split and targets fixed before tuning, gated in CI and on the node with the real model; when the embedding server is down it must fall back to word ranking and log that it did.
tripwire: src/tests/fixtures/card-questions.json (242 questions, every third held out); cardRanking.test.ts pins the word-fallback floors; cardBlend.test.ts (embedder down → words, logged; at most two cards); src/scripts/cardRankingCheck.ts as smoke check 11 with the real model (owner-named 10/10).
owner_decision: Blend word + meaning (Recommended) — supersedes the earlier choice 'Fix the word-matching (Recommended)'
applies_to_new_node: maybe — applies if the new assistant ranks curated cards or guides; the evaluation discipline applies regardless

class: offline evaluation bypasses a live pipeline stage
what_happened: The node check reported owner-named questions 10/10, but it fixed the intent to 'explain'; live, 'Restart All said failed, what now?' was classified unclear@0.3, its best card fell under the 0.40 unclear bar, and the guide section with that exact title ranked 15th in Chroma because its text was mostly the 2 October history.
root_cause: The evaluation skipped the real classifier, and a guide section mixed its answer with a long history that drowned the question in embedding search.
lesson: Assistant evaluations must run the same classifier and thresholds as production, and guide sections must lead with the answer (history under its own heading) so retrieval finds them.
tripwire: Guide fixed (history moved under its own heading; chunk rank 15th → 2nd). Stated, not changed: cardRankingCheck measures intent 'explain' only — a full-pipeline evaluation should exist.
applies_to_new_node: yes — any assistant evaluation must go through the real routing

class: feature keyed on a value the client never sends
what_happened: The page-category boost for the Dashboard was keyed on '/dashboard', but the Dashboard's real route is '/', which is what the chat sends as location.pathname, so the boost never fired.
root_cause: The key was written from an assumed route name and never checked against what the frontend actually sends.
lesson: Context keys shared between frontend and backend (routes, page ids) must come from one shared definition or be tested end to end with the value the client really sends.
tripwire: pageBoostFor/pageLabelFor map '/' to '/dashboard' (slimKnowledge tests); acceptance run with pageContext '/'.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the rebuilt frontend/backend contract should share route identifiers

class: secret printed into an agent transcript by a config read
what_happened: While looking for LND's tor settings, an agent ran grep on /root/.lnd/lnd.conf inside the lnd container, which printed tor.password=<value> into its tool output; it was not shown in the owner's chat but went into the session transcript (stored locally and sent to the model provider). With it, a process on the node's Docker network could add or remove onion services through tor's control port.
root_cause: A secret lives inline in a general config file (lnd.conf) that agents read for ordinary settings, and the read went through a container exec that no guard treated as a secret read.
lesson: The node must keep secrets out of general config files (dedicated secret files referenced by path, unreadable to the assistant), and any secret that reaches a transcript or log must be rotated.
tripwire: None added (an operation record). Should exist: secrets only in dedicated files covered by the guard's secret globs, and a check that no general config file carries a password value.
owner_decision: 7. Is rotating LND's tor password is better for security, then yes.
applies_to_new_node: yes — LND and tor still need a control password; keep it in a secret file the sandboxed assistant cannot read

class: secret rotation across several copies and single-file bind mounts
what_happened: The tor control password lived in three places (data/lnd/secrets/tor_control_password, lnd.conf tor.password, torrc.base HashedControlPassword). One python process generated 24 random bytes and the tor S2K hash and rewrote all three files in place; tor then LND were restarted, LND's onion and all five static onions were checked end to end, and the backups holding the old password were deleted.
root_cause: torrc.base is a single-file bind mount into the tor container, so a new file (new inode) would not reach the container; and a secret duplicated in three files must change in all of them together.
lesson: Secret rotation must keep the secret out of argv, logs and output, update every copy (in place where a single-file bind mount is used), verify by an authenticated end-to-end check, and delete backups that hold the old secret; prefer one secret source over copies.
tripwire: Live checks: inodes unchanged; tor's runtime HashedControlPassword equals torrc.base's (compared by hash, neither printed); LND 'Tor v3 enabled' with no auth error; `rikuri-tor-recover.sh --check` all onions answer end to end. A stale legacy configs/torrc with an old hash was left (tor does not read it).
applies_to_new_node: yes — single-file bind mounts behave the same way under podman

class: new version exhausts a kernel resource (ephemeral TCP ports)
what_happened: A scratch probe of Electrs 0.12 against the live bitcoind failed in 13 s: its bindex fires many parallel REST block requests and exhausted the container's ephemeral ports ('Cannot assign requested address (os error 99)'). As shipped, the upgrade would have failed on this node; 0.12 has no concurrency option.
root_cause: Electrs 0.12 switched to parallel REST block fetches, which the container's default local port range and TIME_WAIT handling could not sustain.
lesson: The Electrs 0.12+ service must set net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1 and net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range='1024 65535', and every new service version must first be characterized in an isolated scratch container against the real backend before the switch.
tripwire: The 0.12 compose migration (dashboard/backend/src/config/upgradeMigrations.ts) adds both sysctls; upgradeMigrations tests; the verifier saw both sysctls on the running container after the upgrade.
applies_to_new_node: yes — for the x86 full node (Electrs needs an unpruned bitcoind); not for the pruned Pi

class: file-descriptor limit too low for a RocksDB index
what_happened: The pre-build container crashed with 'RocksDB failed: IO error: … Too many open files'; Docker restarted it and it recovered. The container's soft nofile limit was 1024 while the index had 2,682 .sst files.
root_cause: The container inherited the default soft nofile 1024, far below what a mainnet RocksDB index opens.
lesson: The Electrs service must run with an explicit open-file limit (nofile soft 65536 / hard 524288), or it will crash in service the same way.
tripwire: The 0.12 migration adds `ulimits: nofile: {soft: 65536, hard: 524288}`; live check after the upgrade: nofile 65536/524288.
applies_to_new_node: yes — x86 full node running Electrs

class: in-place reindex takes the service down for hours
what_happened: Electrs 0.12 needs a new index format (full reindex). Instead of reindexing in place, a scratch container built the 0.12 index in its own volume while 0.11 kept serving, and the upgrade switched onto the ready index (minutes of Electrs downtime instead of hours; the 0.11 index stayed intact for a rollback). The pre-build ran with no memory limit until it was capped live at 4 GB so a runaway could not starve bitcoind or LND.
root_cause: A format-changing upgrade forces a long rebuild; done in place, Electrum wallets and mempool address lookups stop for the whole rebuild.
lesson: An index-format upgrade must build the new index alongside the running service, under an explicit memory cap, and switch only when it is at the chain tip; nodes with too little disk for two indexes need their own plan.
tripwire: The upgrade's stopFirst removes the builder and verifies it is gone before starting the new version; live: Electrum answered from the pre-built index at the tip before the switch.
owner_decision: Yes, let it finish and plan upgrade around the ready index. Nice idea to let the test container build .12 index then upgrade onto it. For nodes with limited SSD, we'll have to add a plan around it, next time.
applies_to_new_node: yes — for the x86 full node; the limited-SSD plan the owner asked for is still owed

class: enabling an unauthenticated interface as an upgrade prerequisite
what_happened: Electrs 0.12 requires bitcoind's REST server (-rest=1), which serves read-only public chain and mempool data without authentication on the RPC port, reachable from host localhost and from containers on bitcoin-net; the cost (no wallet, keys or funds; a heavy query load is the risk; reversible; one bitcoind restart) was stated and the flag was set ahead of the Electrs upgrade.
root_cause: A dependency's new version changed what it needs from bitcoind.
lesson: The node must treat a new bitcoind interface (REST, ZMQ, RPC binds) as a costed, reversible owner choice, keep its exposure on the internal network, and set it ahead of the service that needs it.
tripwire: Prerequisite modelled in the upgrade planner (Electrs 0.12 requires Bitcoin Core 31 and -rest=1; sequence step 1 'rikurinode support'); bitcoind's port published on 127.0.0.1 only.
owner_decision: Do both now.
applies_to_new_node: yes — x86 full node with Electrs

class: health signal depends on a metric a new version removed (monitor goes blind)
what_happened: Electrs 0.12 publishes no electrs_index_height metric. Every reader of Electrs's own height used it — the Health score and service status, the guardian signal electrs.tip_lag_blocks behind the index-lag self-heal (with its own second parser), and the control plane's first-sync phase manager — so after the upgrade Electrs would read unknown, the self-heal would go blind and an 8 GB node would stay in FIRST_SYNC, while the upgrade itself would still 'succeed'.
root_cause: Three copies of the height reader depended on one version-specific metric, and nothing checked that every signal source still existed on the new version.
lesson: Each health signal must have one shared reader with ordered sources chosen by what the service offers (the metric, else Electrum blockchain.headers.subscribe, which on 0.12 is Electrs's own indexed height); unknown must stay unknown, never a made-up number; every upgrade must verify that each signal source still exists.
tripwire: serviceProbes electrsHeightFrom/electrumHeight (pure, tested; serviceProbes 31/31); Rust electrum_height/pick_electrs_height in control-plane/src/electrs_phase.rs with tests; the duplicate parser in signalCollector removed; live: height = tip from source electrum.
applies_to_new_node: yes — x86 full node; the one-reader rule applies to every service

class: revert restores the wrong state
what_happened: Revert restored the compose snapshot only if its path ended in 'docker-compose.yml' (snapshots never do) and re-pinned the tag read from the running container — after a failed upgrade that is the new version — so Revert changed nothing and cleared the failure. After that fix, verifier round 2 found _persistFailedUpgrade picked the OLDEST matching snapshot (an earlier crash-loop attempt's compose, 11 lines different).
root_cause: Revert reconstructed the previous state from current state and a loose history search instead of the exact snapshot the upgrade took.
lesson: Revert must restore the exact snapshot the upgrade itself took, verified by a hash of what the upgrade wrote; if the file changed since, it must refuse and notify rather than guess, and a migrated upgrade must be undone whole.
tripwire: services/revertPlan.ts planRevert (restore whole / restart only / refuse with HIGH notice / re-pin the snapshot's tag) with revertPlan.test.ts; the upgrade records writtenComposeSha; verifier scenario: a failed 0.11→0.12 upgrade reverts to its own snapshot.
applies_to_new_node: yes — OS rollback is handled by the image, but container and app upgrades still need an exact, hash-checked revert

class: concurrent mutations of one service (double press)
what_happened: During the real Electrs upgrade a second press started a second run inside the first run's 90 s watch; it was refused only because the migration's exact-text edit no longer matched. A Revert pressed next logged 'Revert failed for electrs:' with an empty message because the logger dropped its second argument.
root_cause: Nothing serialized upgrade and revert per service, and the page showed the refused second press as 'Upgrade failed', which prompted the Revert press.
lesson: Every mutating operation on a service (upgrade, revert, restart) must hold a per-service lock, refuse a second one with a visible notice, and carry any failure's message to the owner.
tripwire: busyServices set taken in simpleUpgrade and revertUpgrade, released in finally; verifier scenarios: a second press refused, Revert with nothing to revert notifies; Revert failures send a HIGH notice. Follow-up: the Upgrades page still shows a refused second press as 'Upgrade failed'.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: migration keyed on the target only (re-applied to migrated state); test uses live config
what_happened: migrationFor was keyed on the target line only, so every Electrs 0.12.x patch would get the 0.12 migration and be refused because its exact-text edits cannot match an already-migrated compose. Separately, the migration test applied the migration to the live docker-compose.yml, so backend jest went red once the node was really upgraded.
root_cause: The migration ignored the from-version, and its test used the node's live configuration as its fixture.
lesson: Configuration migrations must be keyed on (from, to) and be no-ops inside a line; their tests must run on frozen fixtures, never on the node's live configuration.
tripwire: migrationFor(service, engine, tag, fromVersion) returns null inside the line; migration tests run on a frozen 'node still on 0.11' fixture plus one test asserting the live compose is the migrated service; verifier scenario: v0.12.1 is a plain in-line patch.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: version policy that does not fail closed; two readers of one policy disagree
what_happened: Moving Electrs's supported line to 0.12 made the running 0.11.1 fail the 'every pin inside its line' test; a first fix ('any older line is supported') let a Core 29 tag pass on a Core 31 node. Also the upgrade planner read the raw release-note review, so step 1 showed 'not yet in the rikurinode on this node' for an already reviewed release, while getUpgradeHold filtered reviewed releases.
root_cause: The policy was loosened by a general rule instead of an explicit exception, and the planner re-derived the hold instead of using the same filtered source.
lesson: The node's version policy must fail closed (explicit per-service exceptions, removed once obsolete; an arbitrary older line refused), and every view of an upgrade hold must come from the one function that decides it.
tripwire: Tests: an arbitrary older line (0.10) refused; 0.11.x refused after the upgrade; planner test (seq[0].done); 'HOLDS' tests moved to a hypothetical 0.13 line.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: precondition step's error swallowed (two writers on one volume)
what_happened: The upgrade's stopFirst step ran `docker rm -f` on electrs-prebuild ending in `.catch(() => undefined)`, so a failed removal would go unreported and Electrs 0.12 would start beside a builder writing the same RocksDB volume.
root_cause: A precondition was assumed to succeed instead of being verified.
lesson: Before a service starts on shared data, the node must verify (not assume) that every other writer is gone, and roll back if it is not.
tripwire: simpleUpgrade logs a failed removal, checks with docker inspect that the container is gone, and rolls back ('is still using the shared data'); tests seen failing (2 failed) before the fix.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: probe that can never succeed (negative believed without a positive control)
what_happened: The record first claimed Electrs 0.12's port 50001 'stays CLOSED while indexing', and a background 'index complete' watch never reported completion; both used `exec 3<>/dev/tcp/127.0.0.1/50001` inside a container whose sh is not bash, so /dev/tcp did not exist and the probe could never succeed. 0.12 actually listens on 50001 from every start.
root_cause: The probe was never run against a known-open port before its 'closed' result was believed.
lesson: Every probe or watch must be shown to succeed against a known-positive case before its negative result is trusted or acted on.
tripwire: Correction recorded; later checks used an Electrum client against the container IP. Should exist: a positive control for each health or readiness probe.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: deploy from a shared dirty working tree ships unreviewed code
what_happened: The dashboard builds deployed by this record (22:42, 23:11, 23:12) also shipped another session's uncommitted code from the shared tree (for example an import from an untracked file); it typechecked and the endpoint answered, but it went live without review.
root_cause: Builds were made from the working tree, which several sessions edit at once.
lesson: The node must deploy only builds made from a commit (or a clean worktree of HEAD plus the reviewed change), never from a shared working tree.
tripwire: Recorded only. Later records gate and build on HEAD + staged in a scratch worktree (2026-10-04-gates-run-on-the-commit.md). Should exist: the deploy refuses a dirty tree.
applies_to_new_node: yes — image builds for Fedora IoT should come from commits only

class: self-heal route with no producer (collected signal never acted on)
what_happened: DRB-ELECTRS-INDEX-LAG-01 can never be reached: its issue types (ELECTRS_INDEX_LAG / ELECTRS_SLOW) are produced by no code, and routing sends Electrs issues only to DRB-ELECTRS-DOWN-01, so electrs.tip_lag_blocks is collected but never acted on. Older than this record; left as a follow-up.
root_cause: Alert routes and signal producers were written separately, with no test that each route has a producer.
lesson: Every self-heal or alert rule must have a test proving its trigger is produced by real code from a real signal, and every collected signal must have a consumer.
tripwire: None added (follow-up). Should exist: a registry test that every runbook/alert issue type has a producer and every collected signal has a consumer.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: compatibility check compares unordered results as ordered
what_happened: Replaying the four Electrum calls mempool-api makes against Electrs 0.11 and 0.12 first gave 20/20 identical, then 19/20 on a re-run: one listunspent came back in a different order, which is not stable on either version. Compared as sets: 20/20. The two calls 0.12 changed (server.features, transaction.id_from_pos) are not used by mempool-api (grep of its package).
root_cause: The comparison assumed an ordering the protocol does not promise.
lesson: Compatibility checks between a consumer and a new backend version must replay the consumer's real calls and compare unordered results as sets.
tripwire: Scratch replay script (session scratchpad, not in the repo). Should exist: a repeatable upgrade check that replays the consumer's real calls.
applies_to_new_node: yes — x86 full node with Electrs and mempool

class: global lock shared by concurrent sessions
what_happened: The fix-lock was one file: one session's lock made another session's test writes fail, `on` silently overwrote another record's lock, and `off` released anyone's.
root_cause: Lock state had no owner identity and one shared write target.
lesson: Agent coordination state (locks, claims) must be owned per session; a session's lock binds only that session, and releasing someone else's lock is an owner action.
tripwire: Per-session files .claude/state/fix-locks/<session>.json; a global lock taken outside a session still binds every session; `off --session/--global` always asks; test_guard.py PerSessionLock (10 tests, 7 seen failing first); guard identical in four repos (cmp).
owner_decision: 4. Let's not share fix-lock.
applies_to_new_node: yes — already in Rikuri-PI's shared guard

class: write hidden inside inline interpreter code bypasses a path-based guard
what_happened: A python3 heredoc with a relative path wrote a test file while a lock was engaged, because the guard saw only shell write targets. The first fix read only the first word of the line, and a live drill (`cd … && python3 - <<'EOF' open('src/tests/zz_lockdrill.test.ts','w')`) still got through; only the second fix denied it. After close-out the tripwire produced a false positive by scanning the whole command (a later `npx jest <test path>`).
root_cause: The guard parsed shell syntax only and treated inline code as opaque; the first fix assumed one command shape.
lesson: A guard change must be drilled live through the real hook with the shapes used in practice (cd chains, pipes, heredocs), and its scope must be exactly the inline code, not the whole command.
tripwire: Inline-code tripwire tests (each shape seen failing first) and the recorded live drill ('fix-lock is engaged: inline code in this command writes test/baseline …').
applies_to_new_node: yes — Rikuri-PI shares this guard

class: security patch withheld because only the newest release overall is offered
what_happened: MariaDB 10.11.19 (same supported line, fixes 7 CVEs) was never offered because the checker offered only the newest release overall, 13.0.2, a new line held for review. After the fix it auto-installed live (mempool-db restarted; settings check, watch and dependent check passed, no rollback).
root_cause: The upgrade check had one candidate per service, and the hold on that candidate hid every in-line patch.
lesson: The update checker must find the newest release inside each supported line as well as the newest overall, offer the in-line one under its own gates, and keep the held new line visible with its reasons.
tripwire: Pure helper newestInLine(tags, line, depth) with tests in upgradeRound2.test.ts; the card shows 'Also available: 13.0.2 — needs a rikurinode update first' (newLineHeld).
owner_decision: Do both now.
applies_to_new_node: yes — container images on the new node need the same per-line policy (OS updates come with the image)

class: lookup failure caught and only logged (feature never worked)
what_happened: Since 2025-11-25 the background collector searched GitHub issues for community platforms (umbrel, start9, raspiblitz, mynode, citadel) whose names were never in the GitHub source's REPOS map; every search threw before any network call, producing 135 'Unknown service' errors per collection (891 for umbrel on one day) that nothing reported.
root_cause: A caller passed names a lookup table did not have, and the throw was caught and only logged.
lesson: A background job that fails on every run must surface as a health failure, not as log lines; names passed to a lookup table must be validated against it; and an outbound default nobody chose (MCP_COLLECT_COMMUNITY, ON) must not exist unexposed.
tripwire: mcpCollectorNoCommunity.test.ts (every name collect() passes to searchIssues is in REPOS), later deleted with the whole collector; live journal count of 'Unknown service' 135 → 0.
owner_decision: 1. Remove it.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the class applies to every background job in the rebuilt backend

class: smoke test green while a core module cannot load (liveness is not function)
what_happened: After the Ubuntu 26.04 upgrade the dashboard ran on a Node whose ABI did not match its compiled better-sqlite3 (115 vs 127): node registry, incident closing and guardian activity failed, logged only as WARN, and smoke.sh stayed GREEN (29/1/0). On Node 24 the old better-sqlite3 then aborted the dashboard with a core dump, which smoke would not have reported either.
root_cause: Smoke checked liveness and API answers, not that the service's native dependencies load under the runtime it actually runs.
lesson: The node's smoke/health gate must load each native module with the exact runtime the service uses, fail on native-module load errors in the running service's log, and warn when a process runs a replaced binary or core-dumped this boot.
tripwire: scripts/smoke.sh section 1b: R1 require+open better-sqlite3 with /usr/bin/node; R2 journal signatures ('compiled against a different Node.js version', 'NODE_MODULE_VERSION', 'did not self-register'); R3 /proc/<pid>/exe '(deleted)'; R4 core dump this boot. Drill overrides SMOKE_NATIVE_DIRS and SMOKE_DASH_SINCE proved the FAIL paths (RED on the 142 real failure lines).
owner_decision: 5. Yes add smoke check.
applies_to_new_node: yes — image updates and rollbacks on Fedora IoT can change runtimes; the boot health check should prove native dependencies load

class: OS upgrade silently swaps the application runtime (native ABI break)
what_happened: do-release-upgrade disabled the third-party repos and replaced NodeSource Node 20.20.2 with Ubuntu nodejs 22.22.1 and no npm. The dashboard answered /api/health 200, but better-sqlite3 was built for NODE_MODULE_VERSION 115, so the node registry, incident closing and guardian activity failed — one error line, the rest WARN.
root_cause: The application runtime came from host OS packages, so an OS upgrade changed it underneath natively compiled modules.
lesson: The node must ship its application runtime and native modules together in the image or container (not from host packages), and every OS change must be followed by a check that native modules load.
tripwire: Native modules rebuilt and loaded under the new runtime; CI node-version aligned (ci.yml, dep-audit.yml, drift-digest.yml); smoke section 1b added by 2026-10-03-smoke-catches-broken-native-modules.md.
owner_decision: Node 22 from NodeSource (owner's choice as recorded); then 'maybe we should have moved to Node 24'
applies_to_new_node: yes — Fedora IoT images with automatic rollback should carry the runtime inside the image so update and rollback move it atomically

class: native dependency crashes on a new runtime major
what_happened: On Node 24 the backend's better-sqlite3 11.10.0 aborted when a prepared Statement was garbage-collected (Assertion failed in RemoveEnvironmentCleanupHook); 9 jest suites died with SIGABRT, and live the dashboard core-dumped and was down about 37 s until systemd restarted it.
root_cause: The native module's major version predated the runtime; the repo also carried two majors of the same module (backend 11.x, shared 12.x).
lesson: A runtime major upgrade must pass the full test suite under the new runtime before it reaches the node, and each native dependency must have one version across the repo.
tripwire: Backend better-sqlite3 → ^12.9.0 (one major in the repo); CI runs node-version '24'; full suites under Node 24; smoke 1b R4 warns on a core dump this boot.
applies_to_new_node: yes — whatever runtime the rebuilt backend uses

class: OS major upgrade changes system defaults the node depends on
what_happened: Ubuntu 26.04 changed sudo to sudo-rs, coreutils to uutils, Python 3.12 to 3.14 and the kernel to 7.0, and disabled third-party apt repos. The record checked each one instead of assuming: sudo-rs listed all 47 rikuri NOPASSWD grants with no parse errors, iptables stayed nft, repos were re-enabled in deb822 form, and every host unit and container came back by itself.
root_cause: A distribution upgrade changes several system components at once; any of them can break privileged helpers, firewalling or services.
lesson: An OS upgrade must have a pre-flight (clean stop with bitcoind flush, fresh channel backup, funds exposure checked) and a post-check that proves privileged grants parse, firewall backend, repos, runtimes, host services, identities and smoke; on the new node that post-check should decide the automatic rollback.
tripwire: Plan steps A1–A5 / B1–B8 run and recorded; smoke GREEN; LND synced; `sudo -n -l` lists the grants.
owner_decision: We need to upgrade linux to 26.04.1 LTS with kernel 7.0.
applies_to_new_node: yes — on Fedora IoT these checks become the boot health checks that trigger automatic rollback

class: self-heal fights a planned maintenance stop
what_happened: Before the package swap the stack was stopped with the Dashboard's owner-stop, which holds self-heal so the node does not restart services mid-upgrade; because owner-stop is boot-scoped, the first boot on 26.04 started the whole stack again by itself.
root_cause: Self-heal restarts anything that is down unless an explicit owner stop tells it otherwise.
lesson: A planned stop must suspend self-heal with an explicit, stated scope (until reboot, or a TTL) so automation neither fights maintenance nor leaves the node down after it.
tripwire: Owner-stop holds self-heal and is boot-scoped (B5: 13 host units and 11 containers back after the reboot).
applies_to_new_node: yes — an image update with reboot and possible rollback needs the same explicit hold and scope

class: substring keyword match misclassifies severity and triggers autonomous action
what_happened: isCriticalSecurityUpdate matched plain substrings; its keyword 'rce' matched inside 'force', 'source' and 'resource'. Of 107 real stable releases, 34 were flagged critical, including every LND release ('force close'); LND 0.21.2, 0.21.3 and 0.21.4 were each sent to the owner as CRITICAL security updates with 'Upgrade Now', skipping the 14-day wait. With auto-install on, every LND release would have installed itself on day one.
root_cause: Severity was matched by substrings and never calibrated against real release notes.
lesson: Any classifier that can trigger autonomous action must use whole-word, whole-phrase rules (CVE ids, 'remote code execution', RCE as a word, vendor urgency fields) and be measured against a corpus of real releases before it is enabled.
tripwire: R1 test set (LND 0.21.4 and chroma 'force/source' notes not critical; Redis CVE + RCE critical; tor high-severity 'as soon as possible' and Redis 'Update urgency: SECURITY' critical); corpus re-measure: 19 flagged, all Redis security releases, 0 LND/Bitcoin/mempool/electrs/chroma.
owner_decision: Yes, count them
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: autonomous restart of a money daemon (bounded auto-install)
what_happened: The owner chose automatic installation of critical security releases, default ON, only when every gate passes; on this code tor 0.4.9.13, redis 8.10.2 and mariadb 10.11.19 installed themselves live, each passing the settings check, the 90 s watch and the dependent checks, while mariadb 13.0.2 (critical but held) was announced and not installed.
root_cause: Security fixes otherwise wait for the owner, and a held release must never install.
lesson: Auto-install of security releases must require: critical by the calibrated rule, inside the supported line, not held by notes, sequence or consensus, no owner-stop or maintenance active, the full upgrade gates with auto-rollback, one attempt per version, and notices before and after (dashboard and email); the switch must be visible and step-up protected.
tripwire: upgradeRound2.test.ts (auto-security rules); GET/POST /api/upgrades/auto-security (POST step-up); notifications keyed ':auto-install' and ':critical' in data/upgrade-notifications.json.
owner_decision: Auto-install, only if all gates pass
applies_to_new_node: maybe — for container images; OS security updates come with the Fedora IoT image and its rollback

class: orchestrator call recreates services it was not asked to (config drift by caller environment)
what_happened: The MariaDB auto-install restarted its dependent with `docker compose … up -d mempool-api` (no --no-deps); compose also recreated bitcoind and Electrs and restarted LND, unannounced. The stack's systemd unit loaded the auto-scaled /run/rikuri/memory-limits.env and the dashboard did not, so the same compose file resolved different limits and compose saw changed services.
root_cause: Two callers resolved the same compose file with different environments, and the targeted restart allowed dependency recreation.
lesson: Every caller of the container orchestrator must use one shared environment loader so configuration never drifts by caller, every targeted start must use --no-deps, and an unreadable environment file must be reported, not silently replaced.
tripwire: --no-deps on all 5 orchestrator `up -d` calls and composeControl.composeUp; composeEnv() loads the memory-limits file and warns when it is unreadable; 3 tests seen failing first, plus the verifier-finding test.
applies_to_new_node: yes — podman/quadlet units and the backend must resolve identical settings

class: resource limits not scaled to local hardware after partial recreates
what_happened: Auto-installs and a manual bitcoind recreate ran before composeEnv existed, so six containers (electrs, mempool-api, mempool-db, redis, tor, bitcoin) run on compose's default limits instead of the stack's hardware-scaled ones (for example bitcoin 16G instead of 16998m); only lnd matched.
root_cause: Hardware-scaled limits lived in a runtime env file that only the full-stack start loaded.
lesson: Container resource limits must be derived from the local hardware on every start path, and upgrades must keep the node running, shrinking or stopping something only when RAM requires it.
tripwire: composeEnv() for every dashboard-run compose call; drift table recorded; the six left until the next full stack start by owner choice.
owner_decision: Just leave them. We have enough RAM. If we were doing this as and upgrade for other nodes, then we'll need to keep RAM usage based on the local hardware. Keeping the node running as much as we can, while upgrading. Shotdown or reduce RAM usage if necessary.
applies_to_new_node: yes — essential for the Raspberry Pi 5 node, whose RAM differs from the x86 node

class: cross-service prerequisites and dependent failures not modelled
what_happened: Some releases need another service at a minimum version first (Electrs 0.12 needs Bitcoin Core 31), and a dependent (LND, Electrs, Mempool after a Bitcoin upgrade; mempool-api after MariaDB) could fail after an upgrade with only a Revert offered.
root_cause: Upgrades were judged one service at a time.
lesson: The upgrade planner must show a numbered sequence (node support first, then each prerequisite, then the target), hold the target until every step is done inside the one hold function all entry points use, and roll the upgraded service back automatically when a dependent does not stay up.
tripwire: REQUIRES table and planUpgradeSequence in upgradeSupport; getUpgradeHold kind 'sequence'; orchestrator dependent rollback with HIGH notice (CRITICAL if the rollback does not recover); tests in upgradeRound2.test.ts.
owner_decision: 3. We should have a auto rollback.  Incidently, if the upgrade require a sequeced upgrade (for example, must upgrade to Bitcoin Core 31 before Electrs 0.12; then  our display should say Sequenced upgrad required: start from 1. Rikurinode 1.5; 2. Bitcoin Core 31; 3. Electrs 0.12
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: release-note hold too broad (blocks patches that do not affect the node)
what_happened: Under round 1's rule any breaking-change line held a release, so LND patches (which usually carry a Breaking Changes section) would often be held. The owner relaxed it: HARD findings (reindex or new index format, required version of software the node runs, database migration, cannot downgrade, incompatible) always hold; SOFT findings hold only if they name an identifier found in the node's settings or code; the rest are shown as 'worth knowing'.
root_cause: Prose findings were treated as blocking without checking whether they touch anything the node uses.
lesson: Release-note findings must be split into always-holding ones (reindex, migration, required versions, no downgrade) and conditional ones that hold only when they name a flag or option the node actually uses; non-holding findings stay visible.
tripwire: Classification tests in upgradeRound2.test.ts; findings shown on the card either way.
owner_decision: 1. relax it
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: UI shows a state the server never accepted (swallowed save failure)
what_happened: Verifier round 1 found the Upgrades page's auto-install switch swallowed a failed POST (the switch showed the new state while the server kept the old), a held critical release could still show 'bypass the wait' while its button was hidden, and composeEnv silently fell back to the process environment when the limits file was unreadable.
root_cause: Client state was updated optimistically without confirming the server's answer, and a flag was computed without the final hold decision.
lesson: Every owner-facing control must display the server-confirmed state and show save errors, and every derived flag must use the final hold decision.
tripwire: 4 tests in upgradeRound2.test.ts (autoSecurityError state; criticalSecurityBypass needs readyToUpgradeFinal; composeEnv warns), each seen failing first.
applies_to_new_node: yes — for the rebuilt frontend

class: test reads live mutable node state
what_happened: Several monitoring-loop tests read the real data/maintenance-mode.json: they failed while maintenance was on (21:57–22:01) and passed once it was off.
root_cause: Tests used the node's live state file instead of a fixture.
lesson: A test must never read or write the node's live state; every state path must be injectable and point at a temporary fixture in tests.
tripwire: Listed, not fixed. Should exist: a test-setup guard that fails any test touching the live data directory.
applies_to_new_node: yes — tests run on the node machines

class: upgrade reports success on evidence that cannot fail
what_happened: The owner pressed Upgrade on Electrs (0.11.1 → 0.12.0). The pre-flight ran bare `--help` (passed), the health check accepted the first 'starting' poll and logged 'Upgrade complete! ✓' two seconds later, but every start died with 'An unknown argument --daemon-p2p-addr=bitcoin:8333 was specified'. RestartCount reached 363; the crash-loop runbook ran twice without effect; the owner rolled back by hand about 1 h 40 min later. Siblings found: Telegram replied '✅ upgraded… healthy' on failure, Revert slept 5 s then said 'Reverted Successfully', a MariaDB upgrade left mempool-api stopped.
root_cause: In the record's words: an upgrade path that reports success on evidence that cannot fail — a pre-flight that never fed the new program the node's settings, a health check accepting the first 'starting' poll, no knowledge of which releases need node changes, a UI-only hold, and a Telegram reply ignoring the result.
lesson: An upgrade must (1) prove the new image accepts the node's real settings in an isolated, network-less, data-less container before touching the running one, (2) watch the started container for a fixed window and fail on any restart, exit or unhealthy, (3) roll back automatically and verify the rollback with the same watch, and report the real outcome on every channel.
tripwire: upgradeSafety.ts settings checks (electrs/bitcoind args, lnd flags plus lnd.conf isolated boot, tor --verify-config, redis isolated boot) and the stability watch; wiring guards that failed 9 on the old code; live gate 1 refused v0.12.0 with the exact crash line; gate 2 drilled on a crash-looping scratch container.
owner_decision: Roll back. Then close the three gaps. / Yes, roll back + tell me
applies_to_new_node: yes — every container upgrade on both nodes

class: one-click upgrade offered for releases that need node changes
what_happened: Electrs 0.12.0 needed a bitcoind setting the node did not set, a full reindex and a compose change, yet was offered as a one-click image swap. GitHub release text is often only links (Bitcoin Core always; 48 releases surveyed), so note scanning alone would miss most breaks.
root_cause: The version policy had no idea which releases the node had been adapted to.
lesson: The node must record, per service, the release line it is tested with; patches inside the line stay one-click, a new line is held ('Needs a node update first', reasons shown, no UI override) until a code change moves the line forward; release notes are still fetched from each project's real notes file and quoted.
tripwire: config/upgradeSupport.ts lines table and checkUpgradeSupport(); live API held Electrs 0.12.0 and MariaDB 13.0.2 while tor/redis patches stayed one-click; upgradeSafety tests.
owner_decision: Supported release lines / Hold it, show why
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: policy gate enforced only in the UI (other entry points bypass it)
what_happened: The consensus guard was UI-only: /api/upgrades/simple checked nothing, and the Retry button, /execute and the Telegram upgrade button all called simpleUpgrade without a hold check; /execute pulled the image and asked for approval before any hold.
root_cause: The rule lived in the page, not in the function that performs the mutation.
lesson: Every policy gate must be enforced inside the single mutation function that every entry point (UI, API, chat bot, retry, assistant) calls, before any side effect such as an image pull.
tripwire: Wiring test 'checks the hold before pulling anything' (checkHold → getUpgradeHold → throw UpgradeStopped before verifyAndPullDockerImage); Telegram input parsed with upgradeSimpleSchema.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the assistant and any chat channel must call the same gated functions

class: waiting period not used to adapt the node
what_happened: The owner widened the intent: when a version is first detected, read the full release notes of every release between running and target, tell the owner to wait for a node update and the waiting period, and use the waiting period to adapt the node. Review found the first implementation saved an unread result for good and counted a GitHub pointer text as 'read'.
root_cause: Upgrade information arrived only at button time, too late to adapt the node.
lesson: On first detection of a version, the node must fetch and review every intervening release's real notes (redo unreadable reviews, never count a pointer as read, track whether the range is complete), notify the owner with the review, and when the waiting period ends while still held, send 'waiting period over, still needs a node update' instead of 'Ready'.
tripwire: services/upgradeRequirements.ts with upgradeRequirements.test.ts (per-project notes sources, rangeComplete, hourly retry of unreadable reviews); data/upgrade-reviews.json (gitignored); notices in upgradeNotificationService.
owner_decision: We have a waiting period for each services. I think we should search for documentation for upgrade requirement when the notice to upgrade waiting period first appears. Then send notice to inform the user to wait for rikuri update and the waiting period to be over before upgrading. This will give us time to make any needed changes to rikurinode, during the waiting period.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: release-note hold too broad (blocks patches that do not affect the node)
what_happened: R9 held even an in-line patch whose notes mentioned a reindex, required setting, removed option, migration or breaking change, until a reviewer recorded it in REVIEWED_RELEASES; the verifier showed LND 0.21.3 → 0.21.4 would be held for a 'Breaking Changes' section (legacy commitment type) that did not affect the node.
root_cause: Any breaking-change prose was treated as blocking.
lesson: Hold rules from release notes must separate findings that always matter from ones that matter only if they name something the node uses.
tripwire: Raised as open owner question 1; resolved by the HARD/SOFT classification in the round-2 record.
owner_decision: when the release notes show…, hold
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: credential header sent to every outbound host
what_happened: An independent review found the release-note fetcher sent GITHUB_TOKEN to non-GitHub hosts (the new notes sources include gitlab.torproject.org and mariadb.com).
root_cause: The auth header was added per request without checking the destination host.
lesson: Credentials must be attached only for an allowlist of exact HTTPS hosts, tested against look-alike hosts, and fetched content must be size-capped.
tripwire: requestHeadersFor (https api.github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com only) with a look-alike-host test; fetch size cap 16 MB.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: exemption in a security monitor based on a chosen name
what_happened: The settings-check probe containers run through execFile with an argv array (no shell), --network none, --rm, read-only mounts, tmpfs data dirs, no-new-privileges, a label and a 5-minute sweep. To stop a false alarm, the privilege scan was changed to accept root in containers named rikuri-settings-check-<digits>-<lowercase alnum>, so any root container given that name is exempt from the root scan (accepted; logged at info).
root_cause: The privilege monitor alarmed on the new probe containers and was quieted by a name pattern.
lesson: Probe and sandbox containers must be isolated (no network, no data, no shell, no new privileges, labelled and swept), and exemptions in security monitors must not rest on a name anyone can choose.
tripwire: upgradeSafety.test.ts 'buildSettingsChecks' and 'settings-check containers' tests; live: 0 leftover rikuri-settings-check containers.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: self-heal can act during an upgrade; watch window shorter than the healthcheck
what_happened: The independent review found no maintenance window during the roughly 3-minute upgrade, so self-heal could act on services the upgrade had stopped, and an 'unhealthy' state could never be reached inside the 90 s watch given the services' healthcheck timing.
root_cause: The upgrade and the self-heal loop did not coordinate, and the watch was shorter than start_period plus interval × retries.
lesson: An upgrade must enter maintenance with a TTL and leave it in finally (only if it entered), and must follow health in the background until start_period + interval × retries + 60 s, notifying the owner and offering Revert on a later failure.
tripwire: enterMaintenance (15 min TTL) at stage 4 and exitMaintenance in finally; background followHealth; tests in upgradeSafety.test.ts.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: gate run on the working tree, not the commit
what_happened: After the push, CI failed the concept-card ranking floor (0.21594 against 21.8%): the new card had been tuned against the working tree's concept-cards.json, which held another session's uncommitted edit, so the commit carried a combination never tested.
root_cause: Local gates ran on a shared working tree containing other sessions' uncommitted changes.
lesson: Gates must test exactly the content being committed (HEAD plus staged), not a working tree other sessions share.
tripwire: Card fixed and tested in both states; the lesson became the pre-commit index snapshot in 2026-10-04-gates-run-on-the-commit.md.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: recovery path never triggered live (proven only by unit tests)
what_happened: A full failed upgrade with automatic rollback, the Revert button, and 'simpleUpgrade refuses electrs 0.12.0 before any pull' were not run live, because a failure of the hold would really upgrade the mainnet node; they rest on unit and wiring tests plus live API holds.
root_cause: There was no agreed non-mainnet stack where destructive recovery paths could be drilled.
lesson: The node must have a non-mainnet stack (testnet, signet or regtest) where upgrade rollback, Revert and holds are drilled end to end before they are trusted on mainnet.
tripwire: Listed in Skipped items ('with the owner's consent on the testnet stack').
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: security alarm only in logs (cried wolf; real tampering indistinguishable)
what_happened: Every dashboard start since at least 2026-08-08 logged 'CONFIG_TAMPERED: model-registry.json changed since baseline'. The change was legitimate (the 2026-07-21 model upgrade with pinned revision and sha256) but was never re-baselined, and the alarm reached only the log, so a real tampering would have looked the same and nobody would have seen it.
root_cause: A legitimate change to a protected file did not include re-baselining, and the integrity check had no owner-facing channel.
lesson: Integrity alarms must reach the owner through a delivered channel (HIGH, email and dashboard, in plain words: what the file controls and what to do), once per new hash and again if it changes later; a legitimate change to a protected file must re-baseline in the same change; and the notified-store must be separate from the baseline manifest.
tripwire: configIntegrity.ts pendingTamperNotices / markTamperNoticeSent / startConfigIntegrityCheck with configTamperNotify.test.ts (forget sequence v1 → v2 → v1 → v2 must notify; mutant 'store = manifest' caught); journal '5 checked, 0 baselined, 0 tampered' and 'owner notices pending: N'.
owner_decision: 2. Yes, on both recommendation.
applies_to_new_node: yes — integrity checks on node config and the model registry need delivered alarms; OS config is covered by the image

class: notification recorded as delivered without confirmed delivery
what_happened: notificationManager.send() resolves {success:false} when channels fail instead of throwing, and the first design wrote the 'notified' store before sending, so an undelivered notice would be recorded as sent and never retried.
root_cause: Delivery was inferred from the absence of an exception.
lesson: A notice may be marked delivered only when the send result reports at least one channel succeeded; 0 channels, a rejection or a missing summary must be logged and retried.
tripwire: deliverTamperNotice tests with fake send results (1 succeeded → marked; 0 → not; rejection → not, no throw; no summary → not); mutants '>= 0' and 'mark before send' caught.
applies_to_new_node: yes — every owner alert path

class: startup awaits an external side effect (an alarm can cause a restart loop)
what_happened: Round 3 made startup await the owner notice before server.listen. READY=1 is sent in the listen callback (Type=notify, TimeoutStartUSec=3min, Restart=on-failure) and the email transport sets no timeouts (nodemailer defaults: connect 2 min, socket 10 min), so a pending notice plus a stalled SMTP server could pass 180 s, systemd would restart the service, nothing would be marked, and the next start would block the same way.
root_cause: A network delivery was awaited on the startup critical path, and the transport had no timeouts.
lesson: Startup must never await external delivery (email, webhooks, model calls); such work runs after readiness, and every outbound transport must set explicit timeouts.
tripwire: startConfigIntegrityCheck returns at once with delivery pending; test: a never-resolving send returns in under 500 ms. Follow-up: the nodemailer transport still has no timeouts for other callers.
applies_to_new_node: yes — on Fedora IoT a boot-time block could also fail the boot health check and trigger a rollback

class: text-matching wiring tests pass mutants; evidence printed before the code it proves
what_happened: Verifier rounds 2–4 broke the tests with mutants: a regex over server.ts let 'mark unconditionally first' and 'successful >= 0' pass, then 'send nothing' and 'dashboard only, no email', then a notified path equal to the manifest; the live journal line cited as proof that the step runs was printed before the call, so an `if (0)` mutant printed it too.
root_cause: Wiring was proven by matching source text and by a log line outside the code path.
lesson: Behaviour must be proven by tests that call the code with fakes and are mutation-checked; startup code should be one call into a tested function; live evidence lines must be emitted inside the code path they prove.
tripwire: Mutation checks in a scratch worktree every round (M4/M6/M7/M8, S2–S4, awaited delivery, pending log, advice text), all caught; residual: the single server.ts call line is text-checked.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: module used where an instance was meant (safety feature silently disabled at every start)
what_happened: services.ts calls .on(...) on the approvalManager module (which exports {ApprovalManager, approvalManager}) instead of the instance, so 'Approval notifications not available:' fires at every start and approval requests never notify the owner. Found by verifier round 5, outside this record; surfaced to the owner.
root_cause: An untyped import let a module object stand in for the instance, and the failure was a warning rather than a health failure.
lesson: Owner-approval notifications are a safety path: their wiring must be typed and tested end to end, and a startup warning that a safety feature is unavailable must be a health failure.
tripwire: None added (surfaced). Should exist: a startup test that an approval request produces an owner notification.
applies_to_new_node: yes — approvals for money moves and assistant actions must notify

class: commit gate runs on the working tree, not the staged commit
what_happened: Twice in two days a gate passed locally and failed in CI because another session's uncommitted changes sat in the same tree: the concept-card ranking (2026-10-03) and the quality ratchet (backend_require_calls 1274 → 1275 in CI while the local ratchet held). In the drill the old hook committed a staged type error while the working tree was fixed. The ratchet baseline also had slack: 1274 while HEAD was 1255, so 19 new requires would have passed.
root_cause: The pre-commit typecheck and ratchet read the working tree, and the baseline was not lowered after improvements.
