lesson: Commit gates must run on an export of exactly the index (what is being committed); ratchet baselines must be lowered only from HEAD's counts; a gate that crashes must say it could not run rather than report a counter rise.
tripwire: .githooks/pre-commit exports the index (git checkout-index --prefix) to a temp dir, links node_modules, and runs both typechecks and the ratchet there; precommitGatesOnIndex.test.ts 3/3 (fails on the old hook); live drills D1–D4; CLAUDE.md line 'Gate the commit, not the working tree'.
owner_decision: Ok to run gattes on the commit itself, not on working tree of other sessions and pre-commit step
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's repo is also worked on by several sessions

class: guard judges named arguments, not what a recursive command actually reads
what_happened: A verifier's repo-wide `grep -r` read the contents of .env files (no match, nothing printed): the guard denied only commands that name a secret file, so `grep -r X .` passed, while `grep -r --exclude='*.env' X .`, which would not read them, was denied because '*.env' appeared in its words.
root_cause: The secret check matched words in the command, not the set of files the command would touch.
lesson: A secret-read guard must evaluate the files a recursive search will actually reach (walk its roots, honour its exclude filters) and ask the owner if any secret remains; excluding secrets must never be penalized; tracked-only search (git grep) is the safe default for agents.
tripwire: test_guard.py SecretSearches and the round-2..8 tests (recursive_search, secret_in_tree with a 30,000-entry budget, over budget = ask); verifier.md rule in four repos: never search or read secret files without the owner's permission, use git grep.
owner_decision: Yes, should not be allowed to search or look into .env without permission.
applies_to_new_node: yes — Rikuri-PI shares this guard unchanged

class: rewriting a security filter silently drops existing checks
what_happened: Five verifier rounds each found regressions in the rewritten guard; round 3 found 19, six of them money moves (lncli sendcoins / payinvoice / bitcoin-cli send inside a heredoc run by docker exec, ssh or a subprocess) no longer asked about, after a change treated heredoc bodies as data. A restructuring slip also turned two `continue`s into `return hits`, skipping the protected-path and money checks (caught by the config examples).
root_cause: Each rewrite re-derived the old logic by hand and argued that nothing was dropped, which kept dropping something.
lesson: Never drop a check the previous guard made; only add: a security filter change must run the previous version unchanged (a frozen copy) and return the stricter of the two decisions, with only explicitly owner-approved, narrowly proven relaxations, and must be proven by a differential test against the previous version.
tripwire: guard_base.py (byte-for-byte previous guard.py) runs on every decision and decide() returns the stricter; differential generator over ~70,000 variants of every config example in four repos (0 looser); test_guard.py 87/87 on Python 3.9 and 3.14 in all four repos.
owner_decision: 5 Ok and fix false positive.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the same rule applies to any policy engine in the new node's sandbox or approval layer

class: security check timeout can fail open
what_happened: Nested sh -c / eval commands with many cd targets took up to 12.01 s through the real hook (39 s in-process at depth 5), past the hook's 10 s timeout, where a timeout may fail open; a 9.73 s case came within a quarter second. Round 7 then found an override could still apply after a timeout.
root_cause: The new parsing work had no wall-clock budget, and the override path did not know a timeout had happened.
lesson: Every security check must run under a wall-clock budget that ends in ask or deny, never allow, and no relaxation may apply once the budget is exceeded.
tripwire: 4 s cap for the new checks (_tick), 2.5 s shared cap for search walks, at most 6 folders per command; test_round7_no_override_after_a_timeout; timing tests (10 cds × 5 levels of sh -c under 6 s and not allowed).
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: command-text parsing used as a security boundary
what_happened: After eight verifier rounds the record still lists forms the parser cannot see: `… | xargs grep`, `tar cf - . | strings`, shell commands run from code strings (os.system('cat <secret>')), aliased writers, paths built at run time, env -S/-C forms, nested quoting beyond one level; it states the guard is a tripwire, not a sandbox.
root_cause: Shell and interpreter languages are too expressive for static command-text analysis to bound what a command reads or writes.
lesson: The new node must contain its AI assistant with an OS-level sandbox (no access to secret files, no host shell, scoped writes) and use command-parsing guards only as tripwires on top.
tripwire: Known limits listed in the record. Should exist: a sandbox boundary test proving the assistant cannot read secret files by any command form.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node sandboxes the assistant; this record is the evidence that parsing alone cannot contain it

class: required verification incomplete, accepted with a written gap
what_happened: Verifier rounds 7 and 8 were both stopped by a safety classifier before the adversarial pass on the two narrowed overrides could run; the verdict was FAIL (incomplete), and the owner accepted the change with that gap written down as owed.
root_cause: The verification tool could not complete a required check.
lesson: A required check that could not run must stay 'not yet proven' with an owner and stay visible; only the owner may accept the risk, explicitly.
tripwire: Record status 'ACCEPTED BY OWNER with a known gap'; the owed adversarial pass listed in Skipped items.
owner_decision: Accept as is.  commit and push.
applies_to_new_node: yes — process rule for the new repo

class: producer changed its return shape; consumer silently skips everything
what_happened: Since 2025-11-25 the MCP data collector searched GitHub issues at every start and every 6 h but never stored one: searchIssues had returned an object {closedIssues, openIssues, total…} since 2025-11-04, and the collector checked issues.length (undefined), so every result was skipped and issues.json stayed []. Nobody read its output: its 9 routes under /api/mcp-collector had no caller.
root_cause: An untyped interface between two modules, and no check that the job ever produced anything.
lesson: Inter-module interfaces must be typed so a shape change fails to compile; a periodic job that always produces nothing must raise an absence-of-success alarm; code and routes with no caller must be removed.
tripwire: mcpCollectorRemoved.test.ts (files and mount gone; knowledge service kept); git grep across the whole repo including scripts (prepare-for-distribution.sh still referenced data/mcp); live /api/mcp-collector/status → 404.
owner_decision: 4. remove collector and unused endpoints.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the rebuilt backend should be typed end to end

class: unneeded ingestion of untrusted external text
what_happened: The collector's GitHub searches triggered 20 EXTERNAL_INJECTION_ATTEMPT warnings (html_hidden_instruction) at every start — false positives on issue templates such as romanz/electrs #1315 — and a repo security audit had flagged it as an indirect-injection ingest path; its output fed nothing.
root_cause: A background feature pulled untrusted web content into the assistant's knowledge area with no consumer and no need.
lesson: The node must not ingest untrusted external text into assistant-reachable stores unless a reviewed feature needs it, and every such path must be treated as an injection surface.
tripwire: Live: 0 EXTERNAL_INJECTION_ATTEMPT at start after removal (was 20).
owner_decision: 4. remove collector and unused endpoints.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant's inputs

class: code whose premise disappeared when a dependency was replaced
what_happened: The model warm-up was written for Ollama, which loads a model on first request; the node now uses llama-server, which loads at start, so there was nothing to warm. It also raced: it ran before model discovery finished, with a null model name, logging 'Could not prime primary model' at every start; its text still said 'Phi-3 Mini'.
root_cause: When the model server was replaced, code that existed only for the old server was not removed.
lesson: Replacing a dependency must include removing code that existed only for the old one, and startup steps that depend on discovery must await it.
tripwire: startupBrokenCodeRemoved.test.ts R1 source check; live journal 'Could not prime' 0.
owner_decision: 1. Delete warm-up; why does it need warmup? … 3. Remove
applies_to_new_node: maybe — depends on the assistant's model server

class: edge-triggered automation fires on every start (undefined previous state)
what_happened: The IBD monitor saw a synced node as 'IBD just completed' on every dashboard start because its previous phase was undefined (126 'Post-IBD optimization failed' since 2026-09-25). Its script had failed since 2026-02-27 (a plain node script requiring a module renamed to .ts); had it worked it would, on every start, have rewritten docker-compose.yml (bitcoind -dbcache and memory limit), written .env and run `docker compose up -d --force-recreate bitcoin`, fighting the hardware-scaled limits.
root_cause: A transition detector treated 'unknown' as the previous state, and an automation that rewrites node config and recreates bitcoind had no owner choice.
lesson: Transition-triggered actions must require an observed previous state, and no automation may rewrite node configuration or recreate bitcoind without an exposed, costed owner choice.
tripwire: startupBrokenCodeRemoved.test.ts R2 (monitor, optimizer scripts, unused /api/optimization mount and orphans gone); live: no IBD-monitor lines, /api/optimization/status → 404.
owner_decision: 3. Remove
applies_to_new_node: yes — the Pi 5 pruned node has a long IBD; any post-IBD tuning must be explicit and owner-chosen

class: test resolver more permissive than the production runtime
what_happened: The first version of the class gate (every relative require() in tracked scripts resolves) passed on the two broken scripts, because jest's resolver also finds .ts files while plain node does not; it was rewritten to resolve in a real node process. It then failed with ENOENT in a worktree with an unstaged deletion, because git ls-files still listed the deleted scripts.
root_cause: The check ran under a different module resolver than the one production uses.
lesson: Load and resolve checks must run under the same runtime and resolver as production, and file-list-driven checks must tolerate tracked files missing on disk.
tripwire: startupBrokenCodeRemoved.test.ts R3 (resolves in a real node process; skips tracked files missing on disk), 8/8 failing on HEAD.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the class applies to any language with build-time vs run-time resolution

class: stale build artifacts outlive their deleted source
what_happened: The backend build never cleans dist/, so the three deleted modules' compiled files (and an empty dist/controllers/) stayed there after their sources were removed; they were deleted by hand.
root_cause: Incremental build output is never cleared.
lesson: Builds must start from a clean output directory, and a check must fail if any built file has no source.
tripwire: Manual check '0 dist/*.js without a source file'; follow-up listed, not changed.
applies_to_new_node: yes — image builds should be clean by construction

class: self-heal runbook hardcodes a resource an upgrade changed
what_happened: The reindex self-heal RB-ELECTRS-INDEX-REINDEX-01 hardcoded `docker run -v electrs-data:/data`; since the 0.12 upgrade (index on electrs-bindex) it would have renamed the OLD index and restarted Electrs on the corrupt live one, and after electrs-data was deleted it would have created an empty volume and aborted. Its corruption grep was case-sensitive (missing RocksDB's 'Corruption:') and its restart check relied on 0.11 log words.
root_cause: The runbook encoded a volume name and log wording instead of discovering them from the running service, and no upgrade step re-validated it.
lesson: Self-heal runbooks must discover the live resource from the running service (the volume mounted at /data), fail closed when it is absent, match errors case-insensitively, and be re-validated whenever the service is upgraded.
tripwire: New runbook test (3 cases: reads the mount, case-insensitive corruption, no hardcoded volume) seen failing first; command audit and template tests 39/39; cargo runbook tests 34/34; prechecks and validates run live, read-only, as stored.
applies_to_new_node: yes — x86 full node with Electrs; the rule applies to every runbook

class: wrong baseline for crash-loop detection (restart counter not reset)
what_happened: A throwaway container probe showed that after 2 policy restarts, `docker start` did not reset RestartCount, so a restart counter cannot be the baseline for 'did the restart work'.
root_cause: Docker's RestartCount keeps counting policy restarts across manual starts.
lesson: Restart validation must use uptime since the last start (running and up at least 60 s, no error or panic in the log since then, retried) rather than a restart counter.
tripwire: Runbook step-4 validate: running, up ≥ 60 s since last start, no '^Error|panicked' in the log since then, 8 tries × 30 s; run live (RUNNING).
applies_to_new_node: yes — check the equivalent counter semantics in podman before relying on them

class: irreversible deletion of rollback state
what_happened: The owner deleted the 0.11 index volume (63.92 GB; disk 86% → 83%) after being told that going back to 0.11 would then mean a full reindex. The session first verified that no container mounted it and no failed upgrade was pending a Revert. Older compose snapshots in backups/rollback still declare electrs-data, so restoring one by hand would recreate an empty volume and start a full 0.11 reindex.
root_cause: Rollback artifacts reference state that has since been deleted.
lesson: Deleting rollback state must follow a stated, accepted cost and verified non-use, and every rollback artifact that still references the deleted state must be updated or flagged.
tripwire: Pre-deletion checks: `docker ps -a --filter volume=electrs-data` empty, upgrade_state.json {}; compose valid alone and with the Knots overlay.
owner_decision: 1. Delete the old index.
applies_to_new_node: yes — both image rollback and container rollback depend on retained state, and disk is tight on the Pi

class: test-protection lock covers test files but not tests inside source files
what_happened: Under the fix-lock a python3 heredoc wrote control-plane/src/electrs_phase.rs, a Rust file whose #[cfg(test)] module is test code, and was not refused, while `sed -i` on the same file was.
root_cause: The interpreter-write check compared targets only with test_globs, never with the inline_tests rules.
lesson: Test protection must cover test code embedded in source files (Rust #[cfg(test)] modules) on every write path, not only separate test files.
tripwire: InlineTests.test_inline_code_writes_to_rust_files and test_lock_bypasses_found_by_the_verifier; config examples against HEAD in four repos: 0 weaker, 0 stricter; 91/91 in each repo.
owner_decision: 2. Ok fix the Guard gap.
applies_to_new_node: yes — Rikuri-PI is Rust and shares this guard

class: guard reads the files a command runs (leaks secrets, stalls)
what_happened: Round 2 made the guard scan the script files a command runs; the verifier found that a fake secret run as a script (`perl api.token`) leaked pieces of its contents into deny reasons, a 40 KB untracked script held the real hook 24.9 s (hook timeout 10 s, may fail open), and 'tracked by git' was not 'reviewed'. A first version also denied the guard's own `fix-lock off` command under the lock, caught only by comparing example decisions with HEAD.
root_cause: Reading arbitrary files inside a security hook mixes their contents into its output and its time budget.
lesson: A command guard judges commands and never reads the files a command runs; it must not lock out its own release commands; and every change to it must be compared with the previous version on all config examples, which catches regressions the unit suite misses.
tripwire: Script-file scanning removed; test_huge_inline_code_stays_inside_the_time_budget; test_the_guards_own_commands_run_under_the_lock; 1,032 example decisions compared with HEAD. Known: about 80 KB+ of unclosed `open(` still stalls past 10 s (also in guard_base.py).
applies_to_new_node: yes — shared guard; its stated limits argue again for sandboxing the assistant

class: device classified by where the OS mounts it (mount-root assumption)
what_happened: After the Ubuntu 26.04 upgrade, udisks2 mounted the USB backup stick under /run/media/<user>/ instead of /media/<user>/; isSystemPartition excluded every /run/ mount, so the stick vanished from detection and showed connected:false. The last USB backup was 2026-10-03 19:00; the remount runbook reported SUCCESS, the unmounted-disk repair was exhausted and paged the owner, and its budget was then reported spent every 30 minutes.
root_cause: Drive detection decided what a drive is from the OS's mount path, which udisks2 moved.
lesson: Backup drives must be identified by filesystem UUID, not mount path, and removable-media detection must accept /run/media/<user> (udisks2's media root, Fedora's default) while still excluding other /run mounts.
tripwire: storageDetectionRunMedia.test.ts with the real 26.04 `lsblk -J` fixture (positive cases through scanDevices; every other /run mount stays out); hostMetrics.test.ts /run/media case; live: SCB and hourly config backups landed on the stick.
owner_decision: Core fix + test (Recommended); Leave it to the runbook (Recommended); Include it now (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — Fedora's udisks2 mounts removable media under /run/media/<user> by default

class: repair judged by its own step, not by the consumer's outcome
what_happened: RB-BACKUP-DEVICE-REMOUNT-01 mounted the stick and reported SUCCESS (21:00:01), yet five minutes later DRB-BACKUP-DISK-UNMOUNTED-01 was EXHAUSTED and paged the owner, because the dashboard still could not see the drive; the repair was then skipped once its 2-per-day budget was spent.
root_cause: The runbook's success meant 'the mount happened', not 'the backup engine can use the drive'.
lesson: A repair must validate the outcome the consumer needs (the backup engine sees the selected drive as connected and writable), not that its own command exited 0.
tripwire: None added by this record. Should exist: the remount runbook's validate step queries the selected-device state the backup engine uses.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: untrusted string (drive label, URL value) interpolated into a shell
what_happened: A drive's mount path holds its label, and it reached shell strings in 8 places (df every 5 s, du, umount, lsblk, find, docker cp). Most serious: GET /api/storage/check-initialization/<path>, reachable without login from the LAN through nginx, put the URL value into an lsblk shell string, so a LAN caller could run commands as the dashboard user (present since at least 2026-02-27). The record's first security answer ('no new exec path') was wrong.
root_cause: Commands were built as shell strings with interpolated external values.
lesson: No external value (drive label, mount path, device path, URL or body value) may reach a shell: use argv execution only, and keep a default-deny tripwire over the files that handle such values.
tripwire: mountPathNoShell.test.ts: real-exec cases with a sentinel file (created on the old code), mocked argument checks, and a default-deny source tripwire for the four drive-handling files; verifier's syntax-tree sweep of 390 shell-building calls; live crafted path `sdz$(touch …)` created no file.
owner_decision: Fix all six now (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the rebuilt backend should have no shell execution of external values at all

class: sibling sweep by name misses forms of the class
what_happened: The sweep for '/media/' and '/run' prefixes missed the regex form (mnt|media) in hostMetrics extraDrives, so the drive-space list and the 90%-full alert left the stick out (verifier round 1); the name-based sweep for drive paths in shell strings missed the blocksDest variable, an 8th loginless shell site (verifier round 3).
root_cause: Sweeps searched for known names and spellings instead of the structure of the defect.
lesson: Sweep a defect class by structure (syntax tree, data flow, every call of a kind), not by names, and back the sweep with a default-deny tripwire.
tripwire: CLAUDE.md line 'Sweep a defect class by structure, not by names' (owner approved 2026-10-06); default-deny tripwire in mountPathNoShell.test.ts; syntax-tree sweep.
owner_decision: Include it now (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: negative test that cannot fail
what_happened: The first version of the blockchain-status injection test put the sentinel path in an environment variable; jest's process.env does not reach a child shell, so `touch` got no target and the test could not fail. It was caught before the lock and the path was octal-encoded in the folder name instead.
root_cause: The test's attack payload depended on state the attacked process could not see.
lesson: Every security test must be seen failing against the vulnerable code (here: the sentinel file actually created) before it is trusted.
tripwire: Red runs on the old code recorded (sentinel 'Expected: false, Received: true').
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: recovery searches hard-coded paths that never existed
what_happened: The sibling sweep found the control plane's recovery searching /media/usb{,1}/channel.backup for the LND channel backup — never this node's path — so recovery would not find an SCB on the stick by itself; a legacy backup script and the assistant's path list also hard-wire /media/junc/BACKUP1, and the startup path validator rejects /run/media.
root_cause: Restore paths were written from assumptions and never exercised by a restore drill.
lesson: Recovery must locate channel backups on the actual selected backup drive (by UUID), and the monthly restore drill must prove it finds the SCB there.
tripwire: Skipped item S4 with reactivation 'before the next Restore drill (monthly loop), which must find the SCB on the stick'.
applies_to_new_node: yes — SCB recovery is the most important restore path for an LND node

class: parser assumes an external tool's output types
what_happened: util-linux 2.41 prints rm/hotplug in `lsblk -J` as JSON booleans; storageDetectionService compares them with the string '1', so 'removable' is false for USB drives (only the 'Removable' tag reads it).
root_cause: The parser was written against an older output format with no fixture from the target OS.
lesson: Parsers of system-tool output must be tested against fixtures captured on each target OS version and accept both forms where versions differ.
tripwire: Fixture of the real 26.04 `lsblk -J` shape in storageDetectionRunMedia.test.ts; S5 left as a follow-up.
applies_to_new_node: yes — Fedora ships its own util-linux version

class: external status query returns a stale page
what_happened: Smoke's CI check went RED twice with nothing wrong: GitHub returned an old page of runs (321bedb9 from 2026-08-10, then 9828d977 from 2026-09-15) while six hand-run copies of the same query returned the current successful run first.
root_cause: The check trusted a single answer from an external API.
lesson: A check that depends on an external API must re-query before reporting failure and print what it judged; a false RED is better than a false GREEN but still erodes trust in the gate.
tripwire: Follow-up S12: re-query once before RED and print the run list.
applies_to_new_node: maybe — if the new node's health checks consult CI or other external services

class: outcome classified from text that contains untrusted input
what_happened: ejectDevice decided the result by looking for 'not mounted', 'busy' or 'permission' in umount's error text, which contains the mount path (the drive's label): a stick labelled 'not mounted' was reported 'already unmounted' while still mounted — a false success that invites the owner to pull a mounted drive.
root_cause: Classification matched on text that mixes the tool's message with a user-chosen name.
lesson: Outcomes must be classified only from the tool's own words: remove every occurrence of untrusted values (labels, paths) before matching, and return the tool's text for anything unrecognised.
tripwire: ejectOutcome.test.ts (4 crafted labels red on the old code); mutation sets up to 16/16 red; the verifier ran real umount in an `unshare -rm` namespace with a refusing sudo stub.
owner_decision: Let's also fix S11, 13, and 8.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: substring match on structured output (remount-ro contains 'ro,')
what_happened: The startup scan set isReadOnly from mountLine.includes('ro,'); this node's real USB mount options include 'errors=remount-ro,', so the owner's writable stick was reported read-only. Labels with parentheses or spaces broke the same parsing (a label 'USB DISK' gave a cut-off mount point, and the remount script's findmnt output escaped the space so its write probe failed). Nothing read the scan's output.
root_cause: Mount information was parsed by substring and space-splitting of human-readable text.
lesson: Mount and device state must be read from structured output (findmnt -J / lsblk -J) or exact option lists, never substrings of text that also carries labels; outputs nobody reads should be deleted.
tripwire: ejectOutcome.test.ts scan cases (the real errors=remount-ro line, 'Backup(ro)', 'Back(ro,up)'); the space-in-label sibling and rikuri-backup-remount.sh left as a follow-up.
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: fallback that guesses (prefix match picks the wrong device for a destructive action)
what_happened: privilegedOperations.getDeviceInfo, behind the format route, fell back — when `lsblk -J` did not parse — to the first text line containing the mount path, so '/run/media/junc/BACK' matched the drive at '/run/media/junc/BACKUP' and the format route could get the other drive's device; an lsblk that could not start also threw out of the process (no 'error' listener).
root_cause: A parse failure was answered with a best guess instead of a refusal, on a path that leads to formatting a disk.
lesson: When a lookup behind a destructive action cannot parse or run, it must refuse (404), log why, and never guess by prefix; child-process errors must always be handled.
tripwire: deviceInfoNoGuess.test.ts (hermetic; text or exit-32 output → 404 plus a warning; missing lsblk → 404, process alive, exactly one log line).
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: path containment by startsWith without a separator (host directory listing)
what_happened: GET /api/storage/devices/<path>/browse listed any directory the backend could read: the route checked only that the path existed, and listDirectory compared the target with that same path using startsWith with no separator. In loginless mode any LAN client could list host directories (live counts: /home/junc 82 entries, /etc 269), names only.
root_cause: The route trusted a caller-supplied root and its containment check was not separator-aware.
lesson: File-browsing endpoints must browse only known roots (mount points of detected removable drives), contain paths with a separator-aware check on resolved paths, and require authorization even for reads.
tripwire: Moved to its own record, 2026-10-07-storage-routes-known-drives-only.md (in progress when this record was committed).
owner_decision: Fix now, own record (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: test reaches the live system
what_happened: Round 2's device-lookup test ran real lsblk, udevadm settle and lsblk -no UUID on the owner's real /dev/sda2 through un-stubbed fstab bookkeeping; it was rewritten to be hermetic, and the verifier proved it with a PATH spy and strace (no lsblk or udevadm executed; the same spy caught all three on the earlier test).
root_cause: A helper on the code path shelled out to host tools and was not stubbed.
lesson: A test must never execute host tools against real devices or services on the node; hermeticity must be proven (PATH spy or strace), not assumed.
tripwire: Hermetic deviceInfoNoGuess.test.ts; PATH-spy check with a positive control.
applies_to_new_node: yes — tests and mutation runs execute on the node machines

class: independent slow reads awaited one after another
what_happened: GET /api/status took 7–8 s because the health check made four sequential `docker stats` calls (1.2–2.0 s each) and sometimes hit the 8 s stall watchdog (503). Starting them together cut it to about 2 s; the first version also read stopped or absent containers (which logged errors the old code never produced), fixed by taking one container list and reading only running containers.
root_cause: Independent I/O was serialized on a request path with a hard deadline.
lesson: Independent reads on a request path must run concurrently and only for things that exist and run, and tests should count concurrency rather than time it.
tripwire: healthStatsParallel.test.ts (reads in flight ≥ 4; each container read once; stopped or absent containers not read; each service shows its own figures); live /api/status about 2.0 s.
owner_decision: Fix it now (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: watchdog times out, then the handler answers again (double reply, process crash)
what_happened: Since 2026-10-01 the journal held 97 watchdog 503s on 11 routes and 215 'Cannot set headers after they are sent' lines, 44 of them unhandled rejections; a late next(err) could reset a shared keep-alive socket. During the fix, removing one override let late bodies reach end(chunk), which on a pipelined connection raised an uncaught ERR_STREAM_WRITE_AFTER_END that exits the process; and the audit log had recorded 'SUCCESS (200)' for a login whose reply was dropped.
root_cause: The shared stall watchdog answered 503 but left the response writable by the still-running handler.
lesson: A request watchdog must own the response once it has answered: drop every later header and body write, record the handler's real status for logs and audit, never crash the process, and never cut a reply that started in time.
tripwire: middleware/stallWatchdog.ts with stallWatchdogLateReply.test.ts (every Express reply path, pipelined raw-socket cases, streams not cut, app.ts mounts it with its defaults); mutation set 28/28 red.
owner_decision: Every route (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: maybe — framework-specific, but any rebuilt backend with request deadlines needs the same ownership rule

class: money operation cut by a generic request timeout (ambiguous outcome, double-pay risk)
what_happened: /api/lightning/pay, /channels/open and /api/tapd/send ran under the 8 s stall watchdog: a slow payment got '503 request stalled' (Retry-After: 2) while it carried on, its outcome never reached the page, and a manual retry could pay twice.
root_cause: A generic latency watchdog was applied to every route, including irreversible money operations.
lesson: Money operations must never be timed out into an ambiguous failure: exempt them from generic watchdogs or answer 'pending' with a lookup, and make retries idempotent.
tripwire: Owner moved it to its own record (skip-list change in stallWatchdog.ts).
owner_decision: Exempt money routes, own record now (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes

class: timeout created but never wired; test assumes a port is unused
what_happened: marketplaceOperator.test.ts test 14 assumes nothing listens on 127.0.0.1:8080, but the node runs its local model there, so the test called the real model and timed out under load. Behind it, localizeRationale creates an AbortController with a timer but never passes its signal to llmRouter.chat, so its timeout does nothing.
root_cause: The abort signal was not passed to the call it was meant to cancel, and the test relied on the node's port layout.
lesson: Every timeout must be proven to cancel the call it guards, and tests must inject unreachable endpoints rather than assume a port is free on the machine they run on.
tripwire: None added (follow-up). Should exist: a test that a slow model call is aborted at its timeout, and an injected unreachable URL in the test.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the sandboxed assistant's model calls

class: config drift between sibling proxy sites
what_happened: The nginx site the owner actually used (ryzen.conf: ryzen.local on :80 and :3002) had no `location /socket.io/` while the IP and fleet sites did, so the page logged 6 WebSocket errors per load. nginx answered `/socket.io/` with index.html (200), so socket.io never connected at all; the first diagnosis, 'falls back to polling', was wrong (corrected by the verifier).
root_cause: Three hand-maintained nginx site files serving the same page drifted apart, and the SPA fallback masked the missing proxy location with a 200.
lesson: The node must keep every reverse-proxy site that serves its UI in step (one generated config, or a test that pins the API and WebSocket locations in each), and an API or WebSocket path with no proxy location must not fall through to the SPA's index.html with a 200.
tripwire: dashboard/backend/src/tests/nginxSocketIo.test.ts: each node site has `location /socket.io/` proxying to 127.0.0.1:5000 over HTTP/1.1 with Upgrade and Connection 'upgrade' (comments stripped, no return/try_files inside the block); mutations (block removed, Connection header dropped) red; the verifier proved it live through nginx with a socket.io 4.8.1 stub (candidate: 101 websocket on both ports; old config: 200 index.html).
owner_decision: Own small record, now (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node also serves a web UI with live updates behind a reverse proxy; any second site or port can drift the same way

class: vacuous check that cannot fail on the old behaviour
what_happened: The planned live check ('no /socket.io/ 404 in nginx's log') could not fail, because the broken config answered 200; and the first static test still passed with the new block commented out or with `return 404;` inside it.
root_cause: The checks were written from the expected fix instead of being run against the broken state and against plausible broken fixes.
lesson: Every acceptance check, live or static, must be shown red against the old behaviour and against plausible broken fixes (commented out, short-circuited) before it counts as evidence.
tripwire: The verifier ran each check on HEAD and on the candidate; the live check was replaced by 'GET /socket.io/?EIO=4&transport=websocket answers 101 in nginx's access log'; the test now strips comments and refuses return/try_files in the block, and both mutants were shown red (S1, S2).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new repository is Full tier and its verification depends on checks that can fail

class: gate released before its result is known
what_happened: The fix-lock was engaged, the config edited, the tests run and the lock released in one command, so the release did not wait for the green result; the money-routes record's verifier found the same chaining (engage, edit, tests and release joined with `;`) in that record's 20:38 command.
root_cause: Chaining the steps in one command made the release unconditional on the test outcome.
lesson: A fix-lock (or any gate) release must be its own step, taken only after a green run has been observed.
tripwire: Process rule recorded ('releases are separate steps from here on'); later records log each release as a separate step after a green run. A guard check refusing a release in the same command as a test run would make it deterministic (not part of the record).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new repository uses the same guard and fix-lock workflow

class: untrusted input interpolated into shell text
what_happened: `GET /api/upgrades/status/:service`, served loginless to anyone on the LAN, passed the URL-decoded value (`%3B` becomes `;`) through `getContainerName`, which fell back to the raw input, into `docker inspect ${containerName}` run by a shell: unauthenticated command execution from the LAN. A syntax-tree sweep found 229 shell-text call sites in 60 files, 19 of them reachable with untrusted input (request values, drive file names, peer gossip, model output).
root_cause: Commands were built as shell strings with interpolated values, and validation was per-route and inconsistent (the sibling `/check/:service` allow-listed; `/status/:service` did not).
lesson: The node must run every program with argv (execFile/spawn without a shell), validate every value from a request, drive, peer or model at the boundary (allow-lists for enumerations, nothing starting with '-'), and never let a lookup fall back to the raw input.
tripwire: upgradeStatusNoShell.test.ts and requestValuesNoShell*.test.ts drive the real routers with fake binaries that record argv and a sentinel file for injected commands (`;`, `$(…)`, backticks, newline, `-`/`--`); ratchet counter `backend_shell_interpolations` in scripts/quality-ratchet.mjs (syntax tree: exec*/spawn-with-shell calls whose command is not a plain literal; may only fall: 184, 183, then 180).
owner_decision: Let's also fix S11, 13, and 8. Sweep choices: the assistant's Run = 'Allow-listed, no shell (Recommended)'; code with no caller = 'Delete after proving unused (Recommended)'
applies_to_new_node: yes — the rebuilt backend will still drive the container runtime, bitcoin-cli and lncli; argv-only and boundary validation must hold from the first commit

class: privilege amplification through container-runtime group membership
what_happened: The injection in `/api/upgrades/status/:service` was root-equivalent, not just dashboard-user-level, because the dashboard's user is in the `docker` group (`id -nG junc`).
root_cause: The web backend runs as a user with unrestricted access to the Docker socket, so any command execution in it equals root on the host.
lesson: The node's web backend must not hold unrestricted container-runtime access (docker group or a root socket); container control must go through a narrow, audited interface so that a backend compromise is not host root.
tripwire: None in the record (the injection itself was closed and tested). Should exist: a check that fails if the backend's user can reach the container-runtime socket directly.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the backend is rebuilt cleanly on Fedora IoT, so rootless containers or a privilege-separated helper can be designed in from the start

class: read-only allow-list admits option injection and secret-revealing reads
what_happened: The assistant's read-only Run allow-list admitted `systemctl status -H <user>@<host> nginx` (real systemctl spawned ssh to that host), `docker inspect` of containers whose environment holds passwords, and prototype keys such as `__proto__` (a 500); option values starting with '-' were also accepted.
root_cause: The allow-list matched program and subcommand names but not their options, and treated inspect-style reads as harmless although they reveal secrets.
lesson: An assistant command allow-list must refuse any name or separate option value starting with '-', refuse host-switching, remote and follow flags, exclude reads that reveal secrets (container environment, untruncated command lines), and look programs up by own keys only.
tripwire: dashboard/backend/src/services/aiRunPolicy.ts with aiRunPolicy.test.ts and requestValuesNoShellRound2.test.ts; the verifier ran 117 probes through the real tier gate and step-up with fake binaries (35 allowed, 81 refused, sentinel empty); round-2 mutations 12 of 13 red.
applies_to_new_node: yes — a sandboxed assistant still needs a read-only tool policy wherever it can reach host programs

class: agent executes without an explicit owner action
what_happened: Deploying the allow-list would have let the chat's auto-safe and full-auto modes run read-only commands on their own (each still behind the owner's password), while the guides promised the AI never self-executes. The owner chose that a suggested command runs only on a click, in every mode; the choice was put on the inaccurate premise that auto modes would run 'without a click' (step-up would have asked for the password), and the owner was told afterwards ('Your choice still applies'), not asked again.
root_cause: Auto-run modes existed in the UI and API while the product's documented promise was that the AI never runs anything by itself.
lesson: The assistant must never run a host command without an explicit per-command owner action, in any mode (non-click sources refused and nothing run on mount); owner choices must be put on verified premises, and a corrected premise must be reported with the option to reverse.
tripwire: aiRunPolicy.test.ts (auto-safe, full-auto, missing, case and space variants answer 403 autoRunOff, nothing run, nothing recorded); frontend commandBlockClickOnly.test.tsx (nothing sent on mount in any mode, even after ten minutes of fake time); activityLogNoAutoClaim.test.tsx (the Activity page claims nothing 'auto-executed').
owner_decision: Click required, auto off
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new assistant is sandboxed; any action it proposes on the node must still need the owner's click

class: feature silently dead behind a wrong field name
what_happened: At HEAD, and live, the assistant's Run button ran nothing: `management.ts` read `verdict.allowed` where `validateCommands` returns `verdict.validation.allowed`, so every free-form command was refused without anyone noticing.
root_cause: The route consumed the validator's result by a property the validator does not return, and no test drove a legitimate command through the real route.
lesson: Every user-facing action must have a test through its real route proving the legitimate path actually runs, not only that hostile input is refused; a feature that refuses everything must show up as failing.
tripwire: Round 3 and 4 tests send an allowed command as 'user-approved' through the real router and assert it runs as argv and is recorded; the verifier confirmed clicks of allowed commands run.
applies_to_new_node: yes — applies to every action route of the rebuilt backend

class: option injection into a privileged command after an irreversible step
what_happened: The reboot route passed the owner's reason to `sudo shutdown`; a reason of `-c` cancelled the reboot after the stack had already been stopped (`-P`, `-H` were also accepted). Whether the sudoers rule `/sbin/shutdown -r *` matches under sudo-rs 0.2.13 is unproven; a mismatch would leave the node stopped with no reboot.
root_cause: Free text went into a privileged command's option position, and the stack is stopped before confirming the privileged reboot will be allowed.
lesson: The node must end options with `--` before any free text passed to a privileged command, and must prove a privileged step is permitted (for example `sudo -n -l shutdown -r +5 -- test`) before taking an irreversible step such as stopping the stack.
tripwire: requestValuesNoShell.test.ts asserts the argv `sudo shutdown -r +5 -- <reason>` and the 0–1440 whole-minute delay range; the verifier confirmed `--` ends systemd shutdown's options. The permission preflight was not built (Skipped item).
applies_to_new_node: yes — reboots and image updates on Fedora IoT are privileged steps taken after stopping services

class: untrusted file names from removable media reach a shell
what_happened: `decryptBackupFile` built its openssl command as shell text from the backup file's name: a legacy backup on a drive named `$(touch …)` ran that command on restore (reproduced). The function has no production caller (tests only) and was made argv-only.
root_cause: File names read from a drive were treated as trusted strings inside shell text.
lesson: File names and contents read from removable drives and backups must be treated as untrusted input on every path, restore included: passed as argv, never as shell text.
tripwire: dashboard/backend/src/tests/shellDecryptAndLogSearch.test.ts (the old code created the sentinel); the verifier round-tripped decrypt with real openssl on a path with spaces.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node backs up to and restores from USB drives

class: state-changing command served from a read cache
what_happened: The testnet open-channel, close-channel, fees and sendcoins routes ran lncli through the read cache, so the same open or send within the cache window was answered without running; they also built lncli as shell text from request values.
root_cause: One lncli helper with a response cache served writes as well as reads.
lesson: Money and other state-changing commands must take an uncached path; a response cache may only ever front idempotent reads.
tripwire: testnetLncliNoShell.test.ts (13 failed of 13 on the old routes, including 'a repeat answered from the cache'); the mutation 'the money action from the cache' is red.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's backend will cache LND reads and must keep writes off that path

class: peer-supplied data used without validation
what_happened: `routes/channelManager.ts` used a gossip address (what a remote node advertises, checked by no schema) in an lncli `connect` built as shell text.
root_cause: Lightning gossip from other nodes was treated as trusted configuration.
lesson: Data from peers (gossip addresses, aliases, other advertised fields) must be validated as untrusted input before use; a gossip address is used only if it is a plain host:port.
tripwire: channelManagerLncliArgv.test.ts (`usableGossipAddress` with `lnHost`; mutations 'gossip check removed' and 'accepting anything' red); lncli runs only through services/lncliArgv.ts as argv.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's channel management will consume gossip

class: regression when replacing shell with argv: lost implicit expansion
what_happened: A request could set the fee manager's `rebalanceLndPath` (the program rebalancing runs). After the fix moved rebalance-lnd to argv, two of the four auto-detected locations (`~/.local/bin/rebalance-lnd`, `/home/*/rebalance-lnd/rebalance.py`) were stored literally and failed without a shell (verifier I6).
root_cause: Executable paths were request-settable, and the conversion to argv dropped the tilde and glob expansion the shell had done implicitly.
lesson: Which executable runs must never be settable by a request; when converting shell calls to argv, expand `~` and globs explicitly, store absolute paths, and test every legitimate configured form.
tripwire: requestValuesNoShellRound2.test.ts (rebalance-lnd found at its absolute path in the home folder and under /home/*; mutations 'home folder not looked in' and '/home/* not expanded' red).
applies_to_new_node: maybe — only if the new node bundles an external rebalancer; the argv-conversion rule applies to every shell call it replaces

class: test writes production state through a hard-coded path
what_happened: `ai/chatExecutionLog.ts` wrote `dashboard/data/chat-executions.jsonl` from a `__dirname` path, so the AI Run tests appended 93 fake entries (such as `docker ps;touch /tmp/ai-run-*/PWNED` and `docker restart lnd`) to the owner's live Activity log. About 40 modules write runtime files the same way, and the owner's live `memory.db`, which the AI learns from, already held 14 test rows from an earlier run.
root_cause: Runtime file paths were resolved from `__dirname` or the working directory instead of one configurable data root, so the tests' temporary `DATA_DIR` did not reach them.
lesson: Every runtime file the node writes must resolve from one configurable data root, and a test run must fail if it writes anything outside its own temporary root.
tripwire: Added: the `RIKURI_CHAT_EXEC_LOG` override set in src/tests/setup.ts and a test asserting the owner's log is unchanged by its run (sha256 checked through the gate). Proposed as owned debt: one data root for every runtime file, with a tripwire failing any test run that writes outside it.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the rebuilt backend can resolve every runtime path from one root from its first commit

class: assistant knowledge indexed ahead of the deployed code

class: static tripwire evaded by aliasing
what_happened: The `backend_shell_interpolations` counter followed only five fixed names, so `import { exec as run }`, `promisify(exec)` under another name or `promisify(require('child_process').exec)` passed unseen; once fixed it found four existing sites. The verifier showed it still misses member calls, copied names, `execFile('sh', ['-c', …])`, `spawn(…, { shell: true })` and wrappers from another module, so the claim that it 'keeps the class from growing' was withdrawn.
root_cause: The tripwire matched identifier names instead of the import binding of the dangerous API.
lesson: A static tripwire must be probed with each evasion form (aliases, wrappers, shell options) before it is trusted, and its blind spots must be written beside it instead of claiming the class is closed; prefer a structural rule, such as no shell-capable API imported outside one module.

class: destructive selection by substring match
what_happened: Revoking a remote-access (autossh) client never worked: the `<<<` bash syntax ran under /bin/sh, and the revoke script exists nowhere in the repository. Client names `-e.` or `...` matched every key (on a scratch key file the revoke removed every key), and `ssh` as a client name still revokes every key, the owner's own included, because the script greps case-insensitively for a substring.
root_cause: The destructive operation selected keys by substring search over whole lines instead of an exact match on the key's comment field.
lesson: Destructive operations (revoking keys, deleting backups, closing channels) must select their targets by exact identifier match, refuse names that could match broadly, and be tested on a fixture with several entries including the owner's own.
tripwire: A client name must be 1–64 of word characters and . @ : + -, starting with a letter or digit (requestValuesNoShellRound2.test.ts refuses `-e.`, `...`, `.hidden`, `-`, `--all`). The substring match itself is not fixed (Skipped item: when the script ships, match the comment field exactly).
applies_to_new_node: maybe — only if the new node manages remote-access keys; the exact-match rule applies to every destructive selection

class: generic timeout reports failure while the operation continues
what_happened: The 8 s stall watchdog fronted the routes that move money: a payment, send, channel open or close, PSBT broadcast or hardware-wallet signature slower than 8 s got '503 request stalled' (Retry-After: 2) while it carried on, so its outcome never reached the page and a manual retry could pay twice. Through the real app with 9.5 s fakes the old code answered PAY with 503 at 8,050 ms; ryzen.local also cut every /api request at nginx's 60 s until the 600 s change is installed.
root_cause: A blanket middleware timeout answered on behalf of non-idempotent handlers without cancelling them, and its only exemptions were a method-blind prefix list.
lesson: A request that moves money must answer with its real outcome (or a pending id the page can look up), never a generic timeout while it continues; every layer in front of it (watchdog, reverse proxy, client) must let it finish, and exemptions must be by exact method and path.
tripwire: dashboard/backend/src/tests/moneyRoutesNotCut.test.ts (the watchdog with its production lists, a 30 ms budget and a 120 ms handler: every money POST gets its own answer; a GET beside it, other methods and longer paths keep the watchdog); mutations 30 of 30 red. Proposed (Skipped item): a default-deny test over the real route table.
owner_decision: Exempt money routes, own record now (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new backend will have request timeouts in front of payments, sends and channel operations

class: path policy disagrees with the router's matching
what_happened: Round 1's anchored patterns still cut a trailing slash or another letter case, which Express routes to the same handler, and missed `POST /api/rebalancer/check`, which sends rebalance payments (`checkAndRebalance` → `executeRebalance` → `/v2/router/send`) and still got 503 at 8,004 ms while the rebalance carried on.
root_cause: The money-route list was written from route names instead of from what each handler does, and the patterns did not model the router's case-insensitive, trailing-slash-tolerant matching.
lesson: Any path-based policy (timeouts, auth tiers, exemptions) must be checked against the real route table with the router's own normalisation, and the set of money routes must be derived from the handlers that pay, send, open or close, not from their names.
tripwire: The verifier's routing sweep over the real router (968 routes, five spellings each, 7,673 probes): 0 exemptions reaching a non-money handler, 0 money POSTs not exempt; tests for trailing slash and case (on only 1–2 of 8 patterns, a recorded gap).
applies_to_new_node: yes — any route-based policy in the rebuilt backend has the same failure mode

class: client helper that aborts and re-sends a request elsewhere
what_happened: The frontend exported `smartFetch`, which aborted a request at 5 s and re-sent it to fallback base URLs (the AI service and the Guardian); nothing imported it. The record's first premise blamed `fetchAPI` instead, so the first tripwire guarded the harmless helper and a send through `smartFetch` would have passed.
root_cause: A generic resilience helper treated every request as safe to retry against another backend, and the tripwire was built on an unverified premise.
lesson: The UI must never abort and re-send a request (to the same or another backend) without an idempotency key; money calls wait for their answer, and a tripwire must be built on a verified premise about which code does the dangerous thing.
tripwire: dashboard/frontend/tests/noAbortAndResend.test.ts (no failover helper or second base URL in services/api.ts, no money route through any helper); the verifier confirmed the removal was safe (no importer, no dynamic import). Limit: it checks names only.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new UI will make payment and channel calls

class: path traversal through a caller-chosen base path
what_happened: `GET /api/storage/devices/<path>/browse` listed any directory the backend could read (live, counts only: /home/junc 82 entries, /etc 269), on the default tier, so loginless mode minted a viewer for any LAN client; its containment check compared the target with the same caller-chosen path using a bare `startsWith` (`…/BACKUP` + `../BACKUP2` passed). Three sibling routes also took any path.
root_cause: The routes trusted a caller-supplied mount point as the containment root, and containment used a string prefix instead of resolved paths.
lesson: Routes that read the filesystem must accept only identifiers of drives the node itself detected (404, and no read, otherwise), and containment must use resolved real paths with path.relative, checked before touching the filesystem and again after symlink resolution, with entries listed by lstat.
tripwire: dashboard/backend/src/tests/storageKnownDrivesOnly.test.ts (the real router with a stubbed storage service and real temporary folders: /etc 404, ../BACKUP2, a symlink out and a mount point ending in /.. refused); mutations 9 of 9 and 14 of 15 red (the check-then-read race is not deterministically testable).
owner_decision: Fix now, own record (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node browses and validates USB backup drives

class: error responses leak paths and existence
what_happened: Outside a drive, a missing path answered 500 'ENOENT … realpath <absolute path>' while an existing one answered 'Access denied', so the route was an existence probe that echoed host paths; a repeated `?path=a&path=b` crashed with a 500 TypeError.
root_cause: Raw filesystem errors were passed through to the client, and query parameters were not type-checked.
lesson: Out-of-scope requests must get the same answer whether or not the target exists, filesystem error text must go to the log only, and query parameters must be type-checked (a repeated or object value is a 400).
tripwire: Round-2 tests in storageKnownDrivesOnly.test.ts (missing and existing outside paths answer alike, no path echoed, a repeated `path` answers 400; the route's 403/404/500 mapping pinned). Residual: through a symlink on the drive that points outside, 404 versus 403 still tells existence (Skipped item).
applies_to_new_node: yes — applies to every file-facing route of the rebuilt backend

class: unauthenticated LAN access to default-tier routes
what_happened: Both the drive-browse routes and the shell-injection route of the request-values record (`/api/upgrades/status/:service`) were on the default tier, which loginless mode serves to any LAN client; `/api/storage` mutations also have no `requireAdminForMutation`.
root_cause: Loginless mode grants a viewer to any LAN client, and routes were placed on the default tier without regard to whether they read host state or run programs.
lesson: The node must treat every LAN client as untrusted: a route that reads host state outside its own domain or launches a program must never be reachable without authentication, and loginless access must be an explicit allow-list of harmless reads.
tripwire: Per-route fixes and tests only (storageKnownDrivesOnly.test.ts, upgradeStatusNoShell.test.ts). Should exist: a test over the route table comparing every loginless-reachable route with an approved list.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node will serve its dashboard on the home LAN

class: multiple execution paths with inconsistent validators
what_happened: Besides the Run button, the assistant could run host commands through other paths: loginless chat's orchestrator auto-ran command-database entries marked autoApprove and low risk through a shell with no click (one was a write: the verifier made 'show me a new address' run a fake `lncli newaddress`; the journal since 2026-09-01 shows no orchestrator run); `/api/ai/execute` with a `commandId` ran any database entry (including `docker restart lnd`, `docker system prune -f`) through a shell with no validator; and the agent's prefix whitelist accepted restarts, `compose down`, `curl -o` over a dotfile and `cat` of a private SSH key through a `../..` path.
root_cause: Each path had its own validator or none, labels in a runtime database ('autoApprove', 'low risk') were trusted as authority, and the earlier sweep had covered only the free-form Run.
lesson: The assistant must have exactly one executor that every path goes through (one read-only allow-list, argv only, never a shell, click-only), labels in data and claims in guides ('read-only look-ups') are never authority, and every site that launches a program with request, model, tool or database text must be inventoried and routed through that executor.
tripwire: dashboard/backend/src/tests/assistantExecutionPaths.test.ts (the real orchestrator, `/api/ai/execute` and `/api/ai-agent` routers with fake process launchers; 20 failed and 1 passed on the old code); the verifier's completeness sweep of 86 program-launching files; ratchet `backend_shell_interpolations` 183 to 180.
owner_decision: Own record now (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new assistant is sandboxed, but any bridge that lets it act on the host must be a single policy-checked executor

class: kill switch not wired into every execution path
what_happened: A mutant in which the agent executor skipped the policy was first dismissed as 'equivalent', but it also dropped the emergency stop, the kill signal and the time limit: an approved `docker logs electrs --tail 7` ran to the end 5.9 s after the stop (status 'success'). Nothing tested the stop on the agent path or the signal and time limit anywhere, and approve answered `success: true` when nothing ran.
root_cause: The stop signal and timeout were options each call site had to pass, and no test asserted them per path.
lesson: An emergency stop must refuse new runs and kill running ones on every execution path, every run must carry a time limit, a stopped or failed run must never report success, and a mutant may be called equivalent only after proving it changes no behaviour.
tripwire: Round-2 tests: on a typed click, a database click, both chat sites and an agent approval, every run gets the stop's signal and a time limit; during a stop the agent runs nothing and answers success false. The verifier saw a running command killed (TERM) about 0.3 s after the stop and a hung one at 30.0 s.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new assistant needs a working emergency stop on every path it can act through

class: credentials on command lines leak into logs and answers
what_happened: On testnet4 the resolved bitcoin-cli prefix carries `-rpcuser`/`-rpcpassword`; the new commandId path wrote it into the service log and the execution log, readable through the unauthenticated `GET /api/ai/execution-history`, and (pre-existing) loginless chat answers quoted it ('why is my sync stuck' returned `… -rpcpassword=<password> getblockchaininfo`). The credential is the tracked default and RPC listens on 127.0.0.1 only.
root_cause: RPC credentials were passed as command-line flags, and logs and answers recorded resolved command text instead of templates or ids.
lesson: Credentials must never be put on command lines (use cookie or config-file auth); logs, histories and assistant answers must record ids or templates (such as {{BITCOIN_CLI}}), never resolved command text, with redaction only as a backstop.
tripwire: Round-2 test: on testnet4, commandId and typed commands leave the password in no response, no log call, not in GET /api/ai/execution-history and not in the execution log (which must hold something, so the check is not vacuous); `redactSecrets` covers `-rpcpassword=`, `-rpcuser=`, `-rpcauth=`. Gaps (Skipped items): the space form, `-testnet4.rpcpassword=`, chat's fix database.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node runs bitcoind RPC and an assistant that can read logs

class: configuration captured at import time
what_happened: `ai/diagnosticScripts.ts` and `ai/fixDatabase.ts` build their commands once at module load from `getBitcoinCliPrefix()`, so the network (mainnet or testnet4) is frozen at first import; on testnet4 the fix database's `docker exec lnd lncli pendingchannels` targets the mainnet LND.
root_cause: Network-dependent values were resolved at module load instead of at each use.
lesson: Values that depend on the active network or another switchable setting must be resolved at use, never cached at import, so a switch cannot leave commands pointing at the wrong node.
tripwire: None added (Skipped items, owner Henry). Should exist: a test that switches the active network and asserts generated commands follow it.
applies_to_new_node: maybe — the full node and the pruned node run on separate machines, but any network or node switch inside one backend has the same failure

class: test passes vacuously because its precondition is not asserted
what_happened: One chat case passed against the old code only because the fixture database lacked the triggers the orchestrator normalises to ('block height' to `block_height`), so nothing matched; and four cases asserting that nothing at all ran broke because the real `aiService` runs a fixed `ollama list` whenever its router is loaded.
root_cause: The tests asserted the outcome without asserting that the code path under test was reached, and a module spawns a process at import.
lesson: A test must assert that its path was actually exercised (for example that a database entry matched) before asserting the outcome, and modules should not spawn processes at import time, which makes 'nothing ran' unassertable.
tripwire: Each chat case now also asserts a database entry matched; the corrected file was shown red (20 failed, 1 passed) on the old code; assertions narrowed to what the route ran (`ranByRoute`).
applies_to_new_node: yes — a general testing rule for the new repository

class: test reaches live system
what_happened: On 2026-10-08 mutation runs of the AI Run tests terminated the live mainnet LND three times (08:53, 13:27, 15:29): `aiRunPolicy.test.ts` posted `docker restart lnd` through the real router with the real `child_process`, relying on the code under test to refuse it, and a mutant that skipped the refusal ran it on the node. The node had 0 channels, so no channel or payment was at risk.
root_cause: The test's safety depended on the code it tests, and the test setup isolated data but not the node: `DOCKER_HOST` was unset (the live socket), and `sudo` (with passwordless rules), `systemctl`, `lncli` and `bitcoin-cli` on PATH were the real ones.
lesson: A test, and any mutant of the code it tests, must never be able to reach the live node: before any test worker starts, the harness must put refusing stand-ins first on PATH for every node-changing program and point the container-runtime socket at a path that does not exist; state-changing commands in tests must hit fakes, and mutation testing must never run on a production machine without that layer (better, not on it at all).
tripwire: dashboard/backend/tests/noLiveNode.globalSetup.js and globalTeardown.js (jest globalSetup: stand-ins for docker, sudo, systemctl, shutdown, reboot, lncli, bitcoin-cli, tapcli, hwi, tailscale that exit 126; DOCKER_HOST at a missing socket) with src/tests/testsNeverReachTheLiveNode.test.ts; proof against the exact incident (mutant P1, unmocked test): outer log empty, LND start time unchanged; 36 previously live read-only calls per run now refused. Limits recorded: not network-hermetic (about 200 connections to the live llama-server on 127.0.0.1:8080), `cargo test` has no such setup, and any other harness needs the same outer layer.
applies_to_new_node: yes — tests for the new node must run off the production machines, or in a sandbox with no container-runtime or privileged access

class: isolation applied where child processes never see it
what_happened: The first fix set DOCKER_HOST and PATH in jest's per-file setup; the proof run showed the outer stand-in still catching both `docker` calls, because jest gives each test file a copy of `process.env` and children started by the code inherit the worker's real environment. The tripwire had passed vacuously because it passed `env` explicitly.
root_cause: The isolation was verified from the test's own view (with an explicit environment) instead of from a child started the way the production code starts one.
lesson: Isolation must be proven from the child's point of view (a process started with the default environment, as the code does) and against the exact incident, with an independent outer logging layer showing nothing leaked through.
tripwire: testsNeverReachTheLiveNode.test.ts asks `/bin/sh -c` children with no `env` where each name resolves, before running it; red 12 of 12 against the setup-only fix; under strace the execve hits the stand-in and the outer log stays empty.
applies_to_new_node: yes — any test-isolation layer in the new repository needs the same proof

class: hard-coded absolute program paths bypass PATH isolation
what_happened: `tailscaleService.ts` ran `/usr/bin/tailscale` (status, `set --exit-node`, `logout`, `login`) unless `TAILSCALE_PATH` said otherwise, and a test set it back to `/usr/bin/tailscale`; two mutants ran the real binary, caught only by the verifier's outer layer. `feeManagerService` can run `/usr/local/bin/rebalance-lnd` (which moves funds) by absolute path, and it is not refused.
root_cause: Production code chose node-changing programs by absolute path, which PATH stand-ins cannot intercept, and the builder's sweep for such paths was incomplete.
lesson: Production code must resolve every node-changing program through one overridable resolver, never a hard-coded absolute path, and tests must be scanned for absolute paths to such programs.
tripwire: Round 3: the tripwire asserts the real TailscaleService resolves to the stand-in, and scans every backend test file (224) for quoted absolute paths to the refused programs, rebalance-lnd and /opt/rebalance-lnd (red on 13 quoted forms). Limits: computed paths, /opt/tapd/tapcli, /usr/lib/cargo/bin/sudo, helper files (Skipped items).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the rebuilt backend can route every program launch through one resolver

class: starting state misread as down triggers a self-heal restart
what_happened: After the test-caused stop at 15:29:55, the 5-minute health check saw LND starting with its wallet locked, logged 'CRITICAL: Lightning (LND) is down', sent the alert to 3 of 6 channels (email among them), and the control plane auto-executed RB-CONTAINER-RESTART-01: a fourth LND termination (a 24 s shutdown).
root_cause: The health check did not distinguish a starting, wallet-locked LND from a down one, and self-healing acted on that verdict with no startup grace period.
lesson: Health checks must distinguish starting, wallet-locked and unlocking from down, self-healing must not restart a service that is starting or unlocking (grace period, restart budget), and a false CRITICAL alert is a defect.
tripwire: None added (Skipped item for the owner: self-healing restarts LND while its wallet unlocks). Should exist: a test that a starting, wallet-locked LND is reported as starting and triggers no restart runbook or alert.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node will run LND with wallet unlock and health monitoring

class: self-healing fights a planned maintenance operation
what_happened: During the owner's OS upgrade at 07:30 on 2026-10-08, while the runner had deliberately stopped the stack, the control plane ran restart runbooks for lnd and bitcoin (07:30:30) and for electrs and mempool-web (07:30:59), and afterwards tried `tapd → restart_service` every 5 minutes.
root_cause: The self-heal loop had no notion that an upgrade owned the stack.
lesson: Self-healing must stand down while a planned operation (upgrade, backup, restore, owner stop) owns the stack, and resume only when that operation has finished and reported.
tripwire: None added (reported to the owner). Should exist: a test that no runbook fires while the upgrade's ownership lock is held.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node will have self-healing and OS or image updates

lesson: Every self-heal or runbook target must be resolved from the node's actual service inventory and validated at startup; a target that does not exist is a configuration fault to report then, not something discovered when healing is needed.
tripwire: None added (Skipped item for the owner). Should exist: a startup check that each runbook target exists.

class: maintenance does not restore what it stopped
what_happened: The 07:30 OS upgrade runner's `compose down` left the two testnet containers, fell back to `docker stop`, then ran `compose up` for the mainnet profiles only, so the testnet stack never came back and `rikuri-tapd` failed ('unable to connect to lnd node … lnd version incompatible') and hit systemd's start limit.
root_cause: The runner did not record which stacks were running before teardown and brought back only a fixed set of profiles.
lesson: Any operation that stops services must record exactly what was running before and restore exactly that, reporting anything it could not restore.
tripwire: Added later by 2026-10-09-upgrade-deadlock-and-progress.md: upgradeNoDeadlock.test.ts — testnet is brought back if it was running or is the active network, and stays down if it was not.
