class: promise that never settles freezes a single-flight refresh
what_happened: For 13 hours the dashboard showed 1/8 services up while all 11 containers were healthy: the first score after the dashboard started during a Linux update's Docker restart saw the stack down, and the next calculation never settled. The Electrum probe stays pending when electrs accepts the request and closes cleanly (FIN), because Node cancels the socket timeout on close and emits 'close' with no 'error' (reproduced on Node v24.21.0; the trigger, electrs being recreated, is consistent with the logs but not proven), and the service shares one in-flight promise while the route skips a refresh while one is in flight.
root_cause: A probe settled only on data, error or idle timeout, and the single-flight score calculation had no deadline of its own.
lesson: Every probe must settle on every socket outcome (data, error, close, timeout) under a hard deadline rather than an idle timeout, and a single-flight aggregate must have its own time limit after which it is abandoned (and logged) so the next one runs, with a late result discarded by a generation counter.
tripwire: serviceProbes.test.ts (local Electrum stand-ins that close cleanly, send half an answer, trickle bytes, or answer in full); healthScoreService.test.ts (an input that never arrives is abandoned at the limit, the next one scores, a late finish changes nothing); healthScoreRefresh.test.ts through the real routes/health.ts refresh under fake timers; mutations 6 of 6, 12 of 12 and 4 of 4 red.
owner_decision: Restart dashboard + fix (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node will probe electrs, bitcoind, LND and Tor for a health view
port_candidate: dashboard/backend/src/services/serviceProbes.ts and dashboard/backend/src/services/healthScoreService.ts with src/tests/serviceProbes.test.ts, src/tests/healthScoreService.test.ts and src/tests/healthScoreRefresh.test.ts

class: stale data displayed as current
what_happened: The Services card showed the frozen score's count (1/8) with no regard to the API's `stale: true`. The first fix then regressed: it checked `stale` before 'no counts', so after every dashboard start the card said 'Not updated for over 90 s' instead of 'Checking…' (verifier round 1 FAIL).
root_cause: The card rendered the number without its freshness, and the fix conflated 'not yet calculated' with 'stale'.
lesson: The UI must never show an old measurement as current: a stale value is shown as stale ('Not updated for over 90 s'), and 'not yet measured' is a distinct state ('Checking…'), each tested on the real page.
tripwire: frontend/tests/servicesCardPage.test.tsx (the real Dashboard page: a frozen score shows as stale, a fresh one its count, 'Checking…' before the first score); mutations 'stale ignored by the card', 'Dashboard does not pass stale' and 'stale before no counts' red.
owner_decision: Restart dashboard + fix (Recommended)
applies_to_new_node: yes — every card of the new dashboard needs freshness

class: timeout aligned with the scheduling interval loses a cycle
what_happened: With a 60 s calculation limit and a 30 s refresh tick, the tick two later arrived just before a hung calculation's limit fired (arming the limit lags by about 8 ms, as starting `docker ps` does), saw it still in flight and skipped, so the next score came about 90 s after the hang began. The verifier also found the limit timer not cleared after a finish (every success followed 60 s later by a false 'did not finish') and not unref'd.
root_cause: The limit was chosen without reference to the refresh interval, and timers were not cleared and unref'd when their work settled.
lesson: A watchdog limit must sit strictly between the worst legitimate duration (about 38 s here) and the next scheduling boundary with margin, its value must be put to the owner as a costed choice, and every timer must be cleared when its work settles and unref'd so it can neither fire falsely nor hold the process.
tripwire: healthScoreRefresh.test.ts: through the real refresh under fake timers, a hang started by the 35 s tick; at 96 s three calculations have started and the score is fresh (red at 60 and 65 s, green at 55 s); tests that a finished calculation leaves no limit timer and that timers are unref'd. The lower bound is unguarded (Skipped item).
owner_decision: OK (55 s accepted, 2026-10-10)
applies_to_new_node: yes — any periodic health or score loop in the new node

class: lock held across a restart it waits on
what_happened: On 2026-10-09 the owner's 'Update Linux' runner held the compose lock through `apt-get upgrade`; docker-ce's postinst restarted Docker, systemd first stopped the stack units (`Requires=docker.service`), and their stop scripts waited for the compose lock (`flock -w 300`) held by the runner, which waited for apt, which waited for the Docker restart. It broke only by timeouts after about 9 minutes, with the dashboard down and nothing explaining it; the owner's own `systemctl start rikuri-tapd` was queued behind it.
root_cause: The update runner held a lock across a package install that could restart the container runtime, whose dependent units' stop path takes that same lock.
lesson: An update must never hold a lock across a step that can restart services whose stop or start path takes that lock; ownership of the stack during maintenance must be explicit, so a unit's stop returns at once when the runner has already stopped the stack and its start waits (bounded below the unit's start timeout) until the install is done.
tripwire: dashboard/backend/src/tests/upgradeNoDeadlock.test.ts runs the real runner in a temp root with fake docker, sudo and apt whose postinst replays docker-ce's (the units' stops, then queued starts): old scripts 3 failed, 1 passed; mutations 8/8, 7/7, 12/12 and 8/8 red over four rounds; verifier scenarios A–I (stops rc=0 in 13–18 ms). Not yet proven on real systemd and Docker.
owner_decision: Let's just fix it
applies_to_new_node: maybe — Fedora IoT applies OS updates as images at reboot, so an in-place runtime restart mid-install is less likely, but any runtime or container update path must follow the same lock rule

class: second start path with divergent configuration
what_happened: After the install, the runner brought the stack up with its own `docker compose … up -d`, without the units' `EnvironmentFile=/run/rikuri/memory-limits.env`; the queued `rikuri-stack` start then recreated every container (a different configuration, without memory limits), and LND restarted a second time.
root_cause: The runner and the systemd units started the stack with different commands and environments, so compose saw a configuration change.
lesson: The node must have exactly one canonical way to start its services, the same scripts and environment the boot units use, and every other path (updater, recovery, UI) must call it, so a second start is a no-op rather than a recreation.
tripwire: upgradeNoDeadlock.test.ts: the fake docker logs `RIKURI_UPGRADE_RUNNER` and a marker from the memory-limits file, and the runner's bring-up must carry it; tor and LND restart at most once (8 of 8 three-way bring-ups in verification).
applies_to_new_node: yes — on Fedora IoT the canonical start is the systemd (quadlet) units, and the updater and UI must start through them

class: concurrent repair actions without mutual exclusion
what_happened: Round 2 released stack ownership when the install finished; the runner's bring-up and the queued unit start then both reached the health gate and the onion repair, which ran outside any lock, so tor and LND restarted twice on every Docker-restarting update (verifier round 2 FAIL; round 1 restarted them once).
root_cause: The onion repair, which restarts tor and LND, could be triggered by two paths at once and had no lock or idempotence check.
lesson: Any repair that restarts services must serialise on its own lock and be idempotent (a second run finds nothing to do), and a lock it cannot open must produce a warning and still run the repair rather than skip it silently.
tripwire: upgradeNoDeadlock.test.ts (the fake models tor's published onions: a fresh tor publishes none, a restart publishes all; tor and LND restarted at most once); torRecoverMissing.test.ts (a second repair waits at least 1.5 s and restarts nothing; one that outlasts its wait says so; an unopenable lock warns and runs); `data/tor-repair.lock`.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node publishes LND over Tor onion services

class: ownership probe that mutates what it checks
what_happened: The ownership probe took an exclusive lock, so any other probe at the same moment read as 'an update owns the stack' and a unit's stop was skipped (a plain `flock file sleep 2` made `down` say 'nothing to do'); later the runner's own non-blocking claim (`flock -n`) could lose to a momentary shared check.
root_cause: Checking ownership was done by trying to take the same exclusive lock, so checks and claims raced each other.
lesson: Ownership checks must be non-mutating (a shared lock or a read), 'owned' must mean held by the owner, the owner's claim must tolerate momentary checks with a bounded wait, and an ownership file left by a dead process must read as free.
tripwire: Tests: another shared probe never makes a stop skip; a momentary shared check does not defeat the claim; a stale ownership file stops nothing. The verifier ran 300 simultaneous down+stop pairs (0 skipped) and showed a SIGKILLed holder frees the lock.
applies_to_new_node: yes — any maintenance-ownership mechanism in the new node

class: long operation looks dead, failed run shown as success
what_happened: During updates the owner had no idea how long they would take and the node looked dead for minutes. The progress UI built in response first showed an all-green checklist for a failed update (only the status line said otherwise), kept only the first occurrence of each stage (a failed restore after a failed install showed green), and showed 'Failed' for up to 90 s while the runner still waited for Docker to restore the node.
root_cause: The page had no view of the runner's step state, and the first progress model neither walked every stage nor marked failed or interrupted steps.
lesson: Every long operation must show, on every page, its current step, elapsed time, and steps done and to come from the runner's own state, say 'restarting, reconnecting' when the backend itself restarts, and mark failed and interrupted steps as failed or unknown, never an all-green checklist for a run that failed.
tripwire: dashboard/frontend/tests/osUpdateProgress.test.tsx (the model from the real 2026-10-09 runner state; a failed step marked, an interrupted one unknown, totals ending at the finish; the banner forgets a finished update, remembers 30 minutes, takes 401/403 as up); page mutations 7 of 9 (one equivalent, one gap then covered), then 7 of 7 and 12 of 12 red.
owner_decision: It would be better to have an indicator showing ongoing update process if possible so the node doesn't look dead.
applies_to_new_node: yes — image updates and reboots on the new node are long operations the owner must see progressing

class: management UI hard-depends on the runtime it reports on
what_happened: The dashboard unit has `Requires=docker.service`, so every Docker restart (a docker-ce or containerd update) stops and restarts it; it went down at 03:39:16 during the deadlock. tapd's `Requires=` on the testnet stack (through a drop-in) ends in 'Dependency failed' when that start fails, which its `Restart=` does not cover.
root_cause: Hard systemd dependencies tied the UI's and tapd's lifetimes to the container runtime and stack units.
lesson: The node's management UI must not hard-depend on the container runtime (use Wants= and After=) so it can keep reporting while the runtime restarts, and dependent services need a recovery path from 'Dependency failed'.
tripwire: None added: the change needs a unit reinstall and is the owner's choice (Skipped item); the page now says the dashboard is restarting. Should exist: a unit-file lint that the UI unit does not use Requires= on the runtime.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's services are systemd units on Fedora IoT

class: test shares live lock or state files
what_happened: `torRecoverMissing.test.ts` ran the real repair script in place, so its new lock was the checkout's `data/tor-repair.lock`, the live node's own because the systemd units run the scripts from that checkout; with the lock held elsewhere, 4 tests failed after 122 s, and a gate left the lock file in a worktree.
root_cause: The script's lock location was fixed relative to the checkout and the test did not redirect it.
lesson: Scripts must take their lock and state locations from overridable settings, tests that run real scripts must give them their own locations, and a tripwire must fail any test that runs a lock-taking script with its locks in the checkout.
tripwire: testsNeverReachTheLiveNode.test.ts (round 4): scans `scripts/` for `flock` and fails a test that runs such a script without setting its lock location (comments stripped, the location must actually be set; red on round 4's false negative). Static limits recorded beside it.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's scripts and tests must keep test state away from live state

class: production runs from the development checkout
what_happened: The systemd units run the stack scripts straight from the rikurinode checkout, so any edit in the main tree is live at once: this fix had to be built in a worktree and merged only after verification, and a test that ran a script in place used the live node's own lock file.
root_cause: The node has no install step separating the code it runs from the code being developed.
lesson: The node must run from an installed, versioned artifact (an image or package), never from a development working tree, so that editing, testing or checking out code cannot change the running node.
tripwire: Worked around with worktrees and the round-4 lock-location tripwire; no structural check in the record. Should exist: units and services reference only installed paths.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node ships as images with automatic OS rollback, which removes this class only if nothing points into a checkout

class: test fake diverges from the real process environment
what_happened: Two harness defects made the deadlock test misleading: the fake `sudo` passed the runner's lock descriptors to the units it started (real sudo-rs sets close-on-exec and systemd starts units with none), and the fake's background starts held the installer's output pipe (systemd's units are not the installer's children). A later probe read a waiting unit's momentary `flock` as the runner still owning the lock.
root_cause: The fakes modelled the commands but not the descriptor inheritance, process parentage and timing of the real system.
lesson: Fakes of system components (sudo, systemd, package managers) must model descriptor inheritance, process parentage and timing as the real ones do, and each harness correction must be re-proven red on the old code before it counts.
tripwire: The fake sudo closes FDs 200–202; background starts are detached; the ownership probe checks `/proc/<runner>/fd`; each correction was shown red again on the old scripts before the lock was re-engaged; the verifier confirmed the corrections against PID 1 and sudo-rs 0.2.13 behaviour.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node's update and boot paths will be tested with fakes of systemd and the package or image tool

class: machine state kept in a tracked file
what_happened: An in-app upgrade writes the new image pin into the tracked compose file; `rikuri update --code` (`git pull --rebase`) then refuses ('cannot pull with rebase: You have unstaged changes', exit 128, reproduced on a scratch clone), or, when it takes the upstream history for rewritten, stashes the change and runs `git reset --hard`, so the older pin returns and the next `compose up` downgrades the service. Every in-app upgrade on this node reached git only by hand.
root_cause: The node's own state (which image version it runs) was stored in a git-tracked file that code updates also change.
lesson: The node's image versions and other machine state must never live in tracked files; a code or image update must never change, block on, or downgrade them, the newer of the node's version and the shipped default runs, every reader uses one effective-pin source, revert keeps working, and a refused update says why in plain words.
tripwire: Planned, not built (parked): `docker compose config --images` identical with no node pins; scratch-clone tests that an upgraded node pulls cleanly, keeps its pin and never downgrades, that a newer default replaces an older own pin and that an older default never replaces a newer pin.
owner_decision: C1: (a), the newer one runs (the node's pin is dropped once the default reaches or passes it); C2: 'No other node exists now. So it's OK.'; parked: 'Yes, you can park it'
applies_to_new_node: yes — the record carries these rules to the new repository as design rules from its first commit

class: configuration every caller must opt into fails unsafe
what_happened: A separate pins file through `COMPOSE_ENV_FILES` was tested on compose v5.6.0 and rejected: it works only when exported (set inside `.env` it is ignored, and `--env-file pins` alone drops `.env`, leaving its secrets unset), so about 46 call sites plus any manual `docker compose` would each have to export it, and one that forgot would silently start the repository's older image. An override compose file (`-f`) has the same problem.
root_cause: The mechanism depended on each invocation remembering an extra option instead of applying by default.
lesson: Node-local settings that decide what runs must be picked up by every invocation by default (such as the project's own env file), never by a mechanism each caller must remember, because a caller that forgets fails silently and unsafely.
tripwire: Design experiment recorded (compose v5.6.0, `docker compose config` with DOCKER_HOST at a missing socket); planned: `compose config --images` identical before and after.
applies_to_new_node: maybe — depends on whether the new node uses compose or systemd quadlets; the default-applies rule holds either way

class: in-app upgrade edits tracked settings
what_happened: An in-app upgrade can carry a migration that edits the compose file's settings, not only the pin (`config/upgradeMigrations.ts`, `applyComposeEdits`), so pins kept outside git would not stop a migrated upgrade from modifying a tracked file and blocking the next code update; one such migration exists (Electrs 0.11 to 0.12), and no node needs it.
root_cause: Two mechanisms, in-app upgrades and code releases, could both change service settings.
lesson: In-app upgrades should change only the version pin; settings changes should arrive only through a tested release, and an upgrade that needs one should be shown as 'needs a node update first'.
tripwire: None: open question C3 (recommendation (a)), to be settled in the new repository.
applies_to_new_node: yes — the record hands the C3 question to the new repository

class: non-atomic read-modify-write of a secrets file
what_happened: Planning found that 12 scripts and the engine switch (`bitcoinEngineService.ts:949`, `:1270`) already edit the root `.env`, which holds secrets, non-atomically with an unanchored pattern, and that two dashboard writers could interleave a read-modify-write.
root_cause: Several writers edit the same secrets file in place without atomic replacement, exact key matching or a shared lock.
lesson: Writes to the node's secrets or settings file must be atomic (temp file + rename, same mode and owner), touch only the writer's own anchored keys with every other line byte-identical, be serialised by one lock, and refuse (and say so) if the file cannot be read and rewritten whole.
tripwire: Planned P2 tests on temporary files; not built (parked).
applies_to_new_node: yes — the new node keeps RPC and service secrets in local settings files
